court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Malone Darcy Fleming (a pseudonym) v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (SHEPHERD DCJ)
outcome: Extension of time refused; leave to appeal refused; appeal dismissed. Total effective sentence of 5 years 4 months' immediate imprisonment upheld.
weight: Court of Appeal (three judges) decision, but expressly 'no point of principle' and 'turns on own facts' (Category B). Persuasive on the application of settled principles rather than establishing new law.
tags: possession with intent to sell or supply
oneLine: Court of Appeal upholds a 5 year 4 month total effective sentence for a meth dealer sentenced as 'just under' mid-level, confirming that reoffending while on bail justifies cumulative sentencing and does not breach the totality principle.
whatHappened: FLEMING (a pseudonym) pleaded guilty to three counts. Count 1: possession of a trafficable quantity of methylamphetamine (176.38g, 78-81% purity) with intent to sell or supply, found in a Perth hotel room safe during a search warrant, contrary to Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 (WA) s 6(1)(a) read with s 34(1)(a). Count 2: possession of $17,200 reasonably suspected of being unlawfully obtained (found in a bedside drawer), contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 417(1); the appellant admitted this was proceeds of meth sales. His phone, seized and interrogated in that search, contained messages about the sale and supply of prohibited drugs and paperwork consistent with a tick list. Count 3: possession of methylamphetamine (22.77g) with intent to sell or supply, contrary to Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 (WA) s 6(1)(a) — this offending occurred about six months later while he was on bail, when police searched his vehicle at a regional police station and found the drug plus digital scales, empty clip seal bags, glass smoking implements and two metal spoons. SHEPHERD DCJ characterised him as 'just under a mid-level dealer' and sentenced him to 4 years (count 1), 12 months concurrent (count 2) and 1 year 4 months cumulative (count 3, reduced from 2 years for totality) — a total effective sentence of 5 years 4 months. He appealed on a single ground: that the total effective sentence breached the first limb of the totality principle. The notice was lodged seven weeks late.
whatHeld: The Court refused the extension of time, refused leave and dismissed the appeal. It held the total effective sentence of 5 years 4 months was not unreasonable or plainly unjust and did not infringe the first limb of the totality principle. The individual sentences were not challenged. The Court held it was plainly correct to order partial cumulation for count 3 because reoffending while on bail — with an offence of similar nature — is a significantly aggravating factor showing disregard for the law and enhancing the need for personal deterrence. The reduction of count 3 from 2 years to 1 year 4 months adequately reflected totality. The Court reiterated that for serious drug dealing the major considerations are general and personal deterrence, that quantity and purity matter as indicators of potential harm, and that personal circumstances carry less weight in this class of offence. It found the comparable cases advanced by both sides of limited utility, being either pre-dating the increase to a life maximum or involving couriers rather than dealers, but broadly consistent with the sentence imposed.
whatItMeans: This is a sentencing appeal, so it does not change how you investigate, but it reinforces points worth knowing. The investigative work here — search warrant on the hotel room with the seizure and interrogation of the phone (sale/supply messages, tick list), and six months later the vehicle search at a regional police station while he was on bail — built a clear commercial-dealing case, and the admission that the $17,200 was drug proceeds supported both the s 417(1) count and the finding of an ongoing enterprise. Note how strongly the courts treat reoffending while on bail: it is significantly aggravating and justifies cumulative punishment, so flag any suspect who offends while on conditional release. The case confirms that purity and quantity evidence, and material showing commerciality (tick lists, scales, packaging, cash in mixed denominations), materially strengthen the seriousness of a drug charge.
verdict: AWARENESS only — this is a sentencing/totality appeal that turns on its own facts and states no new point of principle; it does not alter investigative or charging practice.
flags: The District Court file number and exact sentencing date are not specified in the judgment (stated only as 'last year'/'IND XXXX of 20XX').
Offending dates are given only as 'mid-2023' (counts 1 and 2) and 'a little over six months' later (count 3); no exact dates in the text.
The appellant's identity is suppressed by pseudonym; a confidential memorandum on 'other matters' was published only to the parties.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Cooper v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (BURROWS DCJ)
outcome: Leave to appeal refused; appeal against sentence dismissed. Total effective sentence of 6 years 8 months confirmed.
weight: Court of Appeal (three judges) applying settled parity principles from Ngo, Green and House v King. Binding and authoritative, but applies well-established law to its own facts rather than creating new principle.
oneLine: Court of Appeal upholds a co-offender's sentence, confirming that a 'mastermind' and a 'willing participant' can be equally culpable for what happened at the scene despite different roles beforehand.
whatHappened: On 25/05/2018, five men — Paul BONNER (the 'mastermind'), the appellant James COOPER, Shannon BONNER, Waylon KELLS and Darryl PEARSON — carried out a premeditated vigilante home invasion in Kununurra as revenge for a perceived wrong against Paul BONNER's son. In the weeks before, Paul BONNER and KELLS phoned the victim Amanda QUARTERMAINE and threatened her and her partner Corbin CLYDEN. Paul BONNER and KELLS travelled to Kununurra from Shepparton, Victoria; Shannon BONNER recruited COOPER and the two travelled together from Darwin, each using stolen numberplates on their vehicles to avoid detection at state borders; the attack was staged from PEARSON's Kununurra workshop. Shortly after 3.50am, masked and dressed in dark clothing, they kicked in the locked front door and bedroom door while the couple and four children slept. At least three men struck CLYDEN with poles to the head, body, arms and legs; QUARTERMAINE was struck on the arm. CLYDEN needed nine sutures to his scalp. After a nine-day trial, all five were convicted of aggravated home burglary with intent (s 401(1)(a)), assault occasioning bodily harm (s 317(1)), and doing an act likely to endanger life, health or safety (s 304(1)(b)). COOPER was sentenced to a total effective 6 years 8 months; Paul BONNER to 7 years 6 months. COOPER appealed on the sole ground that the 10-month gap was too small and breached the parity principle.
whatHeld: The appeal was dismissed and leave refused. The Court held the 10-month difference between the sentences did not offend the parity principle and would not engender a legitimate or justifiable sense of grievance in an objective observer. Although Paul BONNER was the mastermind who made the threats, had the motive, was the oldest and had a significant record for violent offending, the sentencing judge found each co-offender equally culpable for the offending at the house because each acted pursuant to a common purpose and the assaults were a probable consequence of that plan. The Court accepted the finding that COOPER was not 'roped in' but a willing and enthusiastic participant — travelling from Darwin with 48 hours to reconsider. The distinction in roles existed only before the offence; on the day itself there was no difference. The 10 months adequately reflected BONNER's mastermind role, his violent antecedents and COOPER's youth. The Court also stressed that at age 25 youth carries only little weight as a mitigating factor.
whatItMeans: This is chiefly an awareness case, but it reinforces evidential themes useful to your casework. First, common purpose (probable consequence) means every participant can be held equally culpable for the violence at the scene, even where you cannot prove which individual struck the blows — the judge here could not identify who hit whom, yet all five were convicted. Build the case around the shared plan, not just who wielded the weapon. Second, physical evidence tying a suspect to preparatory acts is powerful: COOPER's fingerprint was found on the stolen numberplate fitted to the vehicle he and Shannon BONNER drove from Darwin, and the Court treated that trip — with some 48 hours to reconsider — as showing a willing and enthusiastic participant, not a man 'roped in'. Preserve and forensically examine vehicles, plates and staging locations. Third, the pre-offence threats, cross-border travel, disguises and stolen plates all evidenced premeditation and consciousness of guilt — document the full timeline, not just the assault. Fourth, an offender aged 25 or over will get little sentencing benefit from 'youth', so don't overstate that concern when assessing a suspect's likely outcome.
verdict: AWARENESS only — this is a sentence-parity appeal that does not change investigative or charging rules, but it usefully reaffirms common-purpose culpability and the value of forensic links to preparatory acts.
flags: Judgment notes the sentencing judge incorrectly referred to 18/05/2018 for a threat phone call; the correct date found was 12/05/2018.
Sentence figures and section numbers are taken directly from the judgment; the s 304(1)(b) and s 317(1) maxima are stated as 7 years each and s 401(1)(a) as 20 years.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: The State of Western Australia v Matanga
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (BLACK DCJ)
outcome: Leave to appeal granted on grounds 1-5; appeal allowed; original conditionally suspended sentence set aside; respondent resentenced to a total effective 3 years 6 months' immediate imprisonment, backdated to 20/10/2025, with parole eligibility.
weight: Court of Appeal (three judges) unanimous judgment of the Court; a considered restatement of established authority on prison-conditions mitigation and Bugmy principles. Persuasive and binding as an appellate authority, though grounds 3-5 were not decided.
oneLine: Harsh conditions generally experienced by remand prisoners at Hakea are not a mitigating factor without evidence of hardship personal to the offender, and childhood deprivation only reduces moral culpability if it impairs capacity to behave lawfully.
whatHappened: MATANGA, aged 25, pleaded guilty to five counts of sexual penetration of a child aged 13-16 (contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 321(2)) involving a 14-year-old complainant on three occasions in late 2024/early 2025 in a country town. The pair met at a party, exchanged Snapchat messages, and engaged in sexual activity in his car at a secluded farming property. He knew her true age at the time of counts 2-5. Three occasions involved unprotected penile-vaginal penetration. He was arrested 07/02/2025, bailed, then remanded from 20/10/2025 on a separate pending charge. The District Court (BLACK DCJ) imposed a total effective 3 years 6 months, conditionally suspended for 2 years, treating his remand conditions at Hakea and 'Bugmy principles' as mitigating. The State appealed.
whatHeld: Grounds 1 and 2 established. The sentencing judge erred in fact and law by treating the respondent's remand conditions as a mitigating factor. There was no evidence his conditions were materially more arduous than those of the general prison population; indeed he spent most of his remand (137 days) at Albany, not Hakea (91 days), contrary to the judge's assumption. The Court held that harsh conditions generally experienced by remand prisoners at Hakea are not a mitigating factor — those conditions reflect the general prison population, and concern about them is a matter for the executive (Prisons Act 1981 (WA) s 7) and administrative law remedies, not sentencing. For prison hardship to mitigate, an offender must adduce evidence of hardship personal to them that is more onerous than for the ordinary prisoner. On Bugmy (grounds 3-4, not decided), the Court observed a deprived childhood only reduces moral culpability where it impairs the capacity to behave lawfully; here it merely influenced poor choices and did not impair that capacity. The Court resentenced to the same terms but as immediate imprisonment, backdated to 20/10/2025, with parole eligibility.
whatItMeans: This decision is awareness-level for your casework but useful context on sentencing. When a court considers prison conditions in sentencing, the point of principle is that generalised Hakea conditions are not mitigating — only evidence of hardship personal to the offender counts. For serious child sexual offending under s 321(2), immediate imprisonment remains the usual and expected disposition, even where the child instigated the activity, there was no coercion, and the offender genuinely believed there was a relationship. Note the practical points relevant to your briefs: a good, thorough interview capturing admissions (here the offender admitted knowing her age) and evidence of the offender's knowledge of age (text messages about waiting until she was 18) can be decisive. The 'element of abuse' — harm, exploitation or mistreatment — is the key touchstone; document the age gap, lack of protection, and victim impact fully.
verdict: AWARENESS — a sentencing appeal clarifying that generalised Hakea remand conditions do not mitigate; it does not change how you investigate or charge.
flags: Grounds 3, 4 and 5 were not determined by the Court, as ground 1 was sufficient to require resentencing.
Section 87 of the Sentencing Act referenced in the judgment relates to remand time; note the respondent was remanded on a separate pending charge, not the indicted offences.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Lagdon v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (CURWOOD DCJ), IND 329 of 2025
outcome: Leave to appeal granted on grounds 2 and 3; appeal dismissed. Total effective sentence of 7 years 9 months' imprisonment upheld.
weight: Court of Appeal (three judges) unanimous judgment of the court; authoritative but expressly turns on its own facts.
oneLine: Court of Appeal upholds a firm 7 years 9 months' sentence for a teacher who groomed and sexually abused a 15/16-year-old student and used online deception to procure and expose himself to three interstate 12-13 year olds.
whatHappened: Harry Sing Wan LAGDON, a high school art teacher in a regional WA town, pleaded guilty to 25 counts of sexually motivated offending against four child victims. Counts 1-15 concerned Tanja (a pseudonym), his year 11 student aged 15-16, involving grooming (text messaging, a birthday pendant, escalating physical contact), indecent dealing, oral and unprotected penile-vaginal penetration on and off school grounds, and a large volume of explicit and degrading photos and videos (hundreds of images/videos). Counts 16-25 concerned online communications with three girls aged 12 or 13 living in Queensland (ERO, MO, LRMR), in which LAGDON posed as a 14, 15 or 16-year-old boy, sent explicit messages and videos of himself masturbating, possessed child exploitation material, and procured LRMR to send explicit images. He was 24-27 at the time, 9 years older than Tanja, with no prior record. He was sentenced in the District Court (CURWOOD DCJ) to a total effective sentence of 7 years 9 months' imprisonment, with count 9 (4 years) as the head sentence and cumulative components from counts 11, 19 and 24. He appealed, arguing count 9 was manifestly excessive and the total effective sentence breached the first limb of the totality principle.
whatHeld: Leave to appeal was granted on grounds 2 and 3 but the appeal was dismissed. The court held that although the sentence for count 9 and the total effective sentence were firm, they were not unreasonable or plainly unjust and revealed no implied error. On the argument that offending occurred in a 'consensual relationship', the court held it is not meaningful to describe a child under a teacher's care, supervision or authority as a willing participant; absence of coercion rises no higher than the absence of an aggravating factor. The court noted the initial refusal in count 4 and the element of force in counts 6 and 8. The court reaffirmed that consent is not an element of s 322 offences, that prior good character carries little weight in child sexual offending, and that general and personal deterrence are the primary considerations. It stressed that sentences for child sexual offending have progressively firmed up and older authorities (pre-2010) should be treated with caution as they may not reflect current standards.
whatItMeans: When you investigate and build a brief for sexual offending by a person in a position of trust (teacher, coach, carer), frame the power imbalance and grooming as core aggravating features, not background. Capture the full evidentiary picture: the grooming timeline, gifts, contrived opportunities to be alone, the volume and content of electronic material (here hundreds of explicit and degrading images/videos), and any degrading or threatening text. Do not treat any apparent 'relationship' or willingness as diminishing criminality — consent is not an element of these offences and, for a child under care/authority, it is at best neutral. Still, record any evidence of actual refusal or force (as in counts 4, 6 and 8 here) because that can be aggravating. Preserve and forensically download devices — the phone and laptop downloads quantifying messages, photos and videos were central to establishing seriousness. For online offending, evidence of age deception (posing as a younger boy) and successful procurement of images strengthens the seriousness of s 204B and s 220 charges. Victim impact evidence detailing lasting harm is important.
verdict: AWARENESS — this confirms sentencing severity and the treatment of 'consent' and grooming in trust-based child sex cases, but does not change investigative or charging procedure.
flags: Victim names (Tanja, ERO, MO, LRMR) are pseudonyms/initials used to protect identity.
The judgment references maximum penalties per count in the sentencing table; verify current section numbers and maxima in the Criminal Code (WA) before relying on them for charging.

caseName: Minchin v Director of Public Prosecutions
appealFrom: Magistrates Court of Western Australia (Perth) (MAGISTRATE J SCUTT), FR 9294/2025, PE 47101/2025, PE 47109/2025, PE 47111/2025
outcome: Leave granted; appeal allowed on ground 1. The 12-month sentence was set aside; MINCHIN resentenced to 8 months, backdated to 25/09/2025 and already served.
weight: Single-judge Supreme Court appeal from the Magistrates Court (WHITBY J), delivered the day after hearing and categorised B, with no authorities cited.
oneLine: WHITBY J allowed a sentence appeal because the magistrate wrongly found one burglary was committed while MINCHIN was on bail — a serious aggravating factor — and resentenced him to 8 months.
whatHappened: MINCHIN pleaded guilty on 24/12/2025 in the Perth Magistrates Court to four counts of burglary and commit (stealing) on a place contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 401(2)(c), receiving a total effective sentence of 12 months' immediate imprisonment. On 04/08/2025 he burgled the Reece Plumbing centre and the Coffee Cabinet in Osborne Park, taking $500 from the latter. On 09/08/2025 he broke into the Folk and Merchant Café in Doubleview and stole cash. He was arrested and charged on 10/08/2025 and released on bail. While on bail, on 21/09/2025, he forced entry to the Copper Chimney in South Fremantle and stole a tip jar and an OscarPOS tablet, making full admissions on arrest. He appealed sentence on four grounds, including that the magistrate wrongly treated one burglary as committed on bail.
whatHeld: Leave granted; appeal allowed on ground 1. The magistrate erred in treating the Folk and Merchant Café burglary as committed on bail, when MINCHIN was not yet charged. The respondent accepted the error but argued it was immaterial; WHITBY J rejected that: because the commission of an offence whilst on bail is a serious aggravating factor, the error was capable of affecting the total effective sentence, requiring resentencing; grounds 2 to 4 were not considered. On resentence, his Honour weighed MINCHIN's mental health and substance misuse issues, stable accommodation, remorse and a 25% guilty plea discount under Sentencing Act 1995 (WA) s 9AA against the need for deterrence, applying the totality principle to reach a total effective sentence of 8 months.
whatItMeans: This carries little investigative consequence — it does not change how you interview, caution, search or arrest. Read it for two things. First, the chronology you record is what the court sentences on: the error here was simply a wrong assumption about which charges MINCHIN was on bail for and when, so arrest, charge and bail dates must be accurate for every charge, since offending on bail is a serious aggravating factor capable of shifting the sentence. Second, MINCHIN's admission at arrest that he broke in because he had no food surfaced at resentencing: what a suspect says in interview travels with the file all the way to sentencing, so record the whole account, not just what proves the elements.
verdict: AWARENESS — a single-judge appeal correcting a conceded bail-status error; it applies orthodox principles and does not change how you investigate.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v Blurton
outcome: Interim detention order made under s 46(2)(c)(i); restriction order application listed for 28/01/2027 with expert examinations ordered; interim supervision order application adjourned sine die.
weight: Single judge of the Supreme Court (MCGRATH J) on an interlocutory HRSO preliminary hearing, marked Category B — turns on its own facts. Persuasive first-instance authority.
oneLine: MCGRATH J found reasonable grounds BLURTON might be a high risk serious offender under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA), and detained him on an interim detention order pending the hearing.
whatHappened: Malcolm Stirling BLURTON, 38, is serving 8 years 6 months imposed 06/05/2020, backdated 29/05/2018, release due 28/11/2026. Three of six index counts are HRSO serious offences: he pointed a shotgun at a man's head and stole $35 (aggravated armed robbery, Criminal Code (WA) s 392(c)(d)); the same day he fired at the car of that victim's friend, wounding the driver, who was hospitalised (armed robbery, s 392(c)); and on a different date he entered a house of people known to him with a shotgun, stealing phones and a laptop (acts intended to cause grievous bodily harm or prevent arrest, s 294). The Children's Court dealt with two further HRSO serious offences: robbery and lit fire likely to injure or damage (Bush Fires Act 1954 (WA) s 32). His violent record runs 2007 to 2024: aggravated burglary, threats to kill. The State applied for a s 48 restriction order on 02/07/2026; heard 28/08/2026.
whatHeld: MCGRATH J found there were reasonable grounds for believing the court might find BLURTON is a high risk serious offender, and made an interim detention order under s 46(2)(c)(i). BLURTON conceded that threshold and his Honour accepted the concession was properly made. The court need not be satisfied a restriction order will be made, only that one might be. Reasonable grounds require facts sufficient to induce that state of mind in a reasonable person. The antecedents, criminal record and expert assessments supported the finding: Professor JANCA diagnosed Cluster Personality Disorder (primarily antisocial) and put him at high to very high risk. His Honour found an unacceptable risk of reoffending that could not be sufficiently reduced by an interim supervision order, and adjourned that application sine die.
whatItMeans: This is a post-sentence restriction decision, not a guide to investigation. Look at what the State put before the court: three affidavits, the first annexing his criminal history and reports including psychiatric and psychological assessments. What you record now — particularised charges, breach charges for bail conditions and restraining orders — is what a judge reads later when deciding whether a person is an unacceptable risk. The court made an order under Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA) s 122 allowing the experts to be supplied with audio-visual recordings of interviews, or transcripts. Your recorded interview does not stop working at conviction — it can be handed to a psychiatrist and psychologist afterwards to assess risk, so interview quality and recordings matter beyond the trial.
verdict: AWARENESS — an interlocutory HRSO hearing. It does not change how you investigate; the s 122 order is worth knowing.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (Sweeney DCJ), IND 507 of 2021
outcome: Hung: leave to appeal refused, appeal dismissed. Sang Le: application to adduce additional evidence and application to extend time both dismissed; appeal remains dismissed under the earlier self-executing (springing) order. Additional-evidence applications refused in both.
weight: Unanimous Court of Appeal (MITCHELL, HALL and SEAWARD JJA), Category B, applying settled principles — M v The Queen and Pell v The Queen on unreasonable-verdict review, Gallagher and Mickelberg on additional evidence. Binding WA appellate authority, but it breaks no new ground.
oneLine: Court of Appeal upholds meth importation convictions, confirming covert recordings, IP tracking and corroborated accomplice evidence together proved a commercial-quantity import agreement.
whatHappened: About 20.9 kg (16.8 kg pure) of methamphetamine was concealed in an industrial oven consigned by FedEx from Toronto on 22/12/2018, addressed to "Minh" of a fake kitchen-equipment business (HKM) at a Maddington premises. Federal police intercepted the parcel in Sydney on 03/01/2019, replaced the drug with an inert substance and ran a controlled delivery on 10/01/2019 (no one attended). Minh and the two appellants, Phuoc Sang LE and Thanh Hung NGUYEN (Hung), were arrested on 15/01/2019 and charged under s 307.1(1) of the Criminal Code (Cth). Minh pleaded guilty and testified for a substantial sentence reduction. Both appellants were convicted after a trial that ran from 06/03/2024 to 24/05/2024; Hung was also convicted of failing to comply with a data access order (s 3LA(5) Crimes Act 1914 (Cth)). The prosecution case rested on Minh's accomplice evidence, translated telecommunications intercepts and a listening/tracking device in Hung's car (obtained under TI and surveillance device warrants), FedEx tracking traced to LE's home router/IP address, and items found on search. Both appellants gave evidence denying knowledge — Hung claimed the venture was tobacco/gemstones, LE claimed an ordinary commercial lease and a Ghana gold business.
whatHeld: Hung's appeal was dismissed (leave refused) and Sang Le's application for an extension of time was refused, so his appeal stayed dismissed under the springing order. On its own review of the record the Court found only one reasonable inference open on the evidence as a whole — an agreement to import a commercial quantity of methamphetamine — and called the prosecution case strong and compelling. It may not have been open to convict on Minh's evidence alone, but his account was corroborated by the covert recordings, Hung's movements, the seized items and the FedEx tracking. The covert recordings were admissible against both appellants — as circumstantial evidence of the agreement and, where its requirements were met, as acts or declarations in furtherance under the co-conspirator exception to the hearsay rule. The interpreter was qualified by a combination of study and experience to translate Vietnamese and a childhood rhyming slang; the concession that his evidence was admissible was correctly made. The Court did not decide whether the prosecutor's questions implying the accused should have called corroborating witnesses were improper: the respondent conceded they should not have been asked, and on that assumption the trial judge's clear, repeated no-onus directions meant no miscarriage of justice, so refusing to discharge the jury was plainly correct. The expert-evidence direction was orthodox. Leave to adduce additional evidence was refused: for Hung it was new, not fresh, evidence; for Sang Le the Court left open whether it was fresh, because either way there was no significant possibility of an acquittal.
whatItMeans: For your casework this confirms several practical points. Corroborate accomplice/informer evidence — the Court doubted a conviction on Minh's evidence alone would have been open, so build independent support (intercepts, surveillance, financial and search material). Covert product from properly warranted TI and surveillance devices can run against every party to an agreement, not just the speaker, via the co-conspirator exception — capture the whole picture, because forensic force comes from the totality, not one disputed phrase. Get properly accredited interpreters for covert recordings; capability by study and experience covers dialect/slang, and disputes over a few words go to weight. Digital tracing matters — IP/router attribution (here FedEx web-tracking tied to LE's home router) is strong circumstantial evidence; corroborate with device location and surveillance timing. For data access orders (s 3LA), the live issue is proving the suspect was capable of complying (knew the PIN/password) — gather evidence linking the person to actual use of the device. Finally, never let questioning imply the accused must call evidence or prove anything — the onus stays on the prosecution.
verdict: AWARENESS — an appellate application of settled principles; the practice points on corroborating accomplice evidence, warranted covert product running against every party to the agreement, interpreter qualification and s 3LA capability reinforce rather than change how you work.
flags: Verified case name is "Le v The King" but the substantive appeal decided was Hung's (Thanh Hung NGUYEN); Sang Le's appeal remained dismissed under a springing order.
Quantity stated as ~20.9 kg (16.8 kg pure); Minh's evidence referred variously to ~24 kg and 1–2 kg — figures in the judgment are inconsistent as recorded.
Relevance set at AWARENESS on review (14/09/2026): the decision applies settled principles; its practice points reinforce existing method rather than change it.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Di Ciano v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (MASSEY DCJ), IND 1887 of 2021
outcome: Both appeals dismissed. Conviction appeal: leave granted on ground 1 but ground not established; leave refused on ground 2. Sentence appeal: leave granted, appeal dismissed. Total effective sentence of 7 years 6 months' imprisonment upheld.
weight: Considered, unanimous Court of Appeal judgment (three judges) reviewing directions on implied admissions and prosecutorial conduct — persuasive and useful guidance, though largely applying settled principle to its facts.
oneLine: Court of Appeal upholds convictions and 7½-year sentence for sexual penetration of a young employee, confirming how pretext-call apologies can be run as implied admissions and how prosecutors may fairly test a consent defence.
whatHappened: DI CIANO, a 47-year-old restaurant owner in Highgate, was convicted after a jury trial of three counts of sexual penetration without consent (counts 2, 3 and 4) against a 22-year-old employee working her second shift on 19/12/2020. The offending occurred in a locked storeroom (forced fellatio and penile-vaginal penetration) and later in a function room (digital penetration). He was acquitted of an indecent assault (count 1) and fined for indecent assaults on two other employees. After the complainant reported to police, she made a recorded pretext call to the appellant from the station, in which he repeatedly apologised ("I'm so sorry... I get it") and said he was "probably too aggressive", without ever expressly admitting non-consent. He later denied forcing her by text ("I never forced anyone and never will"). The defence ran consent, and honest and reasonable mistaken belief. He did not give evidence. He appealed conviction (directions on implied admissions; prosecutor's closing) and sentence (totality).
whatHeld: The appeal was dismissed on all grounds. On the directions: the trial judge's direction was sufficient to avoid any perceptible risk of a miscarriage of justice. The court held that a full Edwards-type lie direction was inapposite because the State did not allege the appellant's statements were untrue — it alleged they truthfully acknowledged non-consent. Nor was this a 'silence' case like MMJ, because the appellant responded and was "anything but silent". Where there is no plausible innocent explanation for the admission, a direction listing implausible alternatives could only emphasise its incriminating force. On the prosecutor's closing: it was not improper for the prosecutor to hypothesise what an innocent person might have said, drawing on propositions defence counsel had put to the complainant. The prosecutor was not treating those propositions as evidence, and standard directions (that questions and counsel's statements are not evidence) removed any realistic risk of misuse. On sentence: the 7 years 6 months total effective sentence did not infringe the first limb of totality; 5 years on count 3 was moderate and some accumulation for the separate count 4 was justified.
whatItMeans: For your casework, this confirms that a pretext call is a powerful tool even where the suspect never expressly admits the offence. An apology or a failure to deny, in a context where an innocent person would be expected to protest, can be run as an implied admission supporting the complainant's account. Two practical takeaways: (1) let the suspect talk — the value here came from an apologetic, non-denying response to being told the complainant felt scared; and (2) get specifics on record where you can, because the defence exploited the fact that no direct allegation of rape/non-consent was ever put during the call, and that the appellant denied force once a specific written allegation came. A well-run pretext call ideally captures the suspect responding to a concrete, non-consensual allegation. Note also the court's approach: because these were truthful-acknowledgement admissions, not lies, the usual lie/consciousness-of-guilt directions did not apply. The case also reinforces that sexual offending by an employer against an employee is a serious aggravating breach of trust and power imbalance, especially against young, culturally vulnerable, or ESL victims.
verdict: AWARENESS with practical value: it does not change the law but confirms best practice for pretext calls and how apologetic, non-denying responses can be used as implied admissions.
flags: The offence provision listed in the catchwords is Criminal Code (WA) s 325; the judgment text does not expressly state the section for each count — confirm charging section before relying on it.
Sentencing Act reference in the judgment is to s 9AA of the Sentencing Act 1995 (WA) for the 10% plea discount on the indecent assault counts only.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Rose v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: Supreme Court of Western Australia (General Division), HOWARD J
outcome: Application for interim orders dismissed; extension of time to file appellant's case granted to 4.00 pm on 11/09/2026.
weight: Court of Appeal (two judges) reasons on an interlocutory application; persuasive on the limits of the court's power over prison authorities, but the power question was expressly left not fully resolved ('highly doubtful' rather than decided).
oneLine: Court of Appeal refuses a remand prisoner's application for orders directing the prison on how to manage his custody so he can prepare a bail appeal: its power to give such directions is 'highly doubtful' and, even if it existed, this was not a case for it.
whatHappened: Andrew Bo ROSE was serving a 6 year 4 month sentence (backdated to 04/10/2019) for serious offences and was released on parole in July 2024. On 26/03/2025, still on parole, he was charged with two counts of aggravated burglary and two counts of possession of prohibited drugs with intent to sell or supply — all serious offences under sch 2 to the Bail Act. His parole was revoked and he was remanded at Bunbury Regional Prison, with trial listed in the Magistrates Court for 27/10/2026. His third bail application was refused by HOWARD J on 15/05/2026. ROSE appealed under s 15A of the Bail Act and, acting in person, applied for interim orders directing the prison to give him a cell computer, free copying/printing, facilitated calls to businesses to find witnesses, in-cell law books, careful handling of evidential mail, and placement in a prison with an open library. He had not filed a compliant appellant's case.
whatHeld: The Application for interim orders was dismissed and an extension of time to file the appellant's case was granted. The Court held it is highly doubtful the court has any power to direct prison authorities on how a prison or prisoner is managed in order to preserve its appellate jurisdiction — the CEO of the Department of Justice is responsible for prison management under s 7 of the Prisons Act 1981 (WA) and is not a party to the appeal. Adopting the NSW reasoning in Liristis and Hamzy, the Court held its role is to ensure a fair trial and at most an 'irreducible minimum' of resources, not equality of arms, with corrections authorities better placed to weigh security. Even if the power existed, this was not an appropriate case: ROSE was disadvantaged but not denied access to the appellate jurisdiction. The Court also stressed that under s 15B(2) the appeal is confined to the material before the primary judge, so seeking new evidence for the bail appeal had no utility, and that new facts should instead found a fresh s 14(2a) application.
whatItMeans: This is a bail/procedural appeal and does not change how you investigate or charge. It is useful background on the custody framework: a person charged with a sch 2 serious offence while on parole faces the exceptional reasons test for bail (cl 3A, pt C, sch 1), and repeat bail applications require new facts or inadequate earlier presentation under s 14(2a). Practically, it confirms that a remand prisoner's complaints about difficulty preparing a defence in custody are managed by corrections and the trial court, not by orders against police or prisons via the appeal court. If a self-represented accused complains to you about disclosure or preparation, note that adequacy of disclosure is a matter for the trial court (here the Magistrates Court), and the prison controls access to computers, copying and legal resources.
verdict: AWARENESS only — a procedural bail-appeal decision about the court's power over prison management; it does not affect investigative steps, evidence gathering or charging.
flags: The verified citation and body of the judgment refer to the 'Bail Act 1982 (WA)', but the catchwords list 'Bail Act 1981 (WA)' — the correct short title is the Bail Act 1982 (WA); treat the 1981 reference as a typographical error.
Section numbers (s 14, s 14(2a), s 15A, s 15B(2)) and cl 3A of pt C sch 1 are taken directly from the judgment text.
Two-member Court (THOMSON P, MITCHELL JA); orders were made 28/08/2026 with written reasons published the same date.

caseName: DJF v Director of Public Prosecutions
appealFrom: Magistrates Court of Western Australia (MAGISTRATE A. HOCKTON)
outcome: Leave granted; ground 2 dismissed, ground 1 upheld. The sentence of 10 months and 30 days' imprisonment was set aside and DJF resentenced to 8 months, suspended for 18 months from 26/08/2026.
weight: Single judge of the Supreme Court (LUNDBERG J) exercising jurisdiction over a Magistrates Court sentence. Categorised B and turning on its own facts. Applies settled totality and appellate-error principles; persuasive, not binding.
oneLine: LUNDBERG J allowed an appeal and suspended an 8-month term, holding that 10 months and 30 days' imprisonment did not bear a proper relationship to the overall criminality of a naive conduit in an investment fraud.
whatHappened: DJF, with no prior record, was approached in mid-2022 by a friend offering what looked like a legitimate business opportunity. The scheme, engineered by others, persuaded investors they were buying investment bonds: recruits' identity documents were used to open bank and cryptocurrency accounts, prepaid phones relayed verification codes, and funds were disbursed domestically and to Hong Kong and the United Kingdom, never recovered. From September 2022 DJF registered five shell companies and opened bank and cryptocurrency accounts; from February 2023 he recruited others and coached them on answering questions. The loss was at least $765,000. DJF denied involvement to police, then pleaded guilty on 16/04/2026 to seven counts of possessing stolen or unlawfully obtained property (Criminal Code s 417(1)) and one count of, with intent to defraud, knowingly producing a false record (Criminal Code s 424(e)). MAGISTRATE HOCKTON imposed 10 months and 30 days' immediate imprisonment on 24/04/2026. DJF appealed.
whatHeld: Leave was granted. Ground 2, alleging express error, was dismissed. DJF fastened on the Magistrate's remark that 'the criminality is the same throughout', but ex tempore reasons must be read as a whole, not construed minutely with an eye for error. The Magistrate was assessing culpability and had reflected the change in knowledge in the sentence for count 8. Ground 1 (totality) was allowed: the sentence must bear a proper relationship to the overall criminality, and an appellate court needs error to intervene (Markarian v The Queen; Gaskell v The State of Western Australia). DJF's culpability was low: counts 1 to 4 involved $475,000, before actual knowledge; his role was narrow, his gain modest, and psychological evidence of submissiveness lowered moral culpability. Immediate imprisonment was unjust.
whatItMeans: This is a sentencing outcome, not a change to how you investigate. First, the figures did not reconcile: sentencing facts said $815,000, the charges totalled $765,000, and count 8 carried no quantum. Make the money in your statement of material facts reconcile to the charges, count by count. Second, the prosecution particularised three mental states across one course of conduct: reasonable suspicion for counts 1 to 4, recklessness for counts 5 to 7, actual knowledge for count 8. If you charge a course of conduct, evidence what the suspect knew and when it changed. Note the typology: recruits enlisted through friendship and money trouble, their identity documents used to open company, bank and cryptocurrency accounts. The person whose licence is on an account may be a recruit, not a principal.
verdict: AWARENESS - a sentence appeal applying settled totality principles. The material-facts discrepancy and staging of the accused's knowledge are useful for brief preparation.

appealFrom: Magistrates Court of Western Australia (Midland) (MAGISTRATE SULLIVAN), MI 3701/2025
outcome: Respondent's application to adduce additional evidence granted; appellant's application refused. Extension of time refused; leave to appeal refused; appeal dismissed. Conviction, $1,600 fine and six-month disqualification stand; costs reserved.
weight: Single-judge Supreme Court decision (JEYAMOHAN J) under the Criminal Appeals Act 2004 (WA). Category B, turning on its facts. Persuasive single-judge appeal authority on extension of time, apprehended bias and fresh evidence; not binding appellate authority.
oneLine: A self-represented driver's appeal against her Road Traffic Act 1974 (WA) s 64AC(1) drug-driving conviction failed: time was not extended, and neither the magistrate's 'rambler' remark nor a chain-of-custody challenge showed a miscarriage of justice.
whatHappened: On 26/02/2025 Kelly Joanne WILKINSON was driving in Ellenbrook when Sergeant Juan TREJOS stopped her for random drug and breath testing. A preliminary oral fluid test read positive. TREJOS took an evidentiary oral fluid sample, which read positive. The sample was sealed and delivered to the Chemistry Centre (WA), where analyst Ms Melissa DAWES certified it positive for methylamphetamine. WILKINSON was charged under s 64AC(1) of the Road Traffic Act 1974 (WA) and convicted after trial before MAGISTRATE SULLIVAN on 25/09/2025 — $1,600 fine, $300.50 costs, a $200 analysis fee and six months' disqualification. Self-represented, she attacked the storage of the test kit and the chain of custody, cross-examined both witnesses. At the outset the magistrate had disclosed she 'can be a bit of a rambler'. Her notice of appeal was filed 09/12/2025, 50 days out of time, on four grounds: miscarriage of justice, apprehended bias, prosecutorial misconduct and unjust reasoning in verdict; procedural fairness came later, in submissions.
whatHeld: Extension of time refused; leave to appeal refused; appeal dismissed. Applying JAD v McRae — delay, its reasons, the merit of the grounds and prejudice — JEYAMOHAN J found the 50-day delay not satisfactorily explained; Tobin v Dodd was applied to her as a litigant in person. Under s 40(1)(e) of the Criminal Appeals Act 2004 (WA), other evidence is admitted only where it shows a miscarriage of justice or error; her material did neither. The respondent's reconstructed exhibit bundle was admitted after the Midland court destroyed the trial exhibits. On bias, the test is whether a fair-minded lay observer might reasonably apprehend the judicial officer might not bring an impartial and unprejudiced mind; the magistrate had disclosed the remark. Procedural fairness was afforded, and the chain-of-custody complaint was at its highest entirely speculative.
whatItMeans: Drug driving is not your ground, but continuity is. What beat this challenge was TREJOS accounting for the legs he handled: the kit stored cool, the sample sealed, secured and conveyed to the station — not the ChemCentre run, which another officer did, DAWES receiving the container from Officer KAUR on 25/03/2025 and tying it to her certificate. Put that level of handling detail in your statement at the time. The magistrate found no other available inference of tampering or adulteration. The body worn camera footage nearly pushed the trial into another sitting, so timestamp the critical segments in your brief; and the Midland court destroyed the exhibits, so keep your own copies of everything you tender. None of this changes how you investigate child abuse, but the continuity discipline transfers to forensic and device exhibits.
verdict: AWARENESS — settled law on extension of time, bias and fresh evidence. ACTION-adjacent on continuity: a chain-of-custody attack fails against detailed officer evidence, not assertion.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v Moussa [No 3]
outcome: Custody order made under the Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023 (WA); no community supervision order; limiting term set as the duration of MOUSSA's life, taken to have commenced on 04/02/2025.
weight: Single-judge first-instance decision (PALMER J), on the order the State sought and MOUSSA conceded, though on the Court's own assessment. Persuasive, not binding. Applies settled Chokolich principles on limiting terms and the Chief Justice's preliminary view in Smith, followed by others.
oneLine: PALMER J made a custody order under the Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023 for a man acquitted of murder on mental impairment grounds, because murder carries a mandatory life sentence, the limiting term is life.
whatHappened: DAVID NADI LAMIE MOUSSA was charged in the Supreme Court (INS 24 of 2025) with the murder of his father and an omission causing danger to his stepmother, and was taken into custody on 04/02/2025. On 01/05/2026 PALMER J found MOUSSA not guilty of both charges on mental impairment under Criminal Code (WA) s 27(1). That verdict triggered the disposition regime in pt 5 of the Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023 (WA), and the matter was adjourned for reports. Dr BRETT interviewed MOUSSA and diagnosed paranoid schizophrenia; functioning had improved but psychotic phenomena were ongoing. The State Forensic Mental Health Service diagnosed schizophrenia and found symptoms including auditory hallucinations and superficial insight. Neither report supported management. A Predisposition Report and victim impact statements from MOUSSA's sister and brother were before the Court. Both the State and MOUSSA accepted a custody order with a limiting term of life.
whatHeld: PALMER J made a custody order and set the limiting term as the duration of MOUSSA's life. Dealing with a person on two or more charges under pt 5 requires a single order in respect of the accused, not one order per charge (s 46(1)); s 46(2)(a) required a custody order unless the Court was satisfied the risk MOUSSA appears to present could be managed under a community supervision order; it was not. Applying Chokolich, s 50 requires the best estimate of the sentence a court would have imposed assuming a plea at the earliest opportunity and disregarding the mental impairment. Life is mandatory for murder under Criminal Code s 279(4) unless clearly unjust and the person unlikely to be a threat; neither limb was met, the assault being 'unprovoked, brutal and sustained'.
whatItMeans: Nothing changes how you interview, caution, search or charge. Its value is what happens to a file after a mental impairment verdict, and why your evidence still drives the result. An acquittal under Criminal Code s 27(1) is neither the end of the matter nor a release: the Court must deal with the accused under the CLMI Act. In setting the limiting term the judge must disregard the mental impairment — so the seriousness you establish at the scene, in the pathology and statement of material facts, not the psychiatric picture, sets the term. The family are still heard after such a verdict, so keep family liaison running past the finding, and cooperation with police was weighed as mitigation, so record what an accused did or said accurately.
verdict: AWARENESS — a first-instance decision applying settled principles under the CLMI Act; it changes nothing about how you investigate, gather evidence or charge.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v KPB [No 5]
outcome: Contravention proved on the balance of probabilities. Order amended rather than rescinded under s 55(1)(b); no continuing detention order. Supervision order recommences 07/09/2026 for 3 years 6 months. Suppression order made.
weight: Single-judge first-instance decision (PALMER J) in HRSO contravention proceedings, turning on its own facts (Category B); applies Hart, CF [No 2] and Griffiths. Persuasive only; its interest lies in the enforcement tempo it assumes.
oneLine: PALMER J found KPB had repeatedly contravened his supervision order through persistent methylamphetamine use but amended the order rather than rescinding it under High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA) s 55(1)(b).
whatHappened: KPB was declared a high risk serious offender under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA) by DERRICK J on 02/11/2023 and detained; LEMONIS J rescinded that order on 23/04/2025 and imposed a supervision order of 3 years 6 months from 04/06/2025. Between 16/07/2025 and 27/11/2025 KPB contravened the order repeatedly, every breach tied to methylamphetamine and amphetamine use. He pleaded guilty on eight occasions in Perth and Midland Magistrates Courts to contravening a supervision order (s 80 HRSO Act) and drug possession (Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 (WA) s 6(2)), plus two curfew breaches, detected mostly by urinalysis with admissions on arrest. On 28/10/2025 the State applied under s 55 to rescind the order and impose continuing detention; FORRESTER J detained KPB, re-released him on an amended interim order on 18/11/2025 with a 'last chance' warning, then returned him to custody on 04/12/2025 after three further positive tests.
whatHeld: Contraventions were proved on the balance of probabilities, established by KPB's convictions; PALMER J amended the order under s 55(1)(b) rather than rescinding it. Under s 55(3) the paramount consideration is adequate protection of the community; ss 55(1)(b) and (c) are subject to s 29, which bars amending an order unless the court is satisfied the offender will substantially comply with standard conditions (s 30(2)), onus on the offender (s 29(2)). His Honour applied Hart, CF [No 2] and Griffiths: no risk of reoffending need be excluded, only reduced to a reasonably acceptable level, with the least invasive order. Dr PETCH's evidence was bleak — relapse 'almost certain', risk 'fairly uncontainable' when using — but PALMER J found, 'with some hesitation', that monitoring had worked: drug use was caught by urinalysis, so both were satisfied.
whatItMeans: You will meet HRSO subjects on the street before court. KPB was released only because PALMER J accepted a relapse would be detected and acted on fast — PETCH's evidence was that intervention 'took too long'. Treat a positive urinalysis as an immediate escalation, not a paperwork item. Know what the amended order authorises: reporting to the OIC of the Serious Offender Enforcement Squad within 48 hours of release, search of home, vehicle and person on request, urinalysis at the direction of a WA Police officer, and inspection of telecommunication devices with passcodes. Two traps: tell the subject before searching and record it; and the cloud-access authorisation is for monitoring only, 'absence any investigation for any offence' — get separate authority for a criminal investigation.
verdict: AWARENESS — a post-sentence contravention decision applying settled HRSO principles; ACTION-relevant only for the enforcement tempo and search powers it sets out.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v Paraha [No 2]
outcome: Respondent declared a high risk serious offender; supervision order made for 2 years 6 months rather than the 5 years sought, not continuing detention; conditions to be redrafted and start date settled with counsel.
weight: Single-judge first-instance decision of LEMONIS J — persuasive, not binding. It applies settled HRSO principles but goes further, setting out a structured approach to when disputed, uncharged conduct becomes 'acceptable and cogent' evidence.
oneLine: LEMONIS J declared PARAHA a high risk serious offender, holding evidence of disputed, unproved violent conduct must positively satisfy the court it occurred to be acceptable and cogent under High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA) s 7(1).
whatHappened: On 03/12/2024 the State applied for a restriction order against Tony James PARAHA under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA). PARAHA, 60, was finishing a 9-year term for the manslaughter of his eight-week-old daughter Narelle (Criminal Code (WA) s 280) by grave criminal neglect rather than direct violence, committed 13/01/2016; that sentence expired 26/01/2025. His two other serious offences were an aggravated indecent assault on a 22-year-old woman on 04/07/1991 and, on 15/01/2010, sexually penetrating an incapable person, a 39-year-old woman with Down's syndrome. The State sought a 5-year supervision order, relying on eighteen tabled categories of other alleged conduct — incident reports, a Statement of Material Facts, a child protection worker's affidavit, the s 74 reports of Dr WYNN OWEN and Dr YEWERS — to show violence against partners and children. Most was uncharged, much of it disputed; one category was abandoned, four were his 2002 restraining order breach conviction.
whatHeld: PARAHA was declared a high risk serious offender; the other-conduct case succeeded in part. Section 84 goes to admissibility, not proof: admissible evidence need not be 'acceptable and cogent' under s 7(1). On this application, disputed, unproved violent conduct had to positively satisfy the court it occurred, weighing seriousness and his chance to test it. An incident report and conclusory passages failed; the undisputed Statement of Material Facts, his admissions and his 'very violent' comment passed, grounding findings of violence against previous partners. A child's carer-relayed disclosures were expressly left undecided. Experts cannot resolve a factual dispute, and actuarial tools cannot make an allegation cogent; their assessments carried less weight for rejecting his denials as an unreliable historian. Risk: drug use escalating into serious violence; the PSSO too short, 2 years 6 months' supervision was minimum adequate protection.
whatItMeans: Most of what the State relied on was later report and assessment material — psychiatric and psychological reports, a pre-sentence report, a victim statement — not contemporaneous records, and much of it was thin, conclusory or untestable. A police incident report, standing alone, proved nothing: it narrated an allegation, no charge was apparent, and the Court would not find it happened. Record particulars, not conclusions — a report that 'violence ... featured heavily' was discarded: nothing captured what happened. For Child Abuse Squad work, a child's disclosure relayed through a carer gave PARAHA no proper opportunity to test it; get the child's account first-hand, in their own words. Watch your Statements of Material Facts — the Court could not tell whether his admissions covered the charge alone or everything alleged; say precisely what was admitted.
verdict: ACTION: the Court's rulings on what makes disputed conduct 'acceptable and cogent' bear on incident reports, Statements of Material Facts and child-disclosure records you create.

appealFrom: Magistrates Court of Western Australia (Perth) (Magistrate D SCADDAN), PE 5058/2025
outcome: Extension of time granted; leave granted to both parties to adduce additional evidence; leave to appeal granted, appeal dismissed. The $600 fine and refusal of a spent conviction order stand; appellant to pay respondent's costs.
weight: Single judge of the Supreme Court (MCGRATH J), Category B; turns on its own facts. Persuasive first-instance authority applying settled principles on statements of material facts and additional evidence.
oneLine: MCGRATH J dismissed WOOD's appeal against a $600 fine for possessing anabolic steroids, holding the Magistrate sentenced him on an unknown quantity, not seven full vials, because the plea facts specified no quantity.
whatHappened: On 16/01/2025 police executed a search warrant at Bayswater and seized seven vials of anabolic steroids — testosterone, trenbolone, boldenone and trestolone. Detective Senior Constable PLUMMER saw liquid in every vial but did not note how much, later deposing 'a varying degree of liquids in each vial'. Officers took 15 photographs of the vials. On 07/02/2025 the prosecution notice recorded that he 'concedes substance', so there was 'no need for analysis'. On 14/07/2025, at the Perth Magistrates Court, WOOD pleaded guilty to possessing a prohibited drug contrary to s 6(2) of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 (WA). The facts named the substances and vials, not quantity. WOOD asked for a spent conviction; Magistrate SCADDAN imposed a $600 fine and refused one, citing his previous convictions. Self-represented and out of time, WOOD appealed, arguing he was sentenced as though the vials were full when they were nearly empty.
whatHeld: Leave to appeal granted; appeal dismissed. MCGRATH J held the test for admitting additional evidence on appeal is whether a different sentence should have been imposed had it been before the court. On a guilty plea the prosecutor must state the material facts (Criminal Procedure Act 2004 (WA) s 129(3)); those facts are the elements of the offence, and anything beyond an element must be proved or admitted by an unchallenged statement of facts. The facts named vials and substances but no quantity — 'vial' is not a term of measurement — so the Magistrate sentenced on an unknown quantity, not seven full vials. WOOD wrongly assumed the fine reset his spent-conviction clock: a $600 fine is 'minor punishment' under s 11(4) of the Spent Convictions Act 1988 (WA), not restarting the 10-year period.
whatItMeans: The lesson sits at the seizure: PLUMMER saw liquid but did not note how much — the omission behind WOOD's ground; 15 photographs showed no more than 'some amount, although very small'. When you seize a quantifiable exhibit, measure or estimate it and record the figure in your notes and the statement of material facts. Photographs prove existence, not volume. The wider point carries into Child Abuse Squad pleas: the facts the prosecutor reads aloud are the facts the offender is sentenced on, and silence is acceptance. Particularise what drives seriousness — frequency, ages, dates, the acts themselves — and where something is not known, leave the facts silent rather than overstate. Keep the disclosure record: the Court relied on WOOD having the photographs and facts before he pleaded.
verdict: ACTION — the appeal existed because the seizing officer never recorded vial quantities: a lesson on measuring exhibits and statements of material facts.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v Hoskin [No 4]
outcome: Contravention proved; order not rescinded, no continuing detention order made; supervision order amended under s 55(1)(b) for a new single-occupancy address and to limit adult pornography to print form, per Annexure A.
weight: FORRESTER J sitting alone in the Supreme Court on an HRSO contravention application. Persuasive first-instance authority only, categorised B and fact-specific: it applies the settled s 55 framework and states no new principle.
oneLine: FORRESTER J found HOSKIN had contravened his five-year HRSO supervision order by unauthorised internet and device use, but amended rather than rescinded it, satisfied his risk remained manageable in the community with independent accommodation and treatment.
whatHappened: Jason James Paul HOSKIN, a high risk serious offender, was subject to a five-year supervision order made by STRK J from 27/03/2024. Diagnosed with paedophilic disorder, his prior offending involved child exploitation material. Between 11/03/2024 and 06/09/2024 he committed 75 offences of contravening the order contrary to s 80(1) of the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA), plus seven reporting offences contrary to s 63(1) of the Community Protection (Offender Reporting) Act 2004 (WA): unapproved internet access and undeclared devices. He pleaded guilty to all 82 on 02/10/2024, received eight months, and was refused parole. Released 06/05/2025, he committed 13 further contravention offences and three reporting offences between 12/05/2025 and 24/06/2025 — further undeclared devices and pornography searches directed at young people. He was arrested and detained on 24/06/2025; the State applied under s 55 on 04/08/2025, and he was sentenced on 16/09/2025 to 10 months, backdated to 05/06/2025.
whatHeld: Contravention proved; the order was amended, not rescinded. FORRESTER J was satisfied from HOSKIN's own pleas that he had contravened the order, matching Dr HALL's risk markers. Under s 55(1) the Court could rescind and detain, amend, extend, or affirm; the paramount consideration is adequate protection of the community, not punishment. HOSKIN bore the onus of satisfying the Court, on the balance of probabilities, that he would substantially comply with the standard conditions — applying Director of Public Prosecutions for Western Australia v Hart, compliance enabling adequate protection by managing the risk. He did not give evidence; Ms LILLY described his conduct as deliberate and deceptive. But the order had achieved its aim — no serious offence, risk-elevating conduct readily detected — and the move to independent accommodation and resumed intervention made the risk manageable.
whatItMeans: You will meet men like HOSKIN in Child Abuse Squad work — HRSO subjects with paedophilic disorder and a history of child exploitation material. What mattered was monitoring product: device declarations, GPS and diary compliance, CCO performance reports, and digital evidence behind each s 80(1) charge. Note the warning signs the experts identified and the Court adopted: use of legal child images for masturbatory purposes, increasing time online, and covertly acquired devices run through third-party Wi-Fi to defeat detection. Treat those as markers of rising, imminent risk, and record them even without a charge. Annexure A conditions you may enforce include reporting to SOES within 48 hours, police search on request, and no unapproved internet. Independent accommodation, the Court noted, gives more freedom but less prospect of immediate detection.
verdict: AWARENESS — a post-sentence HRSO contravention decision; it does not change how you investigate or charge, but is relevant Child Abuse Squad background.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Frigger v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (GETHING DCJ), IND 1112 of 2019
outcome: Application to issue a witness summons dismissed; leave to appeal refused; appeal dismissed.
weight: Court of Appeal (three judges) — persuasive and authoritative on WA law, though the decision expressly turns on its own facts.
oneLine: A second appeal against a s 169 perjury conviction failed where the proposed 'fresh/new and compelling evidence' was neither fresh nor compelling and had no reasonable prospect of establishing innocence.
whatHappened: On 04/06/2024 FRIGGER was convicted after a jury trial of one count of knowingly making a false statement under oath in a material particular, contrary to s 169 of the Criminal Code (WA). The charge arose from two irreconcilable affidavits she swore (in 2008 and 2010) in civil proceedings involving PSA, Mr BANNING, CAT and Mr KITAY — one of the two statements had to be false. Her first appeal was dismissed on 14/01/2025. On 02/06/2026 she brought a second appeal under pt 3A of the Criminal Appeals Act 2004 (WA), relying on an affidavit and seeking a witness summons to Mr KITAY to produce a 2010 'reconstructed Directors' Loan Account'. She argued (1) the civil proceedings were a nullity because PSA lacked corporate authority to bring them, so no statement could be 'material', and (2) new evidence contradicted the prosecution case about directors' fees.
whatHeld: Leave to appeal was refused, the witness-summons application dismissed and the appeal dismissed. The court held the ground identified no fresh and compelling or new and compelling evidence and, in any event, had no reasonable prospect of succeeding. On particular 1, the 'nullity' argument was not new — it had been run in related litigation before trial and could have been raised with reasonable diligence; deemed civil admissions did not bind the State in the criminal case; superior court orders are valid until set aside so the proceedings were not nullities; and the affidavits were in fact relied on and so were capable of affecting the outcome, making them false in a material particular. On particular 2, evidence of a 2010 reconciliation showing FRIGGER a debtor rather than creditor was not compelling — the prosecution never sought to prove which of the two affidavits was false, only that they were irreconcilable so one must be — and evidence of the Freehills advice was in her possession before trial and remained subject to privilege/confidentiality orders. The court confirmed the prosecutor's disclosure duty is to disclose material in the possession of the investigators, not an obligation to go out and obtain material.
whatItMeans: This is mainly background awareness, but note two practical points. First, on s 169 perjury: a statement is false 'in a material particular' if it is reasonably capable of affecting the outcome of the purpose for which it was made — you do not need to prove the proceedings would have turned out differently, only that the statement could have affected them. Where a person swears two irreconcilable sworn statements, the prosecution can succeed by proving both cannot be true (so one must be false) without pinning down which one. Second, on disclosure: your duty runs to evidentiary material in the possession of the investigating agency. A defence complaint that the DPP failed to go and obtain some external document does not create a disclosure breach — but you should make sure everything the investigation actually holds is captured and passed on.
verdict: AWARENESS — it confirms how materiality under s 169 works and the scope of the disclosure duty, but does not change day-to-day investigative practice.
flags: Conviction date (04/06/2024) and other dates are drawn from the judgment text; confirm against the primary record if relied on.
Detailed factual background is in the First Appeal Decision (Frigger v The State of Western Australia [No 2] [2025] WASCA 7), which was not supplied in full.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Nicoletti v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (MASSEY DCJ), IND 1017 of 2022
outcome: Leave to appeal refused; appeal dismissed. Orders made 19/08/2026, reasons published the same day.
weight: Court of Appeal (three judges: THOMSON P, MITCHELL JA, SWEENEY JA) decision applying High Court authority; authoritative but expressly fact-specific ("Turns on own facts", Category B).
oneLine: Non-consecutive transcript page numbers given to the jury did not create a reasonable apprehension of bias or a miscarriage of justice.
whatHappened: NICOLETTI was convicted on 26/08/2025 in the District Court (MASSEY DCJ) of one count of sexual penetration without consent contrary to s 325 Criminal Code (WA). The count was one of several on a larger indictment; an earlier trial hung on various counts and a later trial of this count was aborted after the jury retired. At the trial that convicted him, the jury got a 'dummy' indictment with only this count and no mention of the earlier proceedings. The complainant's edited recorded evidence (given 19/02/2024) was played, and the jury received a transcript of witness evidence. The transcript pages were not consecutive — witness evidence ran pages 4121–4195 and the complainant's ran 1076–1113 — reflecting editing and the broader proceedings. The trial judge told the jury the numbering would be out and there would be gaps due to editing. NICOLETTI appealed, arguing the page numbers signalled he had been involved in extensive criminal proceedings, raising a reasonable apprehension of bias amplified by media coverage.
whatHeld: The Court of Appeal refused leave and dismissed the appeal, finding the ground had no reasonable prospect of succeeding. Three reasons: (1) the practice of numbering transcript pages consecutively across all proceedings under one indictment is not known to an ordinary juror or fair-minded member of the public, so the numbers communicated nothing about other charges; (2) the reasoning the appellant attributed to the fair-minded lay observer was mere speculation with no objective basis in fact; and (3) it would require the jury to disregard the trial judge's clear directions (not to speculate, decide only on the evidence, transcript is not evidence) and their oaths. Applying HCF v The Queen [2023] HCA 35, an apprehension must have an objective basis in fact, and violation of the juror's oath is not lightly to be inferred; jurors are assumed to understand and conform to directions.
whatItMeans: This is a conviction-appeal ruling with little direct operational impact, but it reinforces useful points. Courts strongly presume juries follow directions and honour their oaths, so claims of prejudice from incidental material need a concrete factual foundation, not speculation. Where a matter involves multiple counts, aborted or hung trials, and media coverage, prosecutors use tools like a 'dummy' indictment and editing to keep extraneous material from the jury — be alert to keeping your brief clean of prior-proceeding references. Incidental artefacts like non-consecutive transcript page numbers were held not to convey prejudicial information to lay jurors. The test for post-verdict apprehension of bias from jury issues comes from HCF: whether a fair-minded, informed member of the public might reasonably apprehend the jury did not decide according to law, on the evidence, and per directions.
verdict: AWARENESS only — this turns on its own facts and changes nothing in how you investigate or charge; it confirms the strong presumption that juries follow directions.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Downes v The State of Western Australia [No 3]
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (BOWDEN DCJ), IND 1527 of 2022
outcome: Application dismissed in its entirety.
weight: Two-judge Court of Appeal bench (THOMSON P and MITCHELL JA), Category B, no cases cited. An interlocutory ruling on an application for production of documents and affidavits within a self-represented appellant's conviction appeal — persuasive on appellate procedure, not a substantive precedent on the merits.
oneLine: Court of Appeal dismissed a self-represented appellant's application for document production and affidavits sought to support his conviction appeal over destroyed cannabis plants.
whatHappened: DOWNES pleaded guilty in the District Court to cultivating cannabis with intent to sell or supply (s 7(1)(a) Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 (WA)) and fraudulently diverting electrical power from Western Power (s 390 Criminal Code (WA)). On 14/08/2022 Department of Fire and Emergency Services officers attended a house fire at Orelia; police were notified of suspicions the house was being used to cultivate cannabis and executed a search warrant on 15/08/2022, finding a hydroponic operation in the laundry and three bedrooms. DOWNES first pleaded guilty in the Magistrates Court on 15/09/2022, after which six plants were kept as samples and the rest were destroyed by police. The pleas did not admit the number of plants: that went to a trial of issues, and on 17/12/2025 GILLAN DCJ found 269 plants had been seized and that they were cannabis sativa. DOWNES was sentenced that day to a total effective 3 years 3 months' immediate imprisonment. He appealed his conviction, arguing the State never proved there were 269 cannabis sativa plants and that unlawful destruction of the plants deprived him of the chance to inspect and count them. In this application he sought orders (Categories C–K) compelling production of documents and affidavits — the unredacted Police Destruction List Report, an affidavit from the JP who witnessed the destruction, proof of the authenticity of a WA Police Manual extract, evidence from a detective and the prosecutor, disclosure of a 'Red Flag' on his police record, and whistle-blower protection under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 2003 (WA).
whatHeld: The application was dismissed in full. The Court held the documents and orders sought had no demonstrated relevance to the issues in the appeal. It was already accepted that not all proper procedures were followed in destroying and storing the plants, so no affidavit or further proof on that point was needed. The refusal of a stay is not directly appealable; such grounds can only run as contentions that a ruling caused a miscarriage of justice. The whistle-blower relief was not properly brought within a criminal appeal and must go to a single judge of the General Division under s 15A of the Public Interest Disclosure Act 2003; in any event, no evidence showed detrimental reprisal action against the appellant.
whatItMeans: This decision is about interlocutory procedure in an appeal, not investigative practice, so its direct effect on your casework is limited. But note the practical warning underneath it: in a drug cultivation case, how you count, sample, store and destroy plant material matters. Here it was not in dispute that not all the proper procedures were followed in destroying and storing the seized plants — the destruction forms under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 (WA) and regulations were not properly completed — and although that did not save the appellant, it became the engine for a stay application, an attempt to withdraw the pleas, a trial of issues and repeated appeals. Retain sufficient representative samples (here six, one from each bag), have the Commissioner's delegate properly decide that it is not reasonably practicable to detain the material, have the destruction overseen by an officer of appropriate seniority, and complete the prescribed destruction forms correctly. Expect the approved botanist's certificates (form MD 14) to be attacked as well: the trial judge relied on the botanist's oral evidence rather than his certificates. Where plants are counted, corroborate the count with video and officers who can give direct evidence of counting — that is what sustained the finding of 269 plants at the trial of issues.
verdict: AWARENESS — a procedural ruling on document production in an appeal; it does not change how you investigate or charge, but it shows how a badly documented destruction of plant material can fuel years of litigation.
flags: Conviction date given as 19/07/2024 in the summary but pleas of guilty were entered on multiple dates (15/09/2022, 02/02/2024, 19/07/2024) — check the operative conviction date.
The appeal against conviction itself was not decided here; this is only the ruling on the production application.
Category J is not addressed in the judgment text (categories jump from I to K) — do not assume its content.
Section 41(1) Misuse of Drugs Act and s 30(3) Criminal Appeals Act 2004 (WA) are referenced only via the appellant's grounds and the Court's framing; verify before relying.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v Van Beek [No 2]
outcome: VAN BEEK declared a high risk serious offender; four-year supervision order under s 48(1)(b) from 18/08/2026. Conditions 27 and 28 amended to a three-contact reporting threshold; conditions 29 to 31 and social-media approval refused.
weight: Single-judge first-instance decision of the Supreme Court (HOWARD J), marked Category B and turning on its facts. Applies settled HRSO principles from Garlett; persuasive, not binding. Its value lies in the reasoning on necessary conditions.
oneLine: HOWARD J declared VAN BEEK a high risk serious offender and made a 4-year supervision order under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA), but refused conditions that went further than necessary.
whatHappened: VAN BEEK finished an aggregate 9-year term on 26/07/2025, imposed in the District Court on 20/10/2017 for seven counts of aggravated sexual penetration without consent contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 326, against his former de facto partner, with whom he shares two children.
