He had breached a violence restraining order, and had two counts of aggravated stalking, repeated VRO and protective bail breaches with aggravated common assault, and a threat to harm her child if she did not continue the relationship. The State applied on 06/05/2025 for a restriction order under s 48; LEMONIS J imposed an interim supervision order on 30/05/2025, and VAN BEEK was released onto it. HOWARD J heard the s 48 application on 11/05/2026, with a s 60 victim submission and cross-examined evidence from psychiatrists Dr WYNN OWEN, Dr BANNISTER and Senior CCO Ms LICO. The real contest was over the conditions.
whatHeld: VAN BEEK was declared a high risk serious offender under s 7(1) and made subject to a four-year supervision order under s 48(1)(b); the Act requires such an order to do no more than is necessary for adequate protection. Both psychiatrists assessed him as high risk of a further serious offence, most likely partner violence at a time of conflict or separation; Dr WYNN OWEN put children in his or a partner's or ex-partner's care in the non-serious category. The respondent bears the onus of substantial compliance; his compliance with the interim order discharged it, undisturbed by minor offending. Applying Edelman J's minimum-intrusion observation in Garlett on additional conditions, extended by HOWARD J to duration, the Court refused proposed conditions 29 to 31 and the social-media approval condition, amended conditions 27, 28 and 38, and imposed the balance.
whatItMeans: This is a post-sentence restriction order: it changes no charge you lay, though you may enforce it. Police may, if requested, search VAN BEEK's person, residence and vehicle to monitor compliance; he must report to the Serious Offender Enforcement Squad within 48 hours of the order starting, then as directed. Those powers are for compliance monitoring — if investigating, use ordinary powers, and record which power you exercised and why. The reporting trigger for a new female friendship or relationship is three contacts; devices and social media must be declared within 48 hours, nothing deleted, and passwords given to a CCO or police on request — so material should exist when you need it. This application was built from VRO breaches, protective bail breaches, stalking and a threat to the victim's child — charge and document properly.
verdict: AWARENESS — a first-instance HRSO decision applying settled principle to its own facts; it does not change how you investigate or charge.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v Hill [No 3]
outcome: Respondent found to remain a high risk serious offender; continuing detention order rescinded; supervision order made for 5 years from 07/09/2026 on conditions in the Annexure; non-publication order over the accommodation address and provider's name.
weight: Single-judge decision of the Supreme Court (FIANNACA J) on the first periodic review of a continuing detention order under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA); persuasive first-instance authority, turning on its own facts.
oneLine: On HILL's first periodic review under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA), FIANNACA J held he remains a high risk serious offender but replaced continuing detention with a 5-year supervision order given changed accommodation.
whatHappened: HILL, 68, has a long history of stalking and family violence, some while subject to Violence Restraining Orders (VROs). His last offence was the manslaughter of his 60-year-old former partner, contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 280. Her VRO against him was in force when they resumed contact after his 2012 release. On 01/08/2012 he entered her property and struck her repeatedly, causing a concussive head injury and traumatic spinal injury; she died three hours later. He was sentenced on 28/03/2014 to 11 years backdated to 02/08/2012, and refused parole. He also has convictions for aggravated stalking (s 338E), assaulting partner AB in 2010, and 48 VRO breaches since 2004. On 15/03/2024 DERRICK J made a continuing detention order (Hill [No 2]), not satisfied HILL would substantially comply with a supervision order's standard conditions, and finding the proposed addresses unsuitable. This was the first periodic review, heard 06/02/2026 and 20/07/2026.
whatHeld: CDO rescinded; 5-year supervision order made. FIANNACA J held HILL remains a high risk serious offender under s 7(1) of the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA): an unacceptable risk of intimate partner violence or stalking, to a high degree of probability. Applying Pindan [No 3], the Hill [No 2] findings are a 'point of departure', not binding: the court must be independently satisfied under s 7. Under s 68(2), the court must choose the least invasive order adequately protecting the community. Section 29 put the onus on HILL to prove substantial compliance on the balance of probabilities; applying Hart, he was satisfied. The changes were personal as well as external: counselling, a changed attitude to supervision, aged care funding, a male-only lodge, and 12 months free of prison incidents relevant to his risk.
whatItMeans: This is a post-sentence review, not a guide to investigation, but the conditions are police-facing: HILL must report to the Serious Offender Enforcement Squad within 48 hours of release, and police may search his person, residence and vehicle on request. Record what you see at the time - incident notes and supervision reports written contemporaneously are exactly what decides these applications. Two points matter for family violence casework. First, a single communication in breach of a VRO may itself constitute the serious offence of stalking (par (e) of 'pursue' in Criminal Code (WA) s 338D) - do not treat one-off breaches as trivial. Second, HILL's victim was content to resume contact while her VRO was in force, and he killed her weeks later; the Court drew no conclusion from that.
verdict: AWARENESS - settled HRSO principle applied to its own facts; it does not change investigation, but the VRO-to-stalking point matters for family violence work.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v TJD [No 2]
outcome: Respondent declared a high risk serious offender; supervision order made for one year from 15/08/2026, not a continuing detention order. SOES reporting condition removed; electronic monitoring and CCO reporting retained.
weight: Single-judge decision of the Supreme Court applying settled HRSO principles; marked Category B. Persuasive, not binding - notable for holding a moderate risk can be unacceptable.
oneLine: WHITBY J declared TJD a high risk serious offender under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA), holding even a moderate risk of a serious offence unacceptable, but limiting supervision to one year.
whatHappened: TJD, 50, has eight convictions for serious offences under the HRSO Act. His pattern is offending against adult female strangers, forcing them into sexual activity by threats and weapons, usually using drugs and precipitated by relationship conflict. His last serious offence was in 2000. He was declared a dangerous sexual offender on 31/03/2011 under the now-repealed Dangerous Sexual Offenders Act 2006 (WA), later returned to detention after contravening supervision, then placed on a 10-year supervision order on 11/03/2014, extended to expire 10/03/2026. Since 30/10/2020 TJD has been convicted of 15 contraventions of that order, and a further contravention on 20/03/2026. On 16/02/2026 the State applied under s 36 of the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA) for a restriction order. The State tendered reports from psychiatrist Dr WOJNAROWSKA and psychologist Dr BANNISTER. TJD gave evidence and contested being a high risk serious offender.
whatHeld: TJD was declared a high risk serious offender and released on a one-year supervision order from 15/08/2026, not a continuing detention order. The State had to prove to a high degree of probability that TJD's risk of a serious offence is unacceptable and a restriction order is necessary for community protection. Dr WOJNAROWSKA's Static-99R score fell from 7 to 2 ('Average Risk'); Dr BANNISTER's VRS:SO score, 35/72, sat in the 'moderate-high risk' band, but both experts assessed his overall risk as moderate. WHITBY J accepted TJD's commitment to not reoffending, supported by over 12 years' substantial compliance, but held that even a moderate risk of a serious sexual offence is unacceptable given the serious harm such offending would cause. The court imposes the least invasive order that still protects the community, requiring satisfaction TJD would substantially comply.
whatItMeans: A post-sentence civil order, not a guide to investigation - it changes nothing about how you interview, caution or charge. From 15/08/2026 TJD's order no longer requires him to report to the Officer-in-Charge of SOES or receive police visits, removed over the State's objection - read the order before acting on any HRSO subject, since conditions relax as risk falls. Powers that survive: on request you may search his person, residence and vehicle, direct urinalysis, interview associates, and disclose his offence history to them. Contraventions are evidence: of fifteen convictions, the one that carried weight was meeting his ex-partner, because the 2000 index offending arose from conflict with her. Record who was involved and how it maps onto the index offending pattern, not just the breach.
verdict: AWARENESS - an HRSO outcome that does not change how you investigate or charge; note the conditions attached to the order.

appealFrom: Magistrates Court of Western Australia (Joondalup), MAGISTRATE SHACKLETON, PE 7716/2026 and PE 7717/2026
outcome: Leave granted; appeal allowed on ground 1 (ground 2 not addressed). Resentenced: count 1, 12 months' imprisonment, recognisance release after 10 months, $2,000 bond; count 2, 12 months concurrent, parole eligible; backdated to 31/01/2026.
weight: Single judge (PALMER J) exercising appellate jurisdiction over the Magistrates Court under the Criminal Appeals Act 2004 (WA); Category B. The error was conceded and the law is settled: persuasive first-instance authority, not new law.
oneLine: A Commonwealth carriage-service charge dealt with summarily carries a 12-month cap under Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) s 4J(3)(a), so the 20-month term imposed on STACK was express error; the charge may need to proceed on indictment.
whatHappened: STACK, 33, was convicted on 15/04/2026 of using a carriage service to menace, harass or offend contrary to s 474.17(1) of the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth), and of breaching a Post Sentence Supervision Order contrary to s 74L of the Sentence Administration Act 2003 (WA). Between 14/01/2026 and 31/01/2026 he sent his former partner 30 to 40 texts a day and made 50 to 100 calls a day. STACK had 84 prior convictions for breaching restraining orders and was a declared serial family violence offender. The PSSO, issued on 03/09/2025, barred intimidating or abusive behaviour towards her. He was arrested on 31/01/2026 and pleaded guilty on 23/03/2026. SHACKLETON imposed 20 months for the Commonwealth count and 15 months concurrent for the PSSO breach, then on 11/05/2026 recalled STACK and replaced the parole order with a recognisance release order after 10 months. STACK appealed on jurisdictional excess and manifest excess.
whatHeld: Leave to appeal was granted on ground 1 and the appeal allowed; ground 2 was not addressed. Section 474.17(1) of the Commonwealth Criminal Code carries a maximum of 5 years, making it an indictable offence. Under s 4J(1) of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) such an offence may be dealt with summarily with the consent of prosecutor and defendant, and s 4J(3)(a) then caps the term of imprisonment at 12 months. Both parties consented to summary disposal; PALMER J observed that the Magistrate could have declined summary disposal. Imposing 20 months was express error. Applying Wallam v Dent, because a lesser sentence necessarily had to be imposed, there was a substantial miscarriage. On resentencing, the offending was aggravated by threats to kill, its persistence across two media over two weeks. A 25% early-plea discount applied.
whatItMeans: What it changes is what you flag. Lay a Commonwealth carriage-service charge under s 474.17(1) and, dealt with summarily, imprisonment is capped at 12 months — PALMER J said he would have imposed a more significant term had the matter gone on indictment. Prosecutor and accused must both consent, but the Magistrate may still refuse summary disposal; your brief shows how bad the conduct is. Persistence was proved by volume and spread. Download handset and app content, get the carrier records, and quantify the daily frequency rather than describing it. The Court quoted the messages verbatim — preserve the text, not a summary of it. Record the victim's words about feeling harassed, offended and fearful. On a PSSO breach, put the order in the brief. Identify the exact condition breached.
verdict: AWARENESS — the ruling corrects a sentencing jurisdiction error and applies settled law, changing nothing about how you investigate.

appealFrom: Court of Criminal Appeal of the Supreme Court of New South Wales (HAMILL J, CAMPBELL J and PRICE A-JA), orders of 09/04/2025
outcome: Appeal dismissed, 5:2. FARRUGIA's 11 years with a 7 year 6 month non-parole period stands. EDELMAN J would have allowed the appeal and remitted to the Court of Criminal Appeal; JAGOT J would have quashed the sentence and remitted to the District Court for re-sentencing.
weight: High Court, seven judges: GAGELER CJ, GORDON, STEWARD, GLEESON and BEECH-JONES JJ; EDELMAN J and JAGOT J dissenting. New on the materiality threshold, adapting Brawn v The King. The appeal statute and conduct rules are NSW; the conflict finding is fact-specific and contested 5:2.
oneLine: High Court dismisses FARRUGIA's sentence appeal 5:2, holding an error or irregularity vitiates a sentence only if it could realistically have affected the reasoning of the sentencing judge; no conflict was proved where one Senior Counsel appeared for both co-offenders.
whatHappened: FARRUGIA pleaded guilty in the Local Court on 28/09/2022 to conspiring to traffic a commercial quantity of controlled drugs between about 17/04/2013 and 07/10/2015. Co-offender KANMAZ pleaded guilty to the same conspiracy. Agreed Facts recorded FARRUGIA sourced and received drugs and moved cash for a share of profits, while KANMAZ stored drugs and cash and ran a front company for a wage. The CDPP submitted in writing that KANMAZ should receive the more substantial penalty; one Senior Counsel appeared for both and submitted the opposite — that FARRUGIA's offending was objectively more serious. The Crown conceded the point orally. On 08/12/2023 FARRUGIA received 11 years with a 7 year 6 month non-parole period; KANMAZ received 9 years with 6 years 6 months. FARRUGIA appealed, alleging Senior Counsel was conflicted, but adduced no evidence of his instructions and maintained legal professional privilege. The Court of Criminal Appeal dismissed the appeal.
whatHeld: Appeal dismissed 5:2. A materiality threshold applies before an error or procedural irregularity vitiates a sentence under ss 5(1)(c) and 6(3) of the Criminal Appeal Act 1912 (NSW): adapting Brawn v The King, whether it could realistically have affected the reasoning of the sentencing judge to the sentence that was imposed. Rule 35 of the Legal Profession Uniform Conduct (Barristers) Rules 2015 (NSW) bars acting without informed consent where there is a conflict or a real or substantial possibility of a conflict; but, per Mills v The Queen, proof will almost invariably require the client's instructions, whether by direct evidence or by inference. FARRUGIA did not discharge the burden. EDELMAN J and JAGOT J dissented: the rr 23, 35 and 42 duties do not depend on instructions, and put Senior Counsel in actual conflict once the Crown's written submissions arrived.
whatItMeans: No change to how you investigate. This is an NSW sentence appeal — treat its scaffolding as foreign and take the High Court principle, which travels. The offences were Commonwealth, prosecuted by the CDPP as in WA. What is worth your attention is how much work the Agreed Facts did. Everything in this appeal ran off a single document describing what each co-offender did. FARRUGIA got two years more than KANMAZ because the facts had him taking a share of the profits while KANMAZ was on a wage. When you have co-offenders, the factual document fixes their relative positions: particularise each person's role, reward, and the number and dates of transactions separately for each of them. That matters in multi-offender child abuse files, where relative culpability will be argued at sentence. Two of seven judges would have allowed the appeal, so a file could be re-opened years later on defence-counsel conduct outside your control — keep the brief airtight.
verdict: AWARENESS — an NSW appeal on counsel's conflicting duties and the materiality threshold; changes nothing you do in an investigation beyond particularising each co-offender's role.

appealFrom: Court of Criminal Appeal of the Supreme Court of New South Wales (WARD P, YEHIA and WEINSTEIN JJ)
outcome: Crown appeal dismissed, 5:2. The Court of Criminal Appeal's orders stand: KO's conviction quashed and the matter remitted to the District Court of New South Wales for retrial. STEWARD and GLEESON JJ would have allowed the appeal and restored the conviction.
weight: High Court of Australia, full bench of seven, split 5:2 (GAGELER CJ, GORDON, BEECH-JONES, EDELMAN and JAGOT JJ; STEWARD and GLEESON JJ dissenting). Binding nationally on the fault element of intention under the Criminal Code (Cth), confining and restating Smith and Afford.
oneLine: A High Court majority holds that proving an accused perceived a real or significant chance a consignment contained a substance does not prove he meant to import it; directions letting a jury slide between the two miscarried; KO gets a retrial.
whatHappened: KO was convicted by a District Court of New South Wales jury (Judge J SMITH) of attempting to import a commercial quantity of border controlled drugs, contrary to ss 11.1(1), 307.1(1) and 311.1(1)(f) of the Criminal Code (Cth), between about 06/09/2021 and 20/10/2021. A 600 kg dough mixer shipped from Toronto held 101 one-kilogram packages; Canadian authorities intercepted it, substituted an inert substance, and it reached an address linked to organiser Mr YANG. KO, a sales employee at freight forwarder EMO Trans Australia, allegedly arranged delivery using a phone in a false name and a laptop from YANG, avoiding his employer. A search warrant recovered both devices; police found no drugs, cash or suspicious transactions, and KO had no record. The defence said he was gullible, at most suspicious, and helping a friend. The Court of Criminal Appeal quashed the conviction over the intention directions and ordered a retrial; the Crown appealed.
whatHeld: Crown appeal dismissed, 5:2. The majority restated Smith v The Queen; R v Afford in three propositions: it is not sufficient to prove intention that the accused merely perceived a real or significant chance he was importing a substance; it is sufficient if that perception is coupled with 'even if the substance is in the object, I am prepared to take the object into Australia'; and a miscarriage may arise where directions leave a real risk the jury would treat awareness of the chance as enough. Here, the judge told the jury that, if satisfied KO perceived that chance, it was 'open' to infer intent, but never that they still had to go on to decide whether he meant to import the substance — a material miscarriage of justice. STEWARD and GLEESON JJ dissented, reading the summing up as adequate.
whatItMeans: Read this for the discipline, not the charge. It is Commonwealth Criminal Code importation law and changes nothing you lay under WA law. What travels is the gap between suspicion and intention. When you build a circumstantial case on someone's state of mind, gather material that shows purpose, not just awareness of a risk. The Crown could never pin down when KO's awareness became intention. Before you sign off a brief saying a suspect 'must have known', ask what actually proves he meant it. What carried: a phone in a false name and avoiding his own employer. What did not: a clean house and financial search — no drugs, cash or suspicious transactions. Record negative results; the defence will use them. The same trap sits behind inferred states of mind in Child Abuse Squad work — a non-offending adult's knowledge, or an accused's intent, in grooming cases. Gullibility and suspicion are not intent.
verdict: AWARENESS — a Commonwealth fault-element decision; it does not change how you investigate or charge, but proof of suspicion is not proof of intention.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Mehrabi v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (Sweeney DCJ), IND 123 of 2023
outcome: Leave to appeal granted on grounds 1 and 3; leave refused on ground 2; appeal dismissed. Convictions on all 21 counts upheld.
weight: Strong. Unanimous in result — QUINLAN CJ and FIANNACA J granted leave on grounds 1 and 3 and dismissed the appeal; THOMSON P would have refused leave on every ground but agreed the appeal failed. Court of Appeal authority directly on s 319(2)(a) causation and the availability of s 24 in drug-facilitated cases. The Court expressly declined to decide whether s 24 can ever apply to fraud-vitiated consent, and treated the counterfactual discussion in HES as obiter, confined to representation-of-fact cases.
oneLine: WA Court of Appeal upholds MEHRABI's 21 convictions, confirming that where a complainant's apparent consent is obtained by covertly drugging her, the State need only prove the drug played a 'material role' in her decision — not a counterfactual — and that honest/reasonable mistake was not available.
whatHappened: Following a jury trial in the District Court before Sweeney DCJ, Farzam MEHRABI was convicted of 21 offences against six young women he met on Tinder and Bumble between February and March 2022. The convictions included four counts of administering a stupefying drug (MDMA) with intent to facilitate an indictable offence, 12 counts of sexual penetration without consent, two counts of unlawful and indecent assault, and three counts of unlawfully impeding breathing (choking Ms POTTER and Ms TURNER). MEHRABI covertly gave several women MDMA (confirmed by blood and hair follicle testing), then engaged in sexual activity. Some complainants said they consciously refused; two (Ms CAMPBELL and Ms TURNER) could not remember or described being 'sluggish' and 'half-aware'. MEHRABI gave evidence claiming consent or honest and reasonable belief in consent. The trial judge directed the jury on three ways the State could prove absence of consent: conscious non-consent, incapacity through intoxication, and consent obtained by deceit or fraudulent means (secret drugging) under Criminal Code (WA) s 319(2)(a). MEHRABI appealed on three grounds concerning these directions.
whatHeld: The Court granted leave on grounds 1 and 3 but dismissed the appeal; Thomson P would have refused leave on all grounds but agreed the appeal failed. Ground 1 (tendency): all three 'pathways' were probative of the same tendency — a tendency to engage in sexual acts with a woman without her free and voluntary consent — and covert drugging was 'particularly probative' given the premeditation. Ground 3 (causation): the direction that the drug must have played a 'material role' in the complainant's decision to consent was correct and sufficient. Where deceit distorts the decision-making capacity itself (rather than distorting information), it is neither necessary nor appropriate to pose the counterfactual of whether the complainant would have consented absent the drug. The Court held the counterfactual approach in HES v The State of Western Australia was obiter and confined to cases involving a representation of fact. Ground 2 (mistake): where consent was obtained by deceitfully drugging the complainant, there was no evidentiary basis for a s 24 honest and reasonable mistake defence — given MEHRABI's knowledge of MDMA's effects, no such belief could be honest or reasonable. The Court declined to decide whether s 24 could ever apply to fraud-vitiated consent.
whatItMeans: For your casework on drug-facilitated sexual assault, this decision strengthens how you build and frame the consent element. You do not need to establish what a victim 'would have done' had she not been drugged — that counterfactual is incoherent where the drug itself distorted her decision-making. Focus your evidence on proving the covert administration and that the drug played a material role in any apparent consent. That makes forensic testing and expert pharmacology evidence important: here, blood and hair follicle results positive for MDMA formed the basis of the drugging counts, and Professor DRUMMER's evidence that MDMA increases sexual desire and can reduce a person's ability to resist sexual advances supported that pathway. Secure toxicology samples promptly; a hair sample taken many months later still confirmed exposure over a period, though not purity or dose. Do not let the science displace the complainants — the Court itself observed that the case was most likely decided on the credibility and accuracy of their accounts, not on the drug pathway — so take detailed statements early. Where a suspect knows the effects of the drug he secretly administered, expect the honest-and-reasonable-mistake defence to fall away. Charging the administering-a-stupefying-drug counts also matters for tendency: the Court treated covert drugging as particularly probative of the tendency because of the premeditation involved.
verdict: ACTION — it directly shapes how you evidence and charge drug-facilitated sexual offences: prove covert administration and a material role, not a counterfactual, and secure the toxicology and expert pharmacology evidence early.
flags: The Court expressly did NOT decide whether s 24 (honest and reasonable mistake) can ever apply where consent is obtained by deceit or fraudulent means — it held only that s 24 had no application on these facts.
Thomson P dissented on whether leave should be granted (he would refuse leave on all grounds) but agreed the appeal should be dismissed.

Section numbers for the substantive charges (s 325 sexual penetration, s 323 indecent assault) appear only in Thomson P's reasons; the catchwords cite s 24 and s 319(2)(a). Confirm exact charging sections against the indictment.
MEHRABI was acquitted of count 15 (administering a drug to Ms VARGAS) and pleaded guilty to the three 'offer to supply' counts (1, 5, 14), which were not tried.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Fletcher v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (GETHING DCJ), IND 484 of 2023
outcome: Leave granted; appeal allowed; sentence set aside and appellant resentenced to identical terms (3 years, 2 years 6 months and 5 years, concurrent - total effective 5 years, parole eligible) but backdated to 03/06/2023, crediting the 87 lost days. Application to adduce additional evidence refused.
weight: Court of Appeal (HALL, ARCHER and SWEENEY JJA), unanimous judgment, Category A. Binding WA appellate authority: substandard conditions suffered by a prison population generally are not mitigatory. The court held the 1999 decision in Bekink has been overtaken by recent authority.
oneLine: Court of Appeal resentenced FLETCHER after an 87-day backdating error and held that substandard prison conditions endured by inmates generally, including the well-publicised lockdowns at Hakea, cannot be treated as a mitigating factor; only hardship personal to the offender counts.
whatHappened: FLETCHER pleaded guilty on 08/07/2024 to two counts of criminal damage by fire (arson) and one of attempted criminal damage by fire, all committed in the early hours of 01/08/2022. His girlfriend Ms OLNEY had left him to stay with her friend Mr HARRIS. Over 30/07/2022 and 31/07/2022 FLETCHER sent OLNEY escalating threats ('Derek's first'; 'Your dog is dead') and at 23.56 made a call from a private number that OLNEY recorded; at 01.20 he texted 'Brace yourself bye'. At about 02.40 he lit two Molotov cocktails on HARRIS's timber verandah at Redcliffe. At 03.37, CCTV at Mr DYER's Belmont address captured him and an unknown companion pouring petrol over three cars and lighting two Molotov cocktails at the end of a petrol trail that never ignited. At about 04.05 he doused and burnt Mr CLARK's car at Carlisle; the fire spread to the roof of the Department of Communities unit, causing $164,343.85 damage, and CLARK escaped. Police arrested him at 10.08 on 05/08/2022 and seized whisky bottles, scissors and a cut T-shirt; cell tower data placed his phone at each scene. GETHING DCJ imposed a total effective 5 years on 22/10/2024, backdated to 30/08/2023 on erroneous advice; the correct backdate was 03/06/2023, leaving 87 days uncredited.
whatHeld: Leave granted, appeal allowed. The State conceded that the misapprehension about the backdate produced a miscarriage of justice; the sentence was set aside and FLETCHER resentenced afresh under s 31 of the Criminal Appeals Act 2004 (WA). The question was whether poor conditions at Hakea Prison could mitigate. The court held they cannot. Reviewing Milenkovski (BUSS JA's distilled principles), Bekink, the court found no support in WA authority for treating conditions suffered by inmates as mitigatory; what mitigates is that an offender, for reasons personal to him, will find prison materially more arduous than the general prison population. Bekink 'has been overtaken by this recent authority'. On the additional material, the test is whether, had it been before the sentencing judge, a different sentence should have been imposed; an appellant is bound by the choices made below and must explain non-disclosure. Most of FLETCHER's material was already before GETHING DCJ (his PTSD, the rescue of Mr HARTZENBERG, the courses, his faith), and the fresh material, including missing his mother's death, did not show hardship personal to him. Family hardship is not mitigatory unless exceptional. The application was refused and identical sentences imposed, backdated to 03/06/2023.
whatItMeans: The holding is a sentencing one and it does not change how you investigate. First, this offending was proved by material an investigator captures or loses: both sides of the message exchange, CCTV, cell tower data, and a search. When FLETCHER complained that only his messages appeared in the statement of material facts, the answer was that screenshots showing both sides were in the tendered brief, which let the judge see not one of her messages was threatening. Download and exhibit the whole thread, not the extracts that suit the charge, because the defence will build provocation out of what you left out. Second, treat threats to property and to pets in a family violence context as escalation: the court characterised this offending as coercive control, punishing the girlfriend by punishing her friends. Third, this appeal existed only because the custody dates were wrong - the appellant challenged the Sentencing Information Unit figure at sentencing and both counsel contradicted him. Keep custody, remand and bail records accurate and legible in your file. The read-across to child abuse work is limited, but the evidence principle bites: get everything relevant before the sentencing court the first time, because an appellate court will not reopen forensic choices made below.
verdict: AWARENESS - a sentence appeal correcting a backdating error and settling that poor prison conditions are not mitigatory. It changes nothing, though the message thread and custody dates belong in the brief.

appealFrom: Magistrates Court of Western Australia (MAGISTRATE C STOCKDALE), PE 23590 of 2025 and PE 43762 of 2025
outcome: Leave refused (grounds 1, 3); granted and allowed (ground 2). The $1,000 costs order is set aside and reassessed at $4,800: $3,000 (assault), $1,800 (bail). No order as to appeal costs.
weight: Single judge (SOLOMON J) exercising appellate jurisdiction, delivered extemporaneously and edited from transcript; Category B. Applies settled costs principles but corrects a common misreading of the 2024 costs determination.
oneLine: Where family violence charges were dismissed for want of prosecution, SOLOMON J set aside a $1,000 costs award because the magistrate wrongly treated the sum claimed as the costs determination's maximum; costs reassessed at $4,800.
whatHappened: Shaddon Murry BIN SAAD was charged (PE 23590/2025) with unlawfully assaulting the complainant on 20/04/2025 and doing her bodily harm in circumstances of aggravation (a family relationship), contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 317(1)(b). At Karratha Magistrates Court that day he was granted bail on condition he not contact the protected person or go within 25 metres of her; he was further charged (PE 43762/2025) with breaching it. Legal Aid appeared at the early mentions and at all three appearances on the assault charge between 01/07 and 11/11/2025; from 01/07/2025 BIN SAAD also had counsel, Mr MACFARLANE. The assault charge was dismissed for want of prosecution on 11/11/2025 (the complainant no longer wishing to give evidence); the bail charge likewise on 26/11/2025. BIN SAAD sought costs of $3,256 (assault) and $1,540 (bail); MAGISTRATE STOCKDALE awarded $1,000 across both on 02/12/2025, and he appealed that quantum on three grounds.
whatHeld: Leave was refused (grounds 1, 3); granted, appeal allowed (ground 2). Leave requires a ground with a real, rational and logical prospect of succeeding. Grounds 1 and 3 failed: the reasons were adequate; counsel's work, not Legal Aid funding, failed to justify the claim. Ground 2 succeeded. A successful accused is entitled to costs under the Official Prosecutions (Accused's Costs) Act 1973 (WA), assessed under the Legal Profession (Official Prosecutions) (Accused's Costs) Determination 2024, whose Item 6 allows an amount which is reasonable in the circumstances - it fixes no maximum. The magistrate twice treated the sums claimed as the 'maximum amounts' - a central error, not mere infelicity. Assessing afresh with a broad brush, SOLOMON J fixed $3,000 and $1,800.
whatItMeans: This costs-quantum appeal shows what happens when a family violence prosecution collapses. A summary charge dismissed for want of prosecution makes the accused a successful accused, generally entitled to costs unless certain circumstances disentitle - here $4,800 across two charges. First, build the family violence brief so it does not stand or fall on the complainant's willingness to testify - body-worn video, injury photographs, medical records, triple-zero audio, admissions and independent witnesses survive a withdrawal. Second, timing matters: preparation for the assault trial, already payable, came just over a month before the listed date and two weeks before discontinuance. If a matter is going nowhere because your complainant has withdrawn, tell the prosecutor early rather than let it drift - the same applies to Child Abuse Squad work.
verdict: AWARENESS - a costs ruling correcting a magistrate's misreading of the 2024 costs determination; changes nothing about how you investigate or charge.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Forth v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: Supreme Court of Western Australia (QUINLAN CJ), INS 14 of 2023
outcome: Leave to appeal granted; appeal against sentence dismissed. The 9-year term for manslaughter (reduced from 10 years for totality) stands, as does the total effective sentence of 12 years' imprisonment.
weight: Court of Appeal (THOMSON P, MITCHELL JA and VAUGHAN JA) — unanimous, binding WA appellate authority applying settled manifest-excess principles from Kabambi to its own facts. Category B.
oneLine: FORTH was not present when Cassius TURVEY was beaten to death, but the Court of Appeal held his culpability under Criminal Code (WA) s 8 was substantial — absence from the fatal acts brings no substantial further mitigation — so 9 years stands.
whatHappened: FORTH, then 24, joined a group who on 09/10/2022 went looking for boys said to be about to 'mob' a 14-year-old associate, forcing Seth FLINN into a car under threat of a knife (count 1), then chasing, bashing and detaining Lucas SHEEAN, 15, warning him not to talk (counts 2 and 3). On 13/10/2022 FORTH and Jack BREARLEY broke trolley poles off with an axe as weapons and Brodie PALMER took knuckledusters; the three confronted schoolchildren walking about after school. BREARLEY, armed with a pole, hit Nick TRAILL, 13, on crutches (count 4); the trial judge found FORTH unarmed but aware BREARLEY was armed. FORTH took TRAILL's crutches and hat (count 5, guilty plea 02/12/2024). They chased the fleeing children across a grassed area; BREARLEY and PALMER ran into bushland; FORTH stopped at the creek line, ran up to Lloyd Street, yelling 'get him'. BREARLEY struck Cassius TURVEY, 15, repeatedly on the head with the pole; he died on 23/10/2022. BREARLEY and PALMER were convicted of murder (life; 22- and 18-year minimums); FORTH of manslaughter under Criminal Code (WA) s 8, sentenced by QUINLAN CJ to 9 years within a 12-year total effective sentence. He appealed only on manifest excess.
whatHeld: Leave granted; appeal dismissed. Applying Kabambi v The State of Western Australia, the question on an implied-error ground is whether the end result is so unreasonable or plainly unjust that a substantial wrong must have occurred, judged against the maximum penalty (life imprisonment), sentencing standards and his circumstances. There is no tariff for manslaughter. The closest comparable was Hishmeh v The State of Western Australia — an s 8 offender who did not strike the deceased — where an 11-year starting point stood under a then 20-year maximum; the present offending was distinctly more serious and carried no plea discount. The Queensland decisions R v Oram; R v Hinds and R v Broadby were of no assistance: for State offences the comparable cases are those of this Court, not interstate sentences imposed in a different statutory context. On seriousness the Court pointed to FORTH's knowledge that weapons were being prepared, his maintenance of the purpose by yelling 'get him', and his affirmation in the celebratory video. His culpability was substantial: that he did not do the acts which killed is already substantially reflected in the manslaughter conviction, so it brings no substantial further mitigation.
whatItMeans: This is a sentence appeal, but it shows what evidence keeps a peripheral offender high on the scale when someone else strikes the fatal blow. FORTH never touched TURVEY, yet three strands carried his culpability: proof he knew BREARLEY was armed — he had helped break the trolley poles off with an axe and had been shown PALMER's knuckledusters; an independent witness, Ms ALI, who heard 'get him' and placed it on the man in the tradie shirt; and post-offence conduct, the video made hours later proclaiming 'We got 'em all'. Treat that as the checklist on any group-violence job: establish who knew who was armed and when, canvass hard for uninvolved bystanders who saw or heard the encouragement (and record what they say the offender was wearing), and secure phones and devices for celebration content before it is deleted. The Court put it objectively: that an innocent person might be targeted should have been obvious to FORTH, given the SHEEAN incident days earlier — so do not work the preceding week's detentions and assaults as separate small jobs. Note also that the group disposed of the poles and TRAILL's crutches and hat: anticipate that, and cover disposal routes early.
verdict: AWARENESS — a manifest excess appeal applying settled Kabambi principles to its facts; useful for the s 8 culpability point, but it changes nothing you do at a scene or in interview.

appealFrom: Supreme Court of South Australia (Court of Appeal)
outcome: Appeal dismissed; convictions on counts 2 and 4 upheld. The covert recording was lawfully made and properly admitted.
weight: High Court of Australia, unanimous five-Justice bench — highest authority, but interpreting South Australian legislation, so persuasive rather than binding on WA provisions.
oneLine: High Court held a wife's covert recording of her husband admitting to raping her while she slept was reasonably necessary to protect her lawful interests and so was lawfully made and admissible.
whatHappened: POTTER (a pseudonym) stood trial in the District Court of SA on four counts of rape against his wife, the allegation being that he had sex with her without consent while she was asleep. He was convicted on counts 2 and 4. Before count 4 occurred, on 14/12/2019 the complainant used her mobile phone to covertly record a conversation in which POTTER admitted "I sexually assaulted you" and "I started having sex with you when you were asleep". Her stated reason was to remind herself never to return to him. The trial judge admitted the recording; the SA Court of Appeal split, with the majority (S Doyle and David JJA) holding the statutory exception was not met but wrongly admitting it as a discretion to admit unlawfully obtained evidence, while Kourakis CJ held the exception was met. POTTER appealed to the High Court.
whatHeld: The High Court (five Justices, unanimous) dismissed the appeal, upholding the Crown's notice of contention. It held the making of the recording was reasonably necessary for the protection of the complainant's lawful interests under s 4(2)(a)(ii) of the Surveillance Devices Act 2016 (SA), so it was not prohibited by s 4(1) and was properly admitted. Key points: "lawful interests" is wider than legal rights, title, duty or liability and is akin to legitimate interests, applied case-by-case. "Reasonably necessary" does not mean "essential" — it is enough that the use was appropriate to protect the interest; a proportionality/"reasonably appropriate and adapted" test was rejected. The assessment is objective but judged on the circumstances the recording party faced at the time, with the person's reasons informing but not determining the analysis. The relevant lawful interest was correctly characterised as the complainant's right to bodily autonomy and integrity and not being raped — an interest deserving "the very strongest protection" — not merely her interest in ending the relationship. Given she was vulnerable, still living with POTTER, had been raped repeatedly, the recording was an appropriate powerful reminder of the peril she faced. The Court also confirmed that once the exception is not met, there is no discretion to admit such evidence — the SDA excludes it (s 12(1)).
whatItMeans: This is a South Australian statute, so it does not bind you directly — WA is governed by the Surveillance Devices Act 1998 (WA), which has its own s 5(3)(d) "protection of lawful interests" exception (and, unlike SA, generally requires a principal party's consent). Treat this as strong persuasive authority on how courts read the "reasonably necessary for the protection of lawful interests" exception. For your casework it means a complainant's covert recording of an offender's admissions may be lawfully made and admissible where it protects a serious interest such as bodily integrity or safety from further offending — even if the complainant made it only as a "note to herself" and not for a prosecution. The test is appropriate, not essential: the fact the complainant could have gone to police, or made a written note instead, does not defeat it. When you receive a victim's covert recording, gather evidence of why and when it was made and the circumstances they faced, because that drives admissibility. Remember the mirror risk: recordings made to trap, pressure or gain leverage (rather than to protect an interest) will not qualify. Also note that if the exception is not satisfied there is no discretion to save the recording — confirm the WA equivalent before relying on any covert recording.
verdict: AWARENESS-level: this interprets SA legislation, not WA law, but gives authoritative High Court guidance on the "reasonably necessary for protection of lawful interests" test that WA courts will find persuasive when assessing covert recordings.
flags: Case interprets the SA Surveillance Devices Act 2016; the WA equivalent is the Surveillance Devices Act 1998 (WA) and differs (e.g. WA generally requires a principal party's consent) — check WA provisions before relying on this.
Party anonymised by pseudonym (POTTER); complainant not named.
The precise standard of proof point: prosecution bears the onus on the balance of probabilities to establish the facts satisfying the exception.

appealFrom: Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Queensland
outcome: Appeal allowed. Orders 2 and 3 of the Queensland Court of Appeal (15/08/2025) set aside; in their place, the appeal to the Court of Appeal dismissed, restoring the sentencing judge's decision that no special circumstances existed.
weight: High authority — unanimous five-member High Court decision (Gageler CJ, Edelman, Gleeson, Jagot and Beech-Jones JJ), binding nationally on the standard of appellate review, though the specific provisions are Queensland youth-justice law.
oneLine: The High Court held an appellate court cannot overturn a sentencing judge's finding that no "special circumstances" existed under s 227(2) of the Youth Justice Act 1992 (Qld) unless the House v The King standard of judicial restraint is met.
whatHappened: On 26/12/2022, HCZ (aged 17 years and eight months) and companions decided to commit theft and entered the Lovells' unlocked home in North Lakes, Queensland. HCZ, armed with a knife, was confronted and pushed outside. In the ensuing struggle he struck out with the knife, stabbed Mrs Lovell in the chest (a 13cm wound penetrating her heart) and stabbed Mr Lovell in the back, then kicked Mr Lovell in the face. Mrs Lovell died. HCZ lied to police and had blood splatter on his shorts. The knife handle was found in a lounge chair at the house where he was staying and the broken blade on the Lovells' front lawn; the Lovells' DNA was on his shoes, under his fingernails and on the tip of the blade, his and Mrs Lovell's DNA on the base of the blade, and his fingerprints and DNA on the Lovells' doorway and his fingerprints on their bedroom door. He pleaded guilty to burglary, murder, unlawful wounding with intent, and assault causing bodily harm in company. The sentencing judge found the murder "particularly heinous" under s 176(3)(b)(ii), imposed 14 years' detention, and concluded no "special circumstances" existed under s 227(2) to reduce the default 70% period before release. The Court of Appeal majority reduced the pre-release period to 60%, finding the judge let the seriousness of offending overwhelm mitigating factors. The Crown appealed to the High Court.
whatHeld: The High Court unanimously allowed the appeal. It held the applicable standard of appellate review of a decision under s 227(2) is the standard involving judicial restraint, restricting intervention to the five House v The King grounds, not a correctness standard. Determining the standard is a question of statutory interpretation; because s 227(2) turns on what the court "considers" special having regard to all the circumstances, using open-ended evaluative criteria that tolerate a range of outcomes, judicial restraint applies. The only available basis for the Court of Appeal to interfere was that the finding was unreasonable or plainly unjust (the fifth House ground). It was not. There was nothing about HCZ's early guilty pleas, deprived upbringing, or rehabilitation prospects that made it plainly unjust for the judge to find no special circumstances, particularly given the seriousness of the murder. The weighing of mitigating factors was a matter for the sentencing judge, and the decision tolerated a range of outcomes.
whatItMeans: This is a sentencing and appellate-review decision, so it does not change how you investigate or gather evidence. Its relevance is awareness: it confirms that where a discretionary sentencing determination turns on open-ended evaluative criteria (like "special circumstances"), a sentencing judge's conclusion is hard to disturb on appeal and will stand unless it is unreasonable or plainly unjust. For your casework, note the strength of the evidence brief mattered: the guilty pleas carried less mitigating weight because they were made against an "overwhelmingly strong Crown case" built on CCTV, DNA, fingerprints, and the recovered knife. Thorough forensic linking of an offender to the scene and weapon supports both conviction and the Crown's position at sentence.
verdict: AWARENESS only — this clarifies the appellate standard for reviewing discretionary sentencing findings and does not alter investigative or charging practice.
flags: Provisions applied are Queensland law (Youth Justice Act 1992 (Qld), Criminal Code (Qld)); confirm equivalent WA provisions before relying on the substantive scheme.
This is a sentencing/appellate-standard judgment with no direct bearing on WA investigative procedure.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Maitland (a pseudonym) v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (BLACK DCJ)
outcome: Extension of time granted. Leave to appeal granted on grounds 1 and 2, refused on grounds 3, 4 and 5. Appeal allowed on totality; sentences set aside and resentenced from 10 years 6 months to 8 years 6 months' imprisonment, parole eligible, commencing 26/10/2022.
weight: Court of Appeal (QUINLAN CJ, MAZZA JA and SWEENEY JA), unanimous joint judgment, Category B. Binding in WA, applying settled principle on totality, manifest excess and mitigation. Its novel contribution is the correction of the sentencing judge's view that structured risk-assessment tools are 'pure logic'.
oneLine: Court of Appeal cut a 10-year-6-month family violence sentence to 8 years 6 months on totality, holding that on these facts neither the 'toxic' relationship nor finding his partner with another man mitigated, and correcting the judge's view that risk-assessment tools are 'pure logic'.
whatHappened: MAITLAND (a pseudonym) was served on 07/10/2021 with a two-year family violence restraining order protecting Ms Eve BARNARD (a pseudonym), his on-off partner. The order did not bar contact or communication; it barred him from her home or within 30 metres of it. At about 7.00 am on 28/08/2022 MAITLAND entered the caravan in BARNARD's South Hedland backyard and found her with Mr Nicholas HARRIS (a pseudonym). He punched HARRIS to the head and face (count 1, assault occasioning bodily harm, Criminal Code (WA) s 317(1)(b)); HARRIS fled. MAITLAND pulled BARNARD from under the bed, punched her repeatedly, fracturing her eye socket (count 2, aggravated assault occasioning bodily harm, s 317(1)(a)), strangled her until she almost lost consciousness (count 3, aggravated strangulation, s 298(b)), then forcefully digitally penetrated her vagina (count 4, aggravated sexual penetration without consent, s 326). He was bailed. On 05/11/2022, still bound by the FVRO and bail, he entered her house through an unlocked sliding door, demanded her car key and phone and punched her to the mouth (count 5). He pleaded guilty on 19/07/2024; BLACK DCJ sentenced him on 23/12/2024 to a total effective 10 years 6 months. He appealed sentence on five grounds.
whatHeld: Appeal allowed on totality. Ground 1 failed: 6 years was 'at the high end of the range... but not outside it'. On these facts neither the 'toxic' relationship nor finding BARNARD with another man mitigated, though it 'is not the law' that confronting infidelity 'could never be mitigatory' in an assault case; that is 'very fact-driven'. 'A vast rationalisation' was the Court's own phrase; Gomboc was distinguished, not applied. No provocation defence was run: MAITLAND pleaded guilty and raised it only in mitigation. The ss 245-247 discussion (assault must be an element; s 281 repealed 2008: Hart, Moffa) was scope, not unavailability. There is no hierarchy of seriousness by type of penetration. Ground 3 failed (Skelly). Grounds 4 and 5 failed because no miscarriage arose: her Honour's risk finding was no less favourable than the reports'. Whether she could substitute it the Court left undecided, noting further that the tools are 'more than pure logic'. Ground 2 succeeded: the total did not bear a proper relationship to the overall criminality (Kabambi); her Honour's sentencing comments made no reference to MAITLAND's dysfunctional upbringing, 'apart from his pleas of guilty' the most powerful factor in mitigation.
whatItMeans: This is sentencing law - nothing changes how you interview, caution or charge. Three things are worth carrying into family violence briefs. First, put the terms of the FVRO in the brief: it did not bar contact or communication, only intimidatory, offensive or emotionally abusive behaviour, entry to her home or within 30 metres. Mitigation was argued on that misreading. He had to comply even if she invited him to attend, so 'she asked me to come' is no answer to a breach. Second, strangulation often leaves very few marks even where life-threatening, and injury may not be visible to the naked eye - vision and hearing changes, sore throat, paralysis, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, dissociation and suicidality. If you record what you can see, you under-record the offence. Ask about those symptoms and get them into the statement and medical evidence. Third, the brief is what tests the mitigation story: the sentencing judge measured the claimed reconciliation against BARNARD's statements on the brief and his own account, and on appeal the Court assumed intimacy in his favour and it changed nothing. Download the phone and take a statement covering the relationship history and contact she initiated, not just the incident.
verdict: AWARENESS — a totality resentencing applying settled principle; it changes no investigative practice. But the strangulation passage and the Court's parsing of the FVRO terms are worth carrying into family violence briefs.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
appealFrom: Supreme Court of Western Australia (SOLOMON J), CIV 1094 of 2026
outcome: Oral adjournment application refused; stay dismissed on the Housing Authority's undertaking not to remove ROE's belongings pending appeal; costs reserved; time to file the appellant's case extended to 4.00 pm on 12/08/2026, under a self-executing order dismissing the appeal with costs on non-compliance.
weight: Court of Appeal (MITCHELL and VAUGHAN JJA), joint reasons, on an interlocutory stay application. Appellate authority in WA, but the stay principles were treated as well established, and the decision was marked Category B. Civil residential tenancy and judicial review — no criminal content.
oneLine: Court of Appeal refuses to stay an already-executed eviction order — a stay has no utility once its operation is complete — confirming Magistrates Court evictions are reviewable only for jurisdictional error or denial of natural justice under Residential Tenancies Act 1987 (WA) s 26(2).
whatHappened: ROSEMARY ROE leased residential premises in North Fremantle from the Housing Authority under a tenancy agreement dated 05/08/2013. On 13/06/2024 the Authority gave ROE a breach notice under s 61 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1987 (WA) stating $6,734.79 in rent arrears. On 06/08/2024 it served a notice of termination requiring vacant possession by 22/08/2024. ROE did not pay; asked why, she said that as a sovereign Aboriginal woman she had a right to ask colonisers to 'come to an agreement'. On 10/12/2025, on the Authority's application under s 71, Magistrate HOCKTON terminated the agreement and ordered possession by 4.00 pm on 30/01/2026 (the Eviction Order). ROE sought statutory judicial review in the General Division under s 36 of the Magistrates Court Act 2004 (WA); SOLOMON J dismissed it on 20/04/2026. A Property (Seizure and Delivery) Order — Real Property issued the next day, and possession was seized on 27/05/2026. ROE had commenced this appeal on 11/05/2026. Told by the Court of Appeal office on 25/05/2026 that the appeal did not stop the eviction, she did not lodge her stay application until 02/06/2026 and had still not filed an appellant's case by the 22/07/2026 hearing.
whatHeld: Stay dismissed, adjournment refused, time to file the appellant's case extended under a self-executing order. No appeal lies from the Magistrates Court to the Court of Appeal; the power to stay instead lay in the court's implicit jurisdiction and O 56A r 3(3)(d) of the Rules of the Supreme Court 1971 (WA), which preserves appellate jurisdiction. Three considerations govern a stay: whether it is necessary to preserve the subject matter of the appeal — whether the appeal would otherwise be rendered nugatory — the appeal's prospects, and the balance of convenience. ROE applied only after the Eviction Order had been fully executed: a stay would not oblige the Authority to return possession, and the balance of convenience — an uninhabitable property, and no evidence of impact on ROE or of alternative accommodation — ran against her. By s 26(2) of the RT Act the primary judge could set the Eviction Order aside only for jurisdictional error or a denial of natural justice, adopting SEAWARD J in Re Magistrate Trevor Darge; Ex parte Snook. Rent-calculation and non-prescribed-form complaints were not jurisdictional, and the transcript disclosed no denial of procedural fairness.
whatItMeans: Nothing here changes how you investigate, caution, search or charge. It is a civil interlocutory ruling in a residential tenancy judicial review with no bearing on child abuse work. Two points transfer. First, timing: an appeal does not of itself stop enforcement. ROE was told exactly that by the Court of Appeal office on 25/05/2026, but lodged her stay six days after possession was seized, by which time the Court held there was nothing left to stay and the bailiff nothing left to restore. If you ever need an order preserving property or a state of affairs, it has to be in before the event, not after. Second, the Court held ROE's draft grounds proceeded on the incorrect assumption that she was entitled to procedural fairness before the Eviction Order was enforced — enforcing a court order is not a fresh hearing. The Court did not decide whether the seizure order was defectively issued or executed; even a defect could not have founded the appeal against SOLOMON J. The magistrate's rejection of her sovereign-Aboriginal-woman argument, and of her age, health, single parenthood and the environment around the premises as reasons to withhold rent, was also left undisturbed.
verdict: AWARENESS — a civil stay ruling in a residential tenancy judicial review that does not change how you investigate, gather evidence or charge.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Marco v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: Supreme Court of Western Australia (WHITBY J), IND 41 of 2023
outcome: Both applications for bail pending appeal dismissed (CACR 134 of 2025 and CACR 135 of 2025); MARCO remains in custody on the 14-year total effective sentence pending his conviction and sentence appeals.
weight: Single judge of the Court of Appeal (SEAWARD JA) refusing interlocutory bail; Category B, turns on its own facts. Applies settled bail principle. SEAWARD JA left ground 2 open for a three-judge coram — the interaction between intent to defraud and s 409(3), as raised here, does not appear to have been judicially considered in this State.
oneLine: SEAWARD JA refused MARCO bail pending appeal against 43 fraud convictions and 14 years' imprisonment: neither ground was strongly arguable enough to be an exceptional reason — whether intent to 'make good' bears on intent to defraud under Criminal Code (WA) s 409 remains open.
whatHappened: MARCO was convicted by a Supreme Court jury on 04/09/2025, after trial before WHITBY J, of 37 offences of fraud and six of aggravated fraud contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 409(1)(a) and s 409(1)(g), the aggravation being a victim aged 60 or over. On 30/10/2025 he was sentenced to a total effective 14 years' imprisonment with parole eligibility. The 43 counts involved nine complainants. The State's case was that MARCO held himself out as a private investor with access to overseas 'private placement programs', each investment documented in a declaration of trust. The deceit was particularised as a representation that he would invest the money in a program straight away or within a few days and would not use it for any other purpose — false, because no such programs existed. The State relied on the complainants, MARCO's bank statements and forensic accountant Mr LANGRIDGE, who traced the money to operational costs and repayments to other investors. MARCO's case was genuine belief: $11 million had gone overseas on 31 occasions, he never missed an interest payment, and performance stopped only when ASIC froze his accounts. He appealed conviction and sentence, and on 04/06/2026 applied for bail pending both.
whatHeld: Both bail applications dismissed. Clause 4A of sch 1 pt C of the Bail Act 1982 (WA) creates a rebuttable presumption against bail for an appellant in custody; bail may only be granted where there are exceptional reasons. Where prospects of success are relied on, the grounds must be strongly arguable and the appeal most likely to succeed (Serukai and Lawson). On ground 2 — the direction that whether MARCO intended to make good, or did make good, was irrelevant to intent to defraud — SEAWARD JA held the direction disclosed no clear error of law on its face. None of Ali, Markarian or Sayed considered the interaction between intent to defraud and s 409(3). The trial judge had put MARCO's genuine-belief case and payment record to the jury, and whether MARCO's belief matched the prosecution case as particularised was itself a live issue. SEAWARD JA declined to decide the point; it may be made out before a three-judge coram. Ground 3 (s 112 Criminal Procedure Act 2004 (WA), applying Greenaway) also failed: read as a whole, the directions identified the deceit alleged and MARCO's case, unlike Greenaway.
whatItMeans: This is an interlocutory bail refusal, and SEAWARD JA declined to decide the legal question underneath it. First, particulars discipline the whole case. The State particularised the deceit narrowly — that MARCO represented he would invest the money straight away or within a few days and would not use it for any other purpose — while his answer was pitched at the general level that he believed in the programs. That mismatch became a live appeal issue. When you draft a statement of material facts, pin the act down to what was said or done, to whom, when and in what document; a loose particular gives the defence room to answer a case you never ran. Second, get the suspect's account of his own state of mind on the record early. The jury here was directed it could use what MARCO said in his interview with Ben HARVEY and what he told ASIC investigators on 01/11/2018 in deciding what his intention was. Those contemporaneous accounts are the material a tribunal reasons from. Finally, a convicted person in custody faces a presumption against bail pending appeal, and the strength of the grounds will rarely displace it.
verdict: AWARENESS — an interlocutory bail refusal that leaves the s 409(3) question for a three-judge coram; it changes nothing about how you investigate. The particularisation point is worth carrying into your briefs.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Humble v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (WALLACE DCJ), IND 1747 of 2023
outcome: Application for bail pending determination of the conviction appeal, brought as an alternative to an expedited hearing, dismissed. Neither conviction ground was found strongly arguable; HUMBLE remains in custody on the 6-year aggravated home burglary sentence.
weight: Single judge of the Court of Appeal (THOMSON P), an interlocutory bail application, delivered ex tempore and edited from the court's record; Category B. Conviction-ground views are preliminary and do not bind the appeal court. Useful on the exceptional-reasons threshold, not the substantive grounds.
oneLine: THOMSON P refused bail pending appeal to a former police officer convicted of aggravated home burglary, posing as police with a fake search warrant, holding none of his conviction grounds was strongly arguable enough to be an 'exceptional reason' under the Bail Act 1982 (WA).
whatHappened: HUMBLE was a former police officer, having left the force before the 09/09/2022 offences. The State alleged he impersonated police and sought to execute a fake search warrant at the complainant's house. In an electronic record of interview HUMBLE accepted he was to be paid $25,000 to inflict serious harm on, or unlawfully assault, the complainant. At trial he denied any reference to a search warrant, claiming he was loudly airing allegations the complainant sexually assaulted a cousin of an acquaintance, and that the complainant asked him inside so others would not hear. The issues were whether consent to enter was obtained by threat or fraud — whether the complainant was led to believe HUMBLE was entitled to enter as police, and whether HUMBLE threatened to arrest him — and whether HUMBLE intended to commit grievous bodily harm on entry. On 16/09/2025 a District Court jury (WALLACE DCJ) convicted him of aggravated home burglary contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 401(1)(ba) and impersonating a public officer contrary to s 87(2)(b); he was sentenced to 6 years and 16 months concurrent. On 11/06/2026, with a two-ground conviction appeal pending, he applied for bail as an alternative to an expedited hearing.
whatHeld: Bail application dismissed. Under cl 4A, pt C, Sch 1 of the Bail Act 1982 (WA), bail pending appeal may be granted only if 'exceptional reasons exist' why the accused should not remain in custody. HUMBLE's case was that his grounds were 'strongly arguable'. THOMSON P held the bail stage allows only a limited assessment: the grounds' strength must be readily apparent without detailed argument, with an outstanding feature required to warrant bail. On ground 1 (no direction on 'consent' to enter a dwelling, left to the jury as an ordinary word), his Honour's preliminary view: consent under s 401(1)(ba) means 'consent which has been procured without threat or as a result of a misrepresentation', so whichever meaning the jury applied was either correct or too favourable to HUMBLE. Ground 1 would not have released him regardless: the 16-month impersonation sentence, commenced 05/11/2025 and unchallenged on appeal, plus 7 months' cumulative sentences, remained. On ground 2 (prosecutor's closing address), it was not possible to say the Liberato submission was obviously wrong; the consciousness-of-guilt invitation was not clearly made, the inflammatory comments fell short of a fundamental miscarriage, and the judge's directions answered the sentencing comment.
whatItMeans: Two things matter here. First, the electronic record of interview. HUMBLE's admission in it — that he was to be paid $25,000 to inflict serious harm on the complainant — held up despite a different trial account. That is the case for a properly conducted, recorded interview even when you expect nothing useful. Second, the door. The aggravated home burglary turned on whether consent to enter was procured by threat or fraud: whether the occupant let HUMBLE in believing he was a police officer entitled to enter, or was threatened with arrest. THOMSON P's view of 'consent' under s 401(1)(ba) is preliminary and settles nothing, so do not carry it into a charge decision as law. What you can take is evidential — where entry is obtained on a claim of authority, get the occupant's account early, in his own words: what was said, what he was shown, and what he understood the person's authority to be. The Court left open the Liberato point — whether a prosecutor may argue that believing the accused means several State witnesses, including police, are lying — a reminder that strong contemporaneous records mean a trial turns less on whose word is preferred.
verdict: AWARENESS — an interlocutory bail refusal on the exceptional-reasons threshold, with all conviction-ground views preliminary. Notable for the s 401(1)(ba) consent issue and the Liberato point; no change to investigative practice.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Kruger v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (CLEARY DCJ), IND 443 of 2025
outcome: Leave to appeal granted; appeal against the count 1 sentence dismissed. The 8 years 7 months' imprisonment for possession with intent stands, as does the total effective sentence of 9 years 1 month, parole eligibility and backdating to 27/12/2024.
weight: Court of Appeal (ARCHER, SWEENEY and SEAWARD JJA), unanimous joint judgment. Binding WA appellate authority, but applying settled manifest-excess and drug-sentencing principles to its own facts (Category B). Most useful for its disciplined treatment of what comparable sentencing decisions can and cannot prove.
tags: possession with intent to sell or supply
oneLine: Court of Appeal dismissed KRUGER's manifest-excess appeal against 8 years 7 months for couriering 993 g of methylamphetamine, holding the sentence was at the high end but not plainly unjust, and that a drug debt from his own use is not meaningful mitigation.
whatHappened: At about 22:30 on 24/12/2024 KRUGER drove his Isuzu work truck to a house in Osborne Park, walked to the front garden and left a dark-coloured jumper concealing a large zip lock bag under bushes beside the driveway. The resident, alerted by the noise, watched him on her CCTV system, went out after he drove off, found the package and called police. Analysis showed 993 g of methylamphetamine at approximately 75% purity. KRUGER was arrested at Hillarys Boat Harbour shortly before midday on 27/12/2024 and, while being escorted away, pulled his mobile phone from his pocket and folded it in half, destroying it. A search warrant at his Girrawheen home produced digital scales, a syringe of methylamphetamine, cannabis and clothing matching the CCTV footage. He told police he was an occasional user and had broken the phone to stop police seeing personal photos. He pleaded guilty to possession of a trafficable quantity with intent to sell or supply (count 1) and wilful destruction of evidence (count 2). CLEARY DCJ sentenced him on 12/08/2025 to a total effective 9 years 1 month. He appealed the count 1 sentence only, as manifestly excessive.
whatHeld: Leave to appeal granted; appeal dismissed. Manifest excess arises only where the end result is so unreasonable or unjust that the court must conclude a substantial wrong has occurred (applying Kabambi). In serious drug cases the dominant considerations are personal and general deterrence; quantity matters, but gravity is not to be assessed solely by weight — role, motive and mitigation count too. The Court stressed what comparable decisions can prove: a refusal of leave on manifest excess (e.g. ATH, Watson) cannot imply an upper limit or approve a sentence as correct; decisions on totality or parity are not comparators; and no single decision is a benchmark. McGrath was distinguished: KRUGER was the sole courier, entrusted with a kilogram, in contact with those behind the transaction, standing to gain forgiveness of a $30,000 debt, and his phone destruction was cool-headed and effective rather than panicked. A drug debt from his own use, absent any threat of violence, cannot amount to meaningful mitigation. The Court noted the courier cases in McGrath predated the increase in the maximum penalty, so higher sentences are expected. The sentence was at the high end but not shown to be erroneous.
whatItMeans: This sentencing appeal changes nothing about how you investigate, caution, search or charge. Three things are worth carrying. First, the phone. KRUGER destroyed his mobile in the seconds after arrest: the sentencing judge could not determine whether the device held evidence of other dealing, and the people directing him were shielded from prosecution. In child abuse work the handset is often the case — get control of the hands and the device at the moment of arrest, and if a device is damaged, record when, how, and what the person said. KRUGER's stated reason (personal photos) was abandoned by his counsel at sentencing. Second, note what built the sentence. The weight of the drug set the frame, but the Court's reasoning turned on role — sole courier, entrusted with a kilogram, in contact with those behind the transaction, paid by forgiveness of a $30,000 debt. If you want a serious sentence to survive appeal, the brief has to prove role, not just quantity: contact with the principals, the arrangement, the benefit. Third, this case was made by a householder's CCTV and a phone call. Canvass for private cameras early and seize the footage before it cycles.
verdict: AWARENESS — manifest-excess appeal applying settled principles to a courier's culpability; it changes nothing in how you investigate. ACTION-flavoured on securing a suspect's phone at arrest, costing the people above the courier.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: GRM v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: Children's Court of Western Australia (QUAIL P)
outcome: Leave to appeal granted on ground 1 (which raised an important matter of principle), refused on grounds 2 and 3; appeal dismissed. The conviction for unlawfully doing grievous bodily harm stands, as does the 10-month juvenile conditional release order.
weight: Court of Appeal (THOMSON P, MITCHELL JA and HALL JA), unanimous judgment, marked Category A. Binding in WA: it adopts French CJ's approach in R v Khazaal to what a 'reasonable possibility' means, a question Khazaal left open, and applies it to the evidential onus.
oneLine: Court of Appeal holds that self-defence must rest on the evidence, not on what might have happened in a gap in it: where the only eyewitness looked away for four to five seconds, it was speculation to suggest the victim lunged with his knife.
whatHappened: On the evening of 08/09/2024 GRM, then 15, was at home with his 15-year-old cousin Marcus TUFNELL when he heard his mother Hannah FRANCIS arguing with her partner Dominic GELLERT (all pseudonyms). GRM fetched a samurai sword, a metre long unsheathed, and swung it about in the kitchen; FRANCIS pushed GELLERT out the front door. GRM followed GELLERT into the road. GELLERT turned back towards him holding a small folding knife, blade out, at his side. Swearing at each other from a little over arm's reach, GRM struck GELLERT to the neck with the sword, causing a large laceration. GELLERT refused to sign a statement and defied a summons to a deposition hearing. FRANCIS, on body-worn camera at the scene, said GELLERT 'was swinging at him first', but refused a statement and later said she had seen nothing; no deposition was attempted for her. TUFNELL, the only witness, looked away for the four to five seconds in which the blow landed. GRM was convicted by QUAIL P in the Children's Court of unlawfully doing grievous bodily harm contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 297(3), self-defence the only issue. He appealed on three grounds.
whatHeld: Leave granted on ground 1, refused on grounds 2 and 3; appeal dismissed. The Court restated the elements of self-defence under Criminal Code (WA) s 248(4) and confirmed the accused's evidential onus is low but real, with Heijne and Hawke warning judges to guard against speculation where the evidence has gaps. A defence must have a foundation in the evidence. Agreeing with French CJ in R v Khazaal — evidence merely consistent with a possibility does not suggest it — the Court held that a reasonable possibility must be founded on evidence at least capable of supporting the inference. 'Reasonable', the Court added, is a limiting word strongly suggesting more than the merely theoretical. Inference must be distinguished from conjecture (R v Baden-Clay): the suggestion that GELLERT lunged was speculation, the only evidence being the knife held down by his side. The prosecution need not disprove every theoretical possibility. Ground 2 failed because 'no fracas or physical contact' described the broader circumstances, not a positive finding about the gap. Ground 3 failed because the prosecutor alone decides who to call and, FRANCIS having given no statement, it was not known what she could say.
whatItMeans: On an assault or grievous bodily harm job where self-defence is live, the defence can build only on what is in the evidence. Your job at the scene is to fix the circumstances the court will reason from — the distance between the parties, what was in each hand and where it was held, whether anything moved, who advanced on whom, who armed first, injuries to both, whether either went to the ground. Treat scene accounts on body-worn camera as fragile: TUFNELL told police that GELLERT swung first, but because he did not adopt that in the witness box it was not evidence of the truth, and went only to his credit and reliability — which the trial judge found it did not undermine. Convert scene accounts into signed statements, and where a witness refuses, attempt the deposition — GELLERT defied his summons, no deposition was attempted for FRANCIS. Record your attempts to get cooperation: the trial judge rejected the defence's adverse-inference argument because he accepted Detective WALLER's evidence, which you may have to give yourself. Your family violence callout reports become defence exhibits, as GELLERT's did; expect the same reluctant relatives and protective parents in your child abuse work.
verdict: ACTION — the holding is doctrinal; the case turns on what police did and did not lock down: body-worn camera accounts never converted into statements, and the scene detail that decided self-defence.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Phoebe Buckley (a pseudonym) v Director of Public Prosecutions [No 2]
appealFrom: Supreme Court of Western Australia (WHITBY J), single-judge appeal from the Magistrates Court of Western Australia; SJA file number anonymised in the published reasons.
outcome: Extension of time to appeal refused; leave to appeal refused on all eight grounds; appeal dismissed. Three applications to adduce additional evidence and to summons Senior Constable BORLASE dismissed. Convictions and the global $1,000 fine, suspended 12 months with spent conviction orders, stand.
weight: Court of Appeal (VAUGHAN, HALL and SWEENEY JJA), unanimous joint judgment, binding in WA though categorised B. Authoritative statement of the Criminal Investigation (Identifying People) Act 2002 (WA) s 16 request-and-detain powers and of when an officer must identify himself.
