oneLine: Court of Appeal upholds public-indecency, false-name and obstruction convictions, confirming an officer reasonably suspecting an offence may request details under Criminal Investigation (Identifying People) Act 2002 (WA) s 16(2) and detain to verify them under s 16(4C); need only identify himself if asked.
whatHappened: Shortly after 11.00 am on 10/12/2023, police received a report of a couple acting indecently at the Rockingham foreshore. Constable Dane CROSSLAND and Senior Constable Andrew BORLASE attended; CROSSLAND activated his body-worn camera on approach. BUCKLEY (a pseudonym) lay on the grass near a busy children's playground while her male companion fondled her breast, over and under her dress. BORLASE told the pair to leave and that they would be issued a move on order under s 27 of the Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA). CROSSLAND told BUCKLEY she had committed an offence and asked for her personal details; she gave the false name 'Karen O'Reilly'. Detained until her identity was confirmed, she walked off, then ran despite a warning of arrest, and was taken to the ground and handcuffed. At a Magistrates Court trial on 09/07/2024, where the State called only CROSSLAND and tendered the BWC and CCTV footage, she was convicted of an indecent act in public (Criminal Code (WA) s 203(1)(a)), failing to give personal details (s 16(6) CIIPA) and obstructing a public officer (s 172(2)). Self-represented, she lost a 63-ground appeal to WHITBY J, then sought leave to appeal on eight grounds, 10 days late.
whatHeld: Leave and extension of time refused; appeal dismissed. On the unreasonable verdict ground, the Court reviewed the CCTV and BWC footage and had no reasonable doubt. An act is indecent if unbecoming or offensive to common propriety, need not involve bodily contact, and depends on time, place and circumstances (the magistrate applying Drago v The Queen); overtly sexual touching beside a busy playground was indecent. Under s 16(2) CIIPA an officer who reasonably suspects an unidentified person has committed an offence may request their name, date of birth and address, and under s 16(4C) may detain them for a reasonable period to verify it; a false name is a failure to comply, and the detention being lawful, running and resisting arrest was obstruction. An officer must give surname and rank only if asked; no request was made, and s 27 CIA does not require it. The prosecutor alone decides who to call; no duty attached to the issuing officer; summonsing him was a fishing exercise. No reasonable apprehension of bias (applying Courtney (a pseudonym) v The State of Western Australia); the medical reports were marginally relevant and inadmissible without their authors or the prosecutor's consent.
whatItMeans: Know s 16 of the CIIPA cold — it is the power this case turns on. If you reasonably suspect a person whose details you do not know has committed an offence, you may request name, date of birth and address, and you may detain them for a reasonable period under s 16(4C) to obtain compliance or verify what they give you. Say on camera what offence you suspect, that the person is detained, and why — CROSSLAND did that, and it made the obstruction charge stick. On identification: you only have to give surname and rank if asked, but failing to do so as soon as practicable is a reasonable excuse for refusing details and will sink a s 16(6) charge. Give it on the BWC anyway. A move on order does not exist until it is written in the approved form under s 27(6) — 'gather your things and leave' is not one — so never charge a breach of one you never issued. Secure and disclose the footage; the CCTV went in unopposed because it was disclosed pre-trial and CROSSLAND could speak to it, and preserve the second officer's BWC — the defence will ask for it.
verdict: ACTION — a binding statement of powers you use daily: demanding details, detaining to verify them, identifying yourself, and that a move on order exists only once written in the approved form.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Sym v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: Supreme Court of Western Australia (FORRESTER J), INS 5 of 2023
outcome: Conviction appeal: leave granted, appeal dismissed (conviction stands). Sentence appeal: leave granted, appeal allowed; 9-year sentence set aside and replaced with 6 years 6 months' imprisonment, eligible for parole, backdated to commence 08/03/2024.
weight: Court of Appeal (three judges: VAUGHAN JA, HALL JA, DAVID AJA) unanimous decision — strong persuasive and binding authority on the warning principle and manifest excess for attempted murder.
oneLine: Court of Appeal confirms no judicial warning about forensic disadvantage from a deficient police investigation was needed where the deficiencies were obvious to the jury and aired by defence counsel; conviction upheld but attempted-murder sentence reduced from 9 years to 6 years 6 months.
whatHappened: SYM was convicted by a Supreme Court jury of attempting to unlawfully kill her husband Kenneth SYM at Joondalup on 15/01/2021, contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 283. Mr SYM, who had vascular dementia and type 2 diabetes, was administered a non-therapeutic dose of exogenous insulin while admitted to Joondalup Health Campus. The only real issues at trial were identity and intent. The State ran a circumstantial case built on opportunity (a roughly 15-minute window between 1.25pm and 1.40pm when SYM was in the room), a vial of Actrapid insulin found in a nearby public bathroom bin bearing SYM's DNA (100 billion times more likely to be her than two unknowns), the fact that this expired 2018 insulin type was not used at JHC but was stocked at Princess Margaret Hospital where SYM worked as a nurse on the date the vial was opened, an orange-capped syringe in the sharps container, and text messages showing her stress and frustration as her husband's carer. SYM denied the offence. The police investigation had notable deficiencies: no statement was taken from carer Ms KAUR until the week before trial (March 2024), no statement from student nurse Ms JAMOLA until August 2021, and pharmaceutical records were never obtained. SYM appealed conviction (failure to warn the jury about forensic disadvantage) and sentence (manifest excess).
whatHeld: On conviction: leave granted, appeal dismissed. The Court accepted SYM suffered some forensic disadvantage from the police delays and failure to obtain records, but held a judicial warning is only required to avoid a perceptible risk of a miscarriage of justice where a feature of the evidence may affect its reliability and that significance may not be apparent to a lay jury (applying Carr, Longman, Eravelly, Tully, DWM). Here the disadvantages were limited and were within the common knowledge of the jury — they were extensively explored in cross-examination and defence counsel's closing address and summarised by the primary judge. The evidence of opportunity was only one part of a broad circumstantial case, and SYM's own admission (that no observations were done while she was present) was the most damaging opportunity evidence. Experienced senior counsel did not request such a warning, supporting the conclusion no warning was needed. On sentence: leave granted, appeal allowed. The 9-year sentence bespoke implied error and was manifestly excessive given reduced moral culpability from the causal link between SYM's emotional fatigue/carer burnout and the offending, her good character, and low reoffending risk. Resentenced to 6 years 6 months.
whatItMeans: When your investigation has gaps — delayed witness statements, records you never obtained, lost lines of inquiry — this case shows the courts will scrutinise them, but a defence argument that the trial judge should have specially warned the jury about resulting "forensic disadvantage" will usually fail if those gaps are obvious and can be argued to the jury by defence counsel. That is not comfort. The better lesson for your casework is preventative: take statements from key witnesses promptly while memories are fresh. Here, delays of seven months to years meant carer KAUR and nurse JAMOLA could only speak to "usual practice," not what actually happened — a real evidential loss the Court expressly acknowledged. Also chase down obvious records (here the pharmacy stock records) to exclude alternative suspects; the detective conceded these were relevant lines of inquiry he missed. In a circumstantial case, a strong DNA link, motive evidence and the accused's own admissions can carry the case despite investigative failings — but you cannot rely on that. Do the easy things properly and early: show witnesses their contemporaneous notes when taking statements, and secure relevant registers before they become an appeal point.
verdict: AWARENESS for the conviction principle; but ACTION-relevant lessons on timely statement-taking and obtaining records. Marked ACTION because it directly warns how investigative delay and unpursued lines of inquiry damage evidence quality.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Donald Atkins (a pseudonym) v The State of Western Australia [No 3]
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (LONSDALE DCJ), IND ALB 69 of 2022
outcome: CACR 112 (conviction): extension of time refused, applications to adduce additional evidence refused, leave to appeal refused, appeal dismissed. CACR 113 (sentence): extension of time granted, leave to appeal granted, appeal dismissed. Total effective sentence of 19 years' imprisonment stands.
weight: Court of Appeal (WA) — three judges (MITCHELL, HALL and SWEENEY JJA), unanimous joint judgment. Authoritative statement of the law in WA, though applying well-established principles.
oneLine: Court of Appeal dismisses ATKINS's conviction and sentence appeals over 25 child sex offences against four stepdaughters, confirming the fresh-versus-new evidence test, the prosecutor's discretion on which witnesses to call, and totality principles.
whatHappened: ATKINS (a pseudonym) was convicted after trial in the District Court (LONSDALE DCJ) of 25 child sexual offences committed over about 10 years against four of his stepdaughters (River, Rowan, Whitney and Margot), aged between 7 and 13. He received a total effective sentence of 19 years' imprisonment. Self-represented, he appealed conviction on two grounds: (1) that one complainant (River) gave false evidence and that additional material (text messages, Department of Communities and Independent Children's Lawyer letters, school reports, van photographs, audio-message transcripts) should be admitted; and (2) that a miscarriage arose because the prosecutor did not call his wife (Gertrude) and Ms ELDERSHAW. He also appealed the sentence as breaching totality. The offending came to light after ATKINS was caught trying to record Whitney in the shower in 2020 (offences he had pleaded guilty to), following which the children moved to their father and disclosed the abuse.
whatHeld: Both appeals failed. On conviction ground 1, the additional material was new evidence, not fresh evidence — it existed and could have been obtained with reasonable diligence before trial. Evidence going only to a complainant's credibility on collateral issues generally cannot establish a miscarriage because it is not direct evidence of whether the acts occurred; here it was largely irrelevant, hearsay, opinion, or added nothing. On ground 2, the prosecutor alone decides which witnesses to call, and a decision not to call a witness only founds an appeal if, viewed against the whole trial, it produces a miscarriage. Neither Gertrude nor Ms ELDERSHAW was an eyewitness; both were available for the defence to call; and the defence made a reasonable forensic decision not to call Gertrude. On sentence, the total of 19 years was high but not unreasonable or plainly unjust given four child victims, offending over a decade, a gross breach of trust, multiple penetrative acts, conviction after trial and no remorse; comparable cases gave only limited guidance. The Court also confirmed general deterrence does not depend on publicity.
whatItMeans: For your casework, the practical lessons are about how evidence is later tested on appeal. First, gather and preserve everything before trial — material that a defendant could have obtained with reasonable diligence will be treated as "new" and is very hard to run later, so completeness in the brief matters. Second, note the cross-admissibility/propensity point: the trial judge allowed each complainant's evidence to show sexual interest, but limited it to offences occurring in the family home — when investigating multi-complainant intrafamilial abuse, be precise about where each act occurred, as location can affect admissibility. Third, understand that the DPP, not you, decides who is called, and that a witness favourable to the accused (like a supportive spouse) need not be called by the State if unreliable or unsupportive of the complainants. Fourth, delayed complaint and continuing family contact do not undermine a case — the Court accepted children may not disclose to a non-supportive parent, so document the family dynamics and reasons for delay. This decision applies settled principles rather than changing investigative practice.
verdict: AWARENESS — it confirms established appellate principles (fresh/new evidence, prosecutor's discretion to call witnesses, totality) rather than changing how you investigate or charge.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v Raven [No 2]
outcome: Respondent declared a high risk serious offender; supervision order made for 3 years from 29/06/2026; no continuing detention order. Curfew condition and associate-disclosure condition removed as unnecessary.
weight: Single-judge first-instance decision of the Supreme Court applying settled HRSO principles; expressly turns on its own facts.
oneLine: WHITBY J declared serial fire-setter Victor RAVEN a high risk serious offender under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA) and made a 3-year supervision order rather than continuing detention.
whatHappened: The State applied on 11/11/2025 for a restriction order against Victor Redvers RAVEN, then serving 3 years for wilfully lighting a fire likely to injure or damage (s 32(2)(a) Bush Fires Act 1954 (WA)) - he tied a match to an incense stick and left it in dried undergrowth behind Albany Senior High School. RAVEN, 69, has a mild intellectual disability, paranoid personality disorder and autism spectrum disorder, and a fire-setting history stretching back to 1972, much of it linked to a long-standing grievance against Albany Senior High School. Two experts (Professor PYSZORA and Dr YEWERS) assessed him as a high risk of further fire-setting if not supervised. Both the State and RAVEN's counsel supported a supervision order over continuing detention.
whatHeld: WHITBY J was satisfied to a high degree of probability that RAVEN is a high risk serious offender: he poses an unacceptable risk of committing a serious fire-setting offence, the potential harm being catastrophic. A restriction order was necessary because NDIS funding and stable accommodation with his brother were not enough to manage the risk. The court chose a supervision order as the least invasive option that still adequately protects the community, being satisfied RAVEN would substantially comply (he had complied with the interim order). A 3-year supervision order was imposed with conditions including electronic monitoring, exclusion from Albany and bushland (except his Kauring block), and prohibitions on possessing fire-starting implements.
whatItMeans: This is an outcome under the post-sentence HRSO regime, not a guide to investigation, but it is useful background. It shows how a persistent fire-setting offending pattern, combined with cogent expert risk assessment, supports a finding of unacceptable risk even where an offender has complied with interim supervision. For your casework, note the practical conditions imposed - electronic monitoring, police search of residence/vehicle/person (on request, to monitor compliance), exclusion zones, and bans on fire-starting implements and flammable substances - which are the kind of conditions you may be enforcing if you encounter an HRSO subject. The judgment also stresses information sharing between agencies and police to detect new grievances before they escalate.
verdict: AWARENESS only - this is a post-sentence civil restriction decision that does not change how you investigate, gather evidence or charge.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v Hosie
outcome: Respondent's application to dismiss the restriction order application refused.
weight: Single-judge Supreme Court decision, delivered extemporaneously and edited from transcript. Persuasive first-instance authority on s 35 timing; not binding appellate authority.
oneLine: An HRSO restriction order application under High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA) s 35 must be filed within one year of a possible release date; competency is judged at lodgement, not the final hearing.
whatHappened: On 26/03/2026 the State filed a restriction order application against Shane Andrew HOSIE under s 35(1) of the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA). At that time HOSIE was serving 18 months for two counts of persistent family violence (Index Offences), with a maximum sentence date of 05/06/2026. He had also been declared a serial family violence offender. He had pleaded guilty to further charges awaiting sentence (procuring/exposing a child via electronic communication and possessing child exploitation material), and faced other charges (aggravated sexual penetration without consent, impeding breathing, and threatening) that had produced a hung jury. HOSIE applied to dismiss the application as incompetent, arguing that once it became clear before the final hearing he could not be released within a year, the application failed s 35(3). After HOSIE was sentenced on 05/06/2026 to 2 years (removing any release possibility before 26/03/2027), he maintained the dismissal application.
whatHeld: WHITBY J refused the dismissal application. The word 'application' in s 35 means the originating process filed to commence the proceeding, not the entire court process including the final hearing. Under s 35(3), an application by the State against an in-custody offender must be formally lodged within one year before the date there is a possibility the offender might be released. 'Possibility' and 'might' set a low threshold — only a low-level chance of release is required. Competency is assessed at the date of lodgement, on the knowledge the State then had. On 26/03/2026 there was clearly a possibility HOSIE might be released on 05/06/2026, so the application complied with s 35. Later events (the 2-year sentence removing release possibility) did not render it incompetent.
whatItMeans: For your casework this confirms the timing rule for HRSO applications: the State must file the application within one year of the offender's earliest possible release date, and that release possibility need only be a low-level chance — not a certainty. Judge competency on the facts known at the date of filing. Where an offender has pending charges, an unknown sentence, or a possible bail/discontinuance outcome, that uncertainty can itself supply the 'possibility' of release. Later developments that push the release date beyond a year do not undo a validly filed application. This matters mainly for the State Solicitor's Office and case coordination; as an investigator, ensure custody/sentence timelines and possible release dates are captured accurately so applications are lodged in the correct window.
verdict: AWARENESS — a statutory construction ruling on HRSO application timing; useful background but it does not change how you gather evidence or charge.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v Bunwarrie
outcome: Interim detention order made under s 46(2)(c)(i); respondent detained until further order; restriction order application listed for final hearing on 12/02/2027 with expert reports ordered.
weight: Single judge decision of the Supreme Court on an interlocutory HRSO application; the court noted the governing law is settled and not in dispute. Turns on its own facts (Category B).
oneLine: Supreme Court made an interim detention order under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA) at a preliminary hearing, finding reasonable grounds that BUNWARRIE might be a high risk serious offender.
whatHappened: BUNWARRIE was serving 3 years and 2 months for four counts of using electronic communication to expose a child under 16 to indecent matter (s 204B Criminal Code) and four counts of failing to comply with reporting obligations (s 63(1) Community Protection (Offender Reporting) Act 2004), with release due 19/09/2026. He had a history of serious sexual offending against children, including indecent dealing with a 12-year-old stranger in a train station toilet, masturbating in front of children in public parks, and indecent acts in public. He had a poor record of complying with court orders, breached a post-sentence supervision order, and had unmet treatment needs. He offended within about six weeks of an earlier release. On 07/04/2026 the State applied for a restriction order under the Act and sought an interim detention order under s 46(2)(c)(i). The matter came before WHITBY J at a preliminary hearing on 26/06/2026.
whatHeld: WHITBY J was satisfied there were reasonable grounds for believing the court might find BUNWARRIE is a high risk serious offender under s 7 of the Act. At the preliminary hearing the threshold is lower than the final test — the court need not be satisfied a restriction order will be made, only that one 'might' be made (something possible), supported by sufficient facts to induce that belief in a reasonable person. Given his offending history, poor compliance with orders, lack of viable accommodation, unmet treatment needs and the high risk of serious sexual offending against a female child, the risk was an unacceptable one that could not be sufficiently minimised by supervision conditions. An interim detention order was appropriate to adequately protect the community pending final hearing.
whatItMeans: This is a settled-law application of the HRSO preliminary hearing test — useful background rather than a change to your practice. It shows how the State builds a restriction order application: through the offender's full criminal history, statements of material facts, breach records, psychological/parole reports and evidence of accommodation and treatment needs. When you investigate and document reportable sex offenders, thorough records of reporting breaches, PSSO breaches and pattern offending directly feed later HRSO applications. Note the emphasis on offending while sober and against strangers, and reoffending soon after release, as markers of unacceptable risk.
verdict: AWARENESS only — this applies settled HRSO principles to its own facts and does not change how you investigate or charge.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: The State of Western Australia v Aiden Santo (a pseudonym)
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (TROY DCJ)
outcome: Extension of time granted; leave to appeal granted; leave granted to adduce the letter of recognition as additional evidence (access restricted); appeal allowed; the 2½-year sentence set aside and SANTO resentenced to 2 years 3 months' immediate imprisonment, backdated to 05/03/2026, eligible for parole.
weight: Court of Appeal (THOMSON P, VAUGHAN JA, SEAWARD JA) — a unanimous judgment, delivered ex tempore. Binding in WA, but applies principles the Court described as well established and declined to restate; the three-month discount is fact-specific and of little comparative value.
oneLine: A WA Police letter of recognition for an offender's assistance never reached the sentencing judge, and the Court of Appeal held that losing it was a miscarriage of justice, allowing the State's own appeal and cutting three months from a methylamphetamine supply sentence.
whatHappened: After midnight on 14/09/2024 police saw SANTO (a pseudonym), then 31, riding an electric scooter along a country road. Two officers stopped him and indicated they proposed to search him. SANTO ran, was apprehended nearby, and two clipseal bags were found in his pockets holding 9.73 g and 14.4 g of methylamphetamine, 24.13 g in total, the larger quantity about 50% pure. He pleaded guilty to possession of a prohibited drug with intent to sell or supply, contrary to Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 (WA) s 6(1)(a). TROY DCJ could not be satisfied how much was for personal use, sentenced him on the basis he intended to sell or supply some of the 24.13 g, allowed a 12% reduction under Sentencing Act 1995 (WA) s 9AA, and imposed 2½ years' immediate imprisonment backdated to 05/03/2026 with parole eligibility after 15 months. SANTO was on bail and an intensive supervision order when he offended and had prior drug convictions, including possession of cannabis with intent to sell or supply. On 16/10/2024 the Assistant Commissioner, State Crime had issued a letter of recognition for assistance SANTO gave WA Police. It never reached the sentencing judge. The State appealed.
whatHeld: Extension of time and leave to appeal granted; the appeal was allowed. Sentencing Act 1995 (WA) s 6(2)(d) requires a sentence to take into account any mitigating factors. The letter was such a factor: it existed and was known to the DPP, but not to SANTO's counsel, and through no fault of SANTO or the judge it never reached TROY DCJ. The Court was satisfied that the sentencing process involved a miscarriage of justice, and SANTO had to be resentenced. The principles on cooperation, summarised in SYL v The State of Western Australia and RXA v The State of Western Australia, are that a substantial discount must be given for useful assistance irrespective of remorse or effectiveness, there is no standard percentage, and the discount must not leave a sentence obviously inadequate or an affront to community standards. SANTO's cooperation — three intelligence reports, no charges laid, no property seized, low risk, no tasking, graded 'grade 3', the lowest category under the DPP–police Joint Protocol — was 'at the very low end', but should be acknowledged. The Court would have imposed TROY DCJ's sentence but for the cooperation, allowing a further discount of three months.
whatItMeans: If you take assistance from someone facing sentencing, the letter of recognition is your paperwork. Under Sentencing Act 1995 (WA) s 6(2)(d) it is a mitigating factor the court must take into account, and if it never reaches the judge, the sentence is a miscarriage of justice, undone on appeal. First, raise the letter and make sure its existence is flagged into the prosecution file. Second, be exact about what the assistance produced — the specific reports, charges and property outcomes — which fixed the grading and discount. Overstate it and you mislead the court; understate it and the person who assisted loses the benefit. Third, do not hold a letter back because the information went nowhere: the Court held the assistance need not have been effective, and said giving information to police should be encouraged even if it does not yield immediate fruit. The letter was restricted to a single hard copy, released only by order of a judge of appeal. None of this touches how you interview a child complainant, but the moment you take information from a person who is before the courts — a co-offender, an associate — this process is yours.
verdict: ACTION — the principle is settled, but the document is one WA Police issues, and the case shows what to raise and record, and why it must not stop at the DPP.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Warren (a pseudonym) v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: Children's Court of Western Australia (QUAIL P), PE 2715, 2716 and 2718 of 2024
outcome: Application for an extension of time to appeal dismissed; leave to appeal refused; appeal dismissed. The roughly 10-month delay was not adequately explained and the appeal lacked merit. Convictions on counts 1, 2 and 3 stand.
weight: Court of Appeal (MITCHELL, HALL and SEAWARD JJA) — unanimous in result, split in reasoning: MITCHELL and SEAWARD JJA relied on the trial judge's advantage, while HALL JA reached the same conclusion without it. Binding WA appellate authority applying settled principles; Category B.
oneLine: Where a suspect aged 10 to 13, Criminal Code (WA) s 29 requires proof he had capacity to know the act was seriously wrong; secrecy alone is equivocal, but a coercive threat strongly supports the inference, and the Court of Appeal upheld the convictions.
whatHappened: WARREN (a pseudonym), then 12 or 13, was convicted after a judge-alone trial in the Children's Court of three counts of sexually penetrating a child under 13, contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 320(2), committed 16/05/2017-01/10/2017. The complainant, 7, lived at a metropolitan house with her aunt and uncle, WARREN's grandparents, treated as her adoptive parents, where he was staying. Count 1: she woke to find him penetrating her vagina with his penis; he covered her mouth, told her to be quiet because her cousin Carol was in another room, and ran when the adults returned. Count 2, days later, was digital penetration in the same bedroom. On count 3, about a week after count 1, he demanded fellatio in the playroom and, when she refused, threatened to tell her mother (his grandmother) that she was starting it all, then forced her head. She said this happened about 20 times; school and border records fixed the dates. WARREN denied the offending. Sentenced on 20/05/2025 to a total effective 2 years 3 months for all four offences (a fourth, committed aged over 14, is not on appeal), he appealed only on 25/03/2026, contending the s 29 presumption was not rebutted.
whatHeld: Extension of time dismissed, leave refused, appeal dismissed. Criminal Code (WA) s 29 makes a person under 14 not criminally responsible unless it is proved he had capacity to know that he ought not to do the act; applying TPL and KNL, that means capacity to know the conduct was seriously wrong according to the ordinary standards of reasonable adults. Applying M v The Queen and, for judge-alone trials, Dansie v The Queen, the court assesses the evidence independently. MITCHELL and SEAWARD JJA held the school records and the mother's evidence added little, and missing contemporaneous parent or teacher evidence of moral development made rebuttal harder. Covering her mouth, persisting over resistance and fleeing when adults returned supported an inference of wrongfulness but not, of itself, the required moral understanding. The threat before count 3 was more significant: WARREN 'could only have perceived the efficacy of the threat' if he knew his conduct was seriously wrong, which strongly supports the inference. With his cross-examination admissions that at 12 he knew such acts were seriously wrong, excluding contrary inferences, only one reasonable inference remained — one the majority could reach only with the trial judge's advantage.
whatItMeans: When your suspect was aged 10 to 13, s 29 also requires proof he had capacity to know the conduct was seriously wrong — not a low standard, the Court repeated. Secrecy will not carry it — telling a child to keep quiet is equivocal. What does the work is the detail around it: repeated demands for silence, threats, coercion, force, stopping when adults return. Take the complainant's account verbatim. Here the threat carried the most weight — to tell the complainant's mother that the 7-year-old was 'starting all of this and making me do everything' — because it only works if the speaker knows his conduct is seriously blameworthy; and it was that threat with his own admissions that closed off other inferences. Record the exact wording of any threat, what he said when she resisted, and what he did when adults approached. Secure contemporaneous capacity evidence: the Court said the absence of parent or teacher evidence of his moral development made rebuttal harder; school records proved little. Take statements from parents, carers and teachers about what the child had been taught. Note how the dates were fixed here: school and border records, when recollections were poor.
verdict: ACTION — where a suspect is between 10 and 14, this tells you what evidence rebuts the s 29 presumption, and it turns on details you can capture at the time.

caseName: Cullen v The State of New South Wales
appealFrom: NSW Court of Appeal
outcome: Appeal dismissed — State not liable
weight: Persuasive principle (HCA); statute is NSW
oneLine: Police owe bystanders a duty of care when they move into a crowd to deal with a public-safety threat — but a proportionate response to a real threat is not negligence, even when someone gets hurt.
whatHappened: On 26 January 2017, an “Invasion Day” protest march of about 5,000 people moved through inner Sydney. CULLEN was watching from the crowd. As officers of the Operational Services Group (OSG) moved in — and while Leading Senior Constable Livermore was arresting a marcher — a melee erupted and CULLEN was knocked to the ground and seriously injured. At trial she was awarded $800,000; the NSW Court of Appeal reversed that. She appealed to the High Court.
whatHeld: The appeal turned on three questions — duty, breach, and scope. Duty — yes: when intervening in the march, the officers owed a duty to avoid physical injury to a class of people that included bystanders foreseeably at risk from the operation. Breach — no: their actions were not unreasonable given the public-safety threat they were responding to at the time. The six-judge joint reasons held that, with no breach, the scope question did not arise; Edelman J, agreeing there was no breach, would have decided scope and held the duty did extend to the appellant. Appeal dismissed (unanimous on the result).
whatItMeans: Read it for the principle, not the charge — this is NSW civil negligence, not WA criminal law, so it changes no offence you lay. But the principle is High Court and it travels: when you intervene operationally (a crowd, a public-order job, an arrest in a tight space) you owe bystanders a duty of care, and you are judged on the reasonableness of your response to the threat as it appeared at the time, not with hindsight. What carried the day was that a decisive response to a real, urgent threat was within the range of reasonable responses — judged in the agony of the moment, not with hindsight. Still, record your threat assessment and why the response was proportionate (running sheet, notes, BWC). WA's Civil Liability Act 2002 has broadly similar breach provisions, but this decision turns on the NSW Act — treat the principle as persuasive, not as authority on WA legislation.
verdict: Useful for use-of-force and civil-liability exposure. It does not change how you investigate, gather evidence, or lay a charge.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
appealFrom: Supreme Court of Western Australia (LEMONIS J), SJA 1072 of 2023
outcome: Application for an extension of time to comply with the springing order dismissed; the appeal remains dismissed by operation of the order of 23/06/2025; the further applications dated 17/03/2026 and 04/06/2026, with their supporting affidavits, refused acceptance for filing.
weight: Court of Appeal (MITCHELL, HALL and ARCHER JJA), unanimous joint reasons, Category B. Binding appellate authority on extending time to comply with a springing order, applying the settled A v C [No 2] factors to its own facts rather than stating anything new.
oneLine: Court of Appeal refused a self-represented appellant an extension of time to comply with a springing order, holding that a springing order is the last opportunity to put a case in order and that he faced no prejudice, having already won below.
whatHappened: REYNOLDS was convicted in the Magistrates Court of three offences: two breach of bail offences (charges AL 2150/2021 and AL 682/2022) and one of breaching a family violence restraining order (charge AL 2097/2021). That charge alleged a breach on 06/10/2021 of an interim restraining order made on 09/04/2021 and served on REYNOLDS on 10/04/2021. He appealed to a single judge of the Supreme Court on 07/08/2023. LEMONIS J set aside all three convictions, acquitted him on AL 2150/2021, and remitted the other two to Albany Magistrates Court for trial before a different magistrate. On 24/02/2025 REYNOLDS, self-represented, appealed those orders to the Court of Appeal. He missed the rules deadline and three extensions; filings attempted on 16/05/2025 and 17/06/2025 were refused as non-compliant with the Supreme Court (Court of Appeal) Rules 2005 (WA). On 23/06/2025 the Court made a springing order: unless a compliant appellant's case was filed by 08/07/2025, the appeal would be dismissed. It was not, and the appeal stood dismissed. REYNOLDS then applied for an extension of time to comply.
whatHeld: The application was dismissed and the appeal remains dismissed. Applying A v C [No 2], failure to comply with a springing order is an egregious breach: such an order is the last opportunity to put a case in order. The discretion turns on how the order came to be made, the reason for non-compliance, the prejudice to each side, and whether there is an arguable case on the merits — though merit alone cannot excuse breach of a peremptory order. Most of those factors told against REYNOLDS. His explanation was inadequate: he had been given the court's Self-Representation Kit, the text of r 32, and the Acting Registrar's letter of 04/07/2025 setting out the defects, yet the late document still failed r 32(4) and r 32(5). He would suffer no prejudice, having already had the convictions set aside and the remitted charges since dismissed. There was no evidence of prejudice to the respondents, but a strong public interest in timely disposition of appeals. None of the proposed grounds had merit; the venue complaint failed because Albany was the nearest registry and the primary judge had preserved his right to seek a Perth trial or recusal.
whatItMeans: Nothing here changes how you investigate, interview or charge — it is appellate housekeeping about an appellant who could not file a compliant appellant's case. Look at why the original convictions fell: the restraining order conviction went because the magistrate used the Criminal Procedure Act 2004 (WA) s 55 procedure to convict, and the breach of bail conviction on AL 682/2022 went because the magistrate improperly fettered REYNOLDS's right to participate in the trial process. Neither was an evidence failure, and neither produced an acquittal — both charges were remitted for trial. When a conviction is set aside for a court-process error, your file has to be capable of being run again, sometimes years later, so keep exhibits, statements and the running sheet in a state that survives a re-listing. Note how the restraining order charge was framed: order made 09/04/2021, served 10/04/2021, breached 06/10/2021. Making, service and breach are the three dates a breach charge stands on — prove service, do not assume it. Much of what REYNOLDS complained about was the accuracy of the court record, including an alleged false entry of 'no appearance'. Complaints of that kind are answered by contemporaneous, accurate records, not by recollection.
verdict: AWARENESS — a procedural ruling on extending time under a springing order; it changes nothing about how you investigate or charge, though a conviction set aside for error is remitted, not ended.

appealFrom: Supreme Court of New South Wales (Court of Criminal Appeal)
outcome: Crown appeal allowed; NSW CCA orders (6,7,8,9 of 03/03/2025) set aside; AR's appeal to the CCA dismissed; convictions on counts 3, 5 and 7 restored.
weight: High Court of Australia decision and binding, applying and reinforcing DPP (Vic) v Roder. Note it was a narrow 4:3 split, so the boundaries in borderline cases remain contestable.
oneLine: HCA (4:3) holds that using evidence of charged acts to prove a tendency is not inconsistent with tendency evidence, and a tendency direction is judged by whether the summing up as a whole created a real risk of undermining proof beyond reasonable doubt.
whatHappened: AR was tried in the NSW District Court on seven child sexual offence counts against a single complainant, GC, aged 10, arising from three separate occasions in 2020. The Crown relied on a tendency that AR had a sexual interest in GC and acted on it by penetrating/touching her when she fell asleep beside him watching a movie. The evidence relied on to prove that tendency was the very same evidence of the charged acts — there were no uncharged acts, and all of it came from GC. AR was convicted on counts 3, 5 and 7 (the two Narara incidents) and acquitted on counts 1 and 2 (the weaker West Gosford incident). The NSW Court of Criminal Appeal set aside the convictions and ordered a retrial, holding the tendency direction risked deflecting the jury from the required standard of proof. The Crown appealed to the High Court, which allowed the appeal and restored the convictions.
whatHeld: By a 4:3 majority (GAGELER CJ, GLEESON, BEECH-JONES JJ and JAGOT J; GORDON, STEWARD and EDELMAN JJ dissenting) the appeal was allowed. The majority held: tendency evidence is a form of circumstantial evidence, and the standard of proof for the evidence said to establish a tendency is governed by the principles applicable to circumstantial evidence — unless the tendency is an indispensable intermediate step in reasoning to guilt, the jury need not be satisfied of those acts beyond reasonable doubt before acting on them to find the tendency. Relying on the evidence of charged acts to establish a tendency, and then deploying that tendency in deciding whether the charges are proved beyond reasonable doubt, is not circular reasoning and not inconsistent with the nature of tendency evidence. Framing the tendency with specificity that mirrors the charged conduct is permissible and is often what gives it significant probative value, especially in a single-complainant case (with the s 97A presumption applying to child sexual offences). Following DPP (Vic) v Roder, the guidance that a judge should avoid inviting the jury to make findings on charged conduct is a recommendation, not a rule; a direction that does so is not automatically a miscarriage. The test is whether, considering the summing up as a whole, there was a real or practical risk of undermining the jury's understanding of proof beyond reasonable doubt. Here the summing up was saturated with correct standard-of-proof directions, so no such risk arose.
whatItMeans: This is mainly about trial directions, but it confirms how tendency evidence works in ways that matter to how you build a brief. Evidence of multiple charged incidents from a single complainant can support a tendency — you do not need separate uncharged acts or an external corroborating witness for the tendency to be legitimate circumstantial evidence going beyond mere credibility. Document the common features across incidents carefully (here: victim asleep, beside the accused, watching a movie), because specificity and repeated common features are what give tendency evidence its significant probative value. For child sexual offences, remember the s 97A presumption that such tendency evidence has significant probative value. The dissent shows the live risk where a tendency is narrow, based on very few incidents, from one complainant, and framed in the same terms as the charges — so give prosecutors a clear picture of every distinguishing detail of each incident to support both the charges and any tendency reasoning.
verdict: AWARENESS — it clarifies tendency-evidence principles and jury directions rather than changing your investigative or charging steps, but it informs how you capture and present evidence of repeated offending.
flags: Narrow 4:3 majority — Gordon, Steward and Edelman JJ would have dismissed the appeal on the basis the specific, single-complainant tendency created a real risk of undermining the standard of proof.
Complainant and accused anonymised (AR, GC, JW); accused was an adult in a relationship with the complainant's mother.
Section references (Crimes Act ss 66C(1), 66DB(a); Criminal Appeal Act s 6(1); Criminal Procedure Act s 161A; Evidence Act ss 97, 97A, 101(2)) are drawn from the judgment text and catchwords.
Case concerns trial process/jury directions; direct application to frontline investigation is indirect.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (HOWARD J), IND 1334 of 2022
outcome: Interlocutory appeal against the refusal of severance: leave to appeal refused, appeal dismissed. All seven counts remain joined on one indictment, with trial listed to commence 08/06/2026.
weight: Court of Appeal — QUINLAN CJ, SWEENEY JA and SEAWARD JA — unanimous joint reasons of the Court. Binding appellate authority in WA on joinder and severance, but it applies settled principles from HTN and JHN to its own facts.
oneLine: Court of Appeal upholds the refusal to sever three dishonesty counts from four disqualified-management counts, because the earlier conduct was cross-admissible on the accused's state of mind rather than as propensity, and prejudice could be cured by jury directions.
whatHappened: PELLEW faces seven Commonwealth charges in the District Court arising from a Perth labour hire business. Counts 1 to 3 allege that on 10/05/2018, 14/05/2018 and 28/05/2018, as sole director of Ochre Training Pty Ltd, she dishonestly used her position to authorise transfers totalling $739,655 to Ochre Workforce Solutions Pty Ltd, a company she had incorporated on 11/04/2018, contrary to Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) s 184(2)(a). The Crown alleges illegal phoenixing: a Federal Court application by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxation to wind up Ochre Training was already pending when PELLEW shifted the business to the new entity, to avoid the outcome of the liquidator's appointment that came on 29/05/2018. Counts 4 to 7 allege that between 13/03/2019 and 21/02/2020, having become an undischarged bankrupt on 20/02/2019 and disqualified from managing corporations, she participated in making decisions affecting the whole or a substantial part of the business of Ochre People Pty Ltd, contrary to s 206A(1)(a). Trial dates were vacated twice. On 12/09/2025 PELLEW applied under Criminal Procedure Act 2004 (WA) s 133 to sever counts 1 to 3 from counts 4 to 7; HOWARD J refused it on the morning of trial. She sought leave to appeal that refusal.
whatHeld: Leave to appeal refused; appeal dismissed. Under sch 1 cl 7(3)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Act 2004 (WA), offences may be charged together if they 'form or are a part of a series of offences of the same or a similar character'; applying HTN v The State of Western Australia, legal character is only one factor. There was a common 'substratum of fact': PELLEW the driving force behind a single 'Ochre' brand labour hire business, moved between entities she controlled. Evidence of the counts 1 to 3 transfers was admissible on her state of mind on counts 4 to 7, where the Crown must prove awareness of a substantial risk her decisions affected Ochre People's business. It involved no propensity reasoning: applying Harriman v The Queen and Ivanoff v The Queen, knowledge from earlier conduct proves an actual state of mind, not a tendency. On prejudice, s 133(5) lets a court hold prejudice curable by direction even where evidence on one charge is inadmissible on another. The dishonesty was the real risk, and the general directions in The State of Western Australia v JHN were only the baseline: two further case-specific directions were called for.
whatItMeans: This is a pretrial ruling about how an indictment is built, on Commonwealth corporate charges a long way from your work, so it changes nothing about how you investigate. First, what kept the counts together was precisely identifying what the earlier conduct proved and by what path of reasoning. When your brief covers several episodes or a course of conduct across years, spell out which fact in issue each piece of earlier conduct goes to and on what reasoning. Hill is cited here for the point that calling something 'context' is not enough — the particular permissible use has to be identified. Second, on juries: because juries routinely follow directions not to reason across charges in sexual and physical violence cases, the Court held that a fortiori they could do so on commercial charges. That is a premise, not a ruling on severance in such matters, which still turns on cross-admissibility and prejudice under s 133. Offences alleged in 2018 and 2019 were first listed for trial in December 2022 and are now set down for June 2026, with trial dates vacated three times and severance argued on the morning of trial. Late pretrial argument is what burns trial dates.
verdict: AWARENESS — a joinder and severance ruling; it does not change how you investigate. The reasoning on why earlier conduct proves a later state of mind is worth carrying into multi-episode briefs.

appealFrom: Supreme Court of New South Wales (Court of Criminal Appeal)
outcome: Appeal dismissed. The Crown (appellant) ordered to pay the respondent's costs of the special leave application and the appeal.
weight: High Court of Australia — binding and authoritative on the interaction of s 53A of the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW), s 16AAA of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) and s 68 of the Judiciary Act 1903 (Cth). Decided 6:1 on the mandatory-minimum point (Jagot J dissenting).
oneLine: The High Court confirmed NSW courts can impose aggregate sentences under s 53A of the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW) for multiple Commonwealth offences, even where one carries a mandatory minimum under s 16AAA of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth).
whatHappened: Andrew Stuart McGREGOR pleaded guilty to four Commonwealth child sex offences (with a fifth taken into account) arising from interactions over about two months via social media with a 15-year-old child in the Philippines while he was in Australia, plus possession of child abuse material relating to other children. One offence — persistent sexual abuse of a child outside Australia contrary to s 272.11(1)(c) of the Criminal Code (Cth) — carried a mandatory minimum of 7 years under s 16AAA. The District Court imposed an aggregate sentence of 11 years 6 months (non-parole 8 years). The NSW Court of Criminal Appeal found a conceded error in applying the guilty-plea/cooperation discount under s 16AAC(3), resentenced to an aggregate 10 years 9 months (non-parole 7 years 6 months), and rejected the Crown's arguments against aggregate sentencing. The Crown appealed to the High Court.
whatHeld: The Court dismissed the appeal. It held that s 53A aggregate sentencing is picked up and applied to Commonwealth offences by s 68(1) of the Judiciary Act 1903 (Cth), and is not inconsistent with the general sentencing scheme in Pt IB of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) (the 'wider' contention). It also held that aggregate sentencing is not inconsistent with the s 16AAA mandatory minimum (the 'narrower' contention): the word 'for' in s 16AAA does not mean 'exclusively for' that offence, so a mandatory minimum can be satisfied within an aggregate sentence provided the sentence is not less than the minimum required. The parenthetical words in s 53A(2)(b) were held to be merely descriptive of the sentencing process, not a source of inconsistency. Jagot J agreed on the wider point but would have allowed the appeal on the narrower ground, holding that s 16AAA requires the minimum term to be imposed for each such offence.
whatItMeans: This is a sentencing-law decision and has no direct effect on how you investigate, gather evidence or charge. Its value is background awareness. Note that Commonwealth child sex offences prosecuted in NSW carry mandatory minimum terms (for example 7 years for s 272.11 offences under s 16AAA), which can be reduced only for a guilty plea and/or cooperation with law enforcement (up to 25% each, 50% combined, under s 16AAC) — a practical point if you are assessing the value of an offender's cooperation. Understand that where you brief multiple Commonwealth offences, a NSW court may impose a single aggregate sentence rather than separate sentences, and that state sentencing procedure applies to federal offenders through s 68 of the Judiciary Act.
verdict: AWARENESS — a sentencing-procedure ruling that confirms how courts sentence federal offenders; it does not change your investigative, evidential or charging steps.
flags: Jagot J dissented on ground one (the mandatory-minimum point), holding s 16AAA requires the minimum term to be imposed for each such offence and would have remitted for resentencing.
The precise operation of the s 16AAC(3) discount (whether the floor is set by the actual or maximum permissible percentage) was noted by Jagot J as unresolved and not before the Court.
Decision concerns sentencing procedure only; verify current legislation before relying on section numbers or minimum-term figures.

caseName: Obeid v The King Obeid v The King Macdonald v The King
appealFrom: Court of Criminal Appeal of the Supreme Court of New South Wales
outcome: Appeals dismissed in all three matters; convictions upheld.
weight: High — unanimous seven-member High Court decision on the elements of conspiracy and misconduct in public office, binding nationally.
oneLine: The High Court confirms a conspiracy to commit misconduct in public office is complete without the conspirators agreeing on the particular acts the public official would perform, provided the agreed conduct necessarily satisfies the elements of the predicate offence.
whatHappened: Edward OBEID, Moses OBEID and Ian MACDONALD were charged on a single count of conspiring that MACDONALD, as NSW Minister for Mineral Resources, would wilfully misconduct himself in public office in connection with the granting of an exploration licence at Mount Penny, favouring the financial interests of the Obeid family who owned nearby property (Cherrydale Park). The Crown did not allege agreement to do specified particular acts, but relied on eight overt acts of misconduct (seeking coal reserve information, providing confidential maps, communicating EOI process details) from which the unlawful agreement was to be inferred. Fullerton J, sitting without a jury in the Supreme Court of NSW, convicted all three. The Court of Criminal Appeal dismissed their conviction appeals. The High Court granted leave on a single ground: whether the Crown put a case capable at law of amounting to conspiracy to commit misconduct in public office where no agreement to do particular acts was alleged.
whatHeld: The appeals were dismissed unanimously. There is no general principle that the object of a conspiracy must be reduced to particular specified acts — courts allow conspiracy to be alleged in fairly general terms. A conspiracy is complete upon agreement being made, even where the precise means or methods are unknown or not agreed. The agreement here was of a conditional kind: that MACDONALD would exercise his ministerial powers over Mount Penny to favour the Obeids' financial interests if and when the occasion arose, whatever the particular acts turned out to be. Because the agreed conduct necessarily fell within cumulative descriptive conditions that satisfied every element of the predicate offence of misconduct in public office, the agreement necessarily entailed that Macdonald would commit that offence. The fifth element (misconduct serious and meriting criminal punishment) is a matter for the tribunal of fact, not something the conspirators must agree upon; given the high office of a Minister, there were no realistic circumstances where acts answering those characteristics would not satisfy it. The prosecution remains constrained by three requirements: an agreement, to do an act that necessarily amounts to a crime, particularised as fully as the subject matter will bear.
whatItMeans: When investigating conspiracy to commit misconduct in public office (or conspiracy generally), you do not need to prove the conspirators agreed on the exact acts the offender would carry out. It is enough to establish an agreement that the official would use their office for an improper purpose in a way that necessarily breaches their duties. The unlawful agreement can be inferred from overt acts done in furtherance of it — so build your brief around documented conduct (requests for confidential information, disclosures, directions) that shows a common goal, even if the plan was open-ended. Focus on establishing: the identity of the public official and their office/powers, the duties owed (here impartiality and confidentiality, sourced from codes of conduct), the improper purpose, and a causal 'but for' link between the conduct and the improper purpose. Remember the more general the alleged agreement, the harder it may be to prove a genuine meeting of minds and that the agreement necessarily involved a crime — so particularise as tightly as the evidence allows. The seriousness element is for the court to assess, not something the conspirators need to have contemplated.
verdict: AWARENESS — this confirms established conspiracy principles and clarifies charging scope for misconduct-in-office conspiracies; it shapes how you frame such briefs rather than changing day-to-day investigative practice.
flags: Conspiracy to commit misconduct in public office is a common law offence; the predicate offence has five elements as stated in Sin Kam Wah and developed by Australian appellate courts
The Court expressly left unresolved whether the 'but for' element from Maitland is a true element of misconduct in public office or merely describes a circumstance
Conduct dates span 2007-2009; judgment relates to a Minister's exercise of powers under the Mining Act 1992 (NSW), Pt 5
cleaner: years LATER than the citation year (decide: legitimate future date, or citator bleed?): 2041: R v Macdonald [No 17] [2021] NSWSC 858 at [2041].

appealFrom: Supreme Court of New South Wales (Court of Criminal Appeal) — WHS No 2 [2024] NSWCCA 242
outcome: Appeal dismissed; convictions on Counts 2 and 5 stand (matter had been remitted to the District Court for resentencing).
weight: High. A unanimous five-judge High Court decision authoritatively construing s 293 (now s 294CB) of the Criminal Procedure Act 1986 (NSW), building on Cook (a pseudonym) v The King and HG v The Queen.
oneLine: The prosecution merely leading a child complainant's age and not adducing evidence of prior sexual experience does not "disclose or imply" a lack of sexual experience so as to unlock cross-examination under s 293(6) of the Criminal Procedure Act 1986 (NSW).
whatHappened: WHS was convicted at a 2023 retrial (the second trial) of four sexual offences against MW, a child under ten. The offending was alleged between 27/01/2010 and 10/11/2012; MW first described the abuse to police on 13-14/11/2012 when aged nine. Before trial, WHS applied to adduce FACS records and a 2017 police interview suggesting MW had displayed sexualised behaviour and been exposed to sexual matters by others (including a young male, AT), and to cross-examine MW about viewing pornographic movies with cousins. This material was said to explain how a nine-year-old could describe the abuse in detail. The trial judge ruled it inadmissible under s 293(3). The Court of Criminal Appeal quashed two convictions (Counts 1 and 4) as unreasonable but upheld Counts 2 and 5, and rejected the s 293 argument and a complaint about the Crown's closing address. WHS appealed to the High Court.
whatHeld: The appeal was dismissed. The "case for the prosecution" in s 293(6) is not confined to the prosecutor's opening or closing address — it embraces the entirety of how the case is presented, including implicit steps in the reasoning towards guilt. However, there is a critical distinction: a prosecution case that discloses or implies a lack of sexual experience is different from the prosecution merely adducing evidence of a complainant whose age alone creates a risk the jury will assume or infer a lack of sexual experience. The latter does not engage s 293(6). The prosecution has no free-standing power to adduce sexual-experience evidence; s 293(3) binds it, so the required "disclosure or implication" ordinarily arises only where the prosecution has obtained a ruling and led such evidence under a s 293(4) exception. A mere risk that the jury might assume or infer a lack of prior sexual experience from the complainant's age and the absence of such evidence is not sufficient. Accepting WHS's argument would engage s 293(6) in effectively every case involving a complainant aged nine or under, gutting the statutory protection for a vulnerable class. On Ground 2, the four excluded FACS documents did not contradict or weaken the Crown's closing submission explaining MW's delay in complaining, so no unfairness or miscarriage was established.
whatItMeans: When you are building a child sexual assault brief in NSW, understand that s 293 (now s 294CB) strongly restricts any evidence of a complainant's prior sexual experience or activity, and this protection is at its strongest for young children. The prosecution cannot freely lead such evidence to bolster the case — it must fit a s 293(4) exception and obtain a court ruling. For your investigative approach, do not assume that material suggesting a child had prior sexual exposure (which might "explain" their knowledge) will ever reach the jury: the defence cannot cross-examine on it just because the child's young age might lead jurors to infer sexual naivety. The pathway to cross-examination only opens where the prosecution actually discloses or implies a lack of experience through evidence led or submissions made — not from age alone or from what evidence was left out. Practically, be careful in your dealings and disclosure obligations: this case grew from earlier convictions being quashed because potentially exculpatory FACS material was not disclosed in answer to a subpoena. Ensure all relevant records are identified and disclosed even where admissibility is contested. Also note a prosecutor's closing that explains delayed complaint must fairly reflect the evidence.
verdict: AWARENESS-level authority: it clarifies the law on admissibility and cross-examination limits rather than changing your day-to-day evidence-gathering, but the disclosure lesson underneath it is directly relevant to how you build a brief.
flags: This is a NSW appeal construing NSW legislation; the sexual assault communications/history provisions differ in WA, so treat the statutory detail as jurisdiction-specific and confirm the WA equivalents before applying.
Section 293 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1986 (NSW) was renumbered as s 294CB from 01/06/2022; the judgment uses the old numbering.
The victim and accused are pseudonymised/de-identified (WHS, MW, DB, JW, AT); reporting restrictions apply.

appealFrom: Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Victoria
outcome: Crown appeal allowed; Court of Appeal orders set aside; convictions restored; sentence leave application remitted to the Victorian Court of Appeal.
weight: High persuasive authority — a unanimous seven-judge High Court decision applying and reinforcing its recent ruling in R v Churchill.
oneLine: Applying R v Churchill, a complainant's distress when making a pre-trial complaint is admissible circumstantial evidence that the offending occurred; in Victoria no "unreliable" direction about it is required or permitted absent substantial and compelling reasons.
whatHappened: TSALKOS was convicted in the County Court of Victoria of two charges of kidnapping and two of rape with aggravating circumstances against two teenage complainants, AB (16) and JJ (15), and of four charges of procuring or inciting an act of gross indecency with a person under 16, each committed against JJ, over events in 1987. AB's mother gave evidence, without objection, that she found AB "very very distressed" at the hospital at the time AB told her she had been raped. The trial judge directed the jury it could use the distress as indirect/circumstantial evidence supporting AB's account, but only if satisfied the distress was caused by the offending and not another reason (such as AB concealing sex work or lying to police). The Victorian Court of Appeal majority allowed TSALKOS's appeal, holding the distress was "intractably neutral" and could not support the account, and ordered a retrial. The King appealed to the High Court.
whatHeld: The appeal was allowed and the convictions restored. Applying R v Churchill, the High Court held that evidence a complainant was distressed at the time of making a pre-trial complaint is ordinarily relevant under s 55 of the Evidence Act 2008 (Vic) and admissible under s 56 to prove the offending occurred, on the basis the jury may find a causal connection between the distress and the alleged offending. The Court of Appeal erred by separating the distress from the content of the complaint, by treating "independent", "indirect" and "circumstantial" evidence as interchangeable, and by applying an abolished common law corroboration rule. The fact there could be another explanation for the distress does not make it irrelevant; that goes to weight for the jury. The distress had substantial probative value and s 137 was not engaged. The prosecutor's description of the evidence as "independent" was not a miscarriage — it meant only that it came from a source other than AB, not that it was independent corroboration.
whatItMeans: This is a Victorian decision on Victorian statutes, so it is awareness only for WA work, but the reasoning is instructive. It confirms that a complainant's observable distress at the time of complaint is not "neutral" filler — where witnessed by another person it can be evidence that the offence occurred, not just a boost to credit. When you take statements from a person present when a complaint was first made (a parent, friend, first responder), record their observations of the complainant's emotional and physical state carefully and precisely, and note the timing relative to the complaint. Do not assume such evidence is worthless because innocent explanations exist — that is a jury question. Check how WA's Evidence Act 1906 and Criminal Procedure Act 2004 treat this before relying on the specific holdings.
verdict: AWARENESS: it sharpens how you gather and value distress/first-complaint evidence, but it turns on Victorian legislation, so confirm the WA position before applying it operationally.
flags: Decision turns on Victorian legislation (Evidence Act 2008 (Vic); Jury Directions Act 2015 (Vic)) — confirm the equivalent WA position before applying operationally
Offending dates from 1987; rape charged as a common law offence at the time
Key holdings rely on and apply R v Churchill (2025) 99 ALJR 719 — read alongside that decision

caseName: Garlett v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Western Australia (part removed into the High Court under s 40 of the Judiciary Act 1903 (Cth))
outcome: That part of the appeal removed into the High Court was dismissed. The HRSO Act was held valid in its application to robbery (item 34).
weight: High Court of Australia, majority decision (5:2). Binding and authoritative nationally; the leading authority on the validity of WA's preventive detention regime for non-sexual, non-terrorism serious offences.
oneLine: The High Court upheld the validity of WA's High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 as it applies to robbery, confirming post-sentence preventive detention/supervision orders do not breach Ch III of the Constitution.
whatHappened: GARLETT, then 23, in company entered a home without consent on 19/11/2017, pretended to be armed with a handgun, threatened violence and stole a pendant and $20. He pleaded guilty to robbery and assault with intent to rob (ss 392 and 393 Criminal Code (WA)) and was sentenced (total effective three years six months, plus a further five months for criminal damage in custody). His release date was 19/10/2021. On 29/07/2021 the State applied for a restriction order under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA), treating robbery as a 'serious offence' under item 34 of Subdiv 3 of Div 1 of Sch 1. GARLETT challenged the validity of the Act in its application to robbery, arguing it breached the Kable principle in Ch III of the Constitution. The Kable ground was removed into the High Court.
whatHeld: By majority (Kiefel CJ, Keane, Steward, Edelman and Gleeson JJ; Gageler and Gordon JJ dissenting), the High Court held the HRSO Act is valid in its application to robbery and does not infringe the Kable principle. The function conferred on the Supreme Court is materially indistinguishable from the Queensland scheme upheld in Fardon. The purpose of the scheme is protective, not punitive: any curtailment of liberty must be supported by the court's own risk evaluation under s 7, must be no greater than necessary to protect the community, and is subject to regular review. The court makes its own evaluative judgment and is not acting under dictation from the executive — the mandatory 'must' in s 48(1) only engages after the court is independently satisfied under s 7. The determination of which offences are 'serious' is a matter for the legislature, and including robbery (with maximum penalties up to life) is not inimical to the court's integrity. The scheme bears the hallmarks of judicial process: onus on the State, rules of evidence, right to be heard, public hearings, reasons, and a right of appeal.
whatItMeans: This confirms the HRSO Act regime is constitutionally sound for robbery offenders, so applications for restriction orders against serious offenders convicted of robbery (and other Sch 1 offences) remain a valid tool. For your casework, note the scheme is protective not punitive — an order is justified only by a forward-looking risk assessment, not as further punishment. Evidence quality matters: the State carries the onus and must prove an unacceptable risk to a high degree of probability by acceptable and cogent evidence (s 7), so build a thorough package — psychiatric/psychological assessments, criminal history, patterns of offending, antecedents, and rehabilitation efforts. Note the majority's emphasis (especially Edelman J) that risk must relate to a specified serious offence the offender has a relevant propensity to commit; an unrelated criminal record may say little about the specified risk. Continuing detention is an order of last resort behind supervision orders. Be aware several judges flagged the breadth of the Act and the risk it could sweep up minor offending and Indigenous offenders disproportionately.
verdict: AWARENESS — this is a constitutional validity ruling confirming an existing tool remains available; it does not change day-to-day investigative method but shapes how you build evidence for restriction order applications.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
appealFrom: Supreme Court of WA
outcome: Appeal dismissed — but on the facts (the schizophrenia was not shown to operate independently of the cannabis), NOT because voluntary intoxication is an absolute bar to ss 27/28.
weight: WA Court of Appeal — binds WA courts below
oneLine: Voluntary intoxication does NOT automatically defeat an unsoundness-of-mind defence: an accused can still rely on s 27 if a mental impairment deprived them of capacity independently of the intoxication — but not where the intoxication itself (or its effect on a condition) caused it. STEFANSKI lost only because his schizophrenia couldn't be separated from his cannabis use.
whatHappened: An appeal against conviction on guilty pleas to two counts of murder. The appellant argued he could not in law be guilty (or was not guilty by reason of unsoundness of mind) where a psychosis had been triggered by his voluntary cannabis use — turning on the construction of ss 27, 28(1) and 28(2) of the Criminal Code (WA). The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. (Your instructor placed the facts at a ‘Greenwood’ murder; the judgment does not name Greenwood — the legal point and citation are what matter.)
whatHeld: The Court of Appeal (Buss P, Mazza JA, Beech JA) construed ss 27, 28(1) and 28(2) of the Criminal Code (WA) and held — rejecting the contrary view in Herbert as 'wrong' — that an accused who intentionally became intoxicated may still rely on s 27(1) if they prove, on the balance of probabilities, a 'mental impairment' that deprived them of a relevant capacity independently of and without regard to the intoxication. What s 28(2) bars is reliance on s 27 where the voluntary intoxication itself — or its effect in triggering or worsening a pre-existing condition — caused the loss of capacity. The appeal was dismissed on the facts: the psychiatric evidence could not show STEFANSKI's paranoid schizophrenia operated independently of his admitted cannabis intoxication, and his guilty pleas were a considered free choice (Meissner).
whatItMeans: The practical lesson survives, but the rule is narrower than the shorthand. Get bloods early — not because a voluntary intoxicant automatically defeats an insanity defence (it does not), but because proving what was in the system goes to the question that actually decides these cases: could the mental impairment have operated independently of the intoxicant? For any serious matter, secure a forensic blood sample before alcohol/cannabis/meth metabolises, so the psychiatric picture can be disentangled. Exam heads-up: the simplified line 'voluntary intoxication can't ground unsoundness of mind' overstates it — that is not what the Court held.
verdict: ACTION — drives an investigative step (early forensic bloods) and corrects a common overstatement of the intoxication/insanity rule.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: ISN v The State of Western Australia [No 2]
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (BIRMINGHAM DCJ), BUN IND 12 of 2019
outcome: Leave to appeal granted on ground 4; leave refused on grounds 1, 2 and 3; appeal dismissed. Convictions and 4 years 6 months' total effective sentence stand.
weight: Court of Appeal (three judges) unanimous judgment of the Court; binding on WA courts below and a clear statement of recognition/identification and circumstantial identity principles.
oneLine: Recognition evidence from a child complainant who knew the accused well, combined with a strong circumstantial case on identity, upheld a conviction for child sex offences despite a pitch-dark room and no facial recognition.
whatHappened: ISN was tried in the District Court before BIRMINGHAM DCJ on an indictment alleging four sexual offences against a girl under 13, called T. Counts 1 and 3 (indecent dealing by kissing) were contrary to Criminal Code (WA) s 320(4); counts 2 and 4 (digital penetration of the vagina) were contrary to s 320(2). The offending occurred at a country town between late 2011 and mid-2013, when T was about 8-10 years old. The accused was a close friend of T's father A and an uncle figure to T, visiting the family home very frequently and often sleeping over, along with his young daughter C, who slept in the same room as T. He was a self-described alcoholic who often drank to excess. T first told her boyfriend what had happened in about November 2017, then her school counsellor in March 2018; the complaint to police was made in April 2018. At trial the only real issue was identity: the defence did not dispute that the acts occurred, but argued the accused was not the offender and that other men also visited and drank at the house. The accused denied the offences in a video record of interview (VROI, 25/10/2018) and did not testify; his daughter C gave defence evidence. On 31/10/2019 the jury convicted on all four counts. He was sentenced to a total effective 4 years 6 months' immediate imprisonment. He appealed conviction on four grounds relating to identity directions and the reasonableness of the verdicts.
whatHeld: The Court of Appeal (BUSS P, MAZZA JA, VAUGHAN JA) refused leave on grounds 1-3, granted leave on ground 4, and dismissed the appeal. On ground 1, T's testimony was properly characterised as recognition evidence (not merely inferential) given her lifelong familiarity with the accused, her very close face-to-face physical contact with the offender, and her evidence of seeing him enter the room and lie next to C; it stood alongside the circumstantial case. On ground 2, a Domican warning is mandated only for identification cases, not ordinarily for recognition cases, because recognition evidence is generally more reliable; the judge properly reminded the jury that honest mistakes in recognition can occur even with close relatives and friends. Although it would have been preferable to specifically isolate the weaknesses in T's recognition evidence, no miscarriage arose given the short trial, the recent closing addresses, and the full Longman direction. On ground 3, the summing up was balanced. On ground 4, the Court held the circumstantial case on identity was the stronger and most compelling category: the only reasonable inference was that the accused was the offender. Evidence based on pure assumption was technically inadmissible but unobjected to and used for the defence's advantage; recognition partly by intuition was admissible (per AK v The State of Western Australia [2008] HCA 8) though of limited weight alone.
whatItMeans: This case shows how identity can be proved without any facial recognition where the complainant knew the offender well and a strong circumstantial case exists. When you build a child sex case turning on identity, focus on assembling the combination of circumstances — opportunity, frequency of access, trusted-family-friend status, prior non-sexual touching, and conduct consistent with the offender's behaviour (here, T's father finding the accused, on occasions, asleep in the bed of the accused's own daughter C — who slept in the same room as T — and the accused being by far the most regular overnight visitor). The Court found the circumstantial case more compelling than the complainant's recognition evidence itself. Note the distinction between recognition evidence (offender previously known to the witness) and identification evidence (first seen at the crime scene): the full Domican warning is mandated for identification but not ordinarily for recognition. Be aware some of T's evidence about how she 'knew' it was the accused was assumption-based and technically inadmissible — the defence chose not to object because it helped them. To strengthen future cases, gather evidence that rules out alternative male visitors (attendance patterns, who slept over, who had any contact with the child) so the innocence hypothesis is closed off. Delay to complaint (offending in 2011-13; first disclosure to her boyfriend in about November 2017, police complaint April 2018) triggered a full Longman direction.
verdict: AWARENESS: This is an appellate application of settled recognition/identification and unreasonable-verdict principles; it reinforces how to build a circumstantial identity case but does not change investigative procedure.
