flags: Complainant, accused and family members anonymised in judgment (T, C, A, P, ISN) — use initials/pseudonyms, do not attempt to identify.
Offence dates are ranges pleaded on the indictment (between 31/12/2011 and 01/07/2013), not precise dates.
The case name in the citation is 'ISN v The State of Western Australia' while the judgment header shows 'ISN v The State of Western Australia [No 2]' — noted for accuracy.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: LNN v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (STONE DCJ)
outcome: Appeal against conviction allowed; convictions on counts 2, 3, 5 and 6 set aside and new trial ordered. Extension of time granted. Appeal against sentence dismissed as redundant.
weight: Court of Appeal (three judges), Category A, delivered 08/03/2021. Binding and applies established principles (Hill, Dann, LNV, Bauer) on uncharged-acts directions. Strong authority on the need for propensity-reasoning directions.
oneLine: Convictions for child sexual offences quashed and a retrial ordered because the jury was never clearly told it could not use evidence of uncharged sexual acts as propensity reasoning.
whatHappened: LNN was tried in the District Court (STONE DCJ) on six counts of sexual offences against two girls, T (born January 2010) and H (born April 2011), both under 13, allegedly committed on one unknown day between 01/01/2015 and 12/05/2017. On 01/04/2019 he was convicted on counts 2, 3, 5 and 6 (penetration of T's mouth, masturbating in T's presence, rubbing his penis on H's genitals, and encouraging H to perform fellatio) and acquitted on counts 1 and 4. He received a total effective sentence of 8 years. Both complainants gave evidence of further sexual acts by LNN that were not charged. The prosecutor invited the jury to treat these as showing an 'unnatural relationship' and 'unhealthy sexual interest' and told them evidence of uncharged acts against one girl could be used across all six counts. He appealed conviction on four grounds and sentence on one.
whatHeld: Grounds 1-3 failed: the recent complaint direction was adequate, the mixed verdicts were reconcilable (count 1 acquittal explained by lack of specificity on penetration; count 4 acquittal by H's later evidence limiting the conduct to the lounge room), and the guilty verdicts were not unreasonable. Ground 4 succeeded. It was common ground the uncharged-acts evidence was not admitted or available as propensity evidence under s 31A Evidence Act 1906 (WA) or at common law. Because the prosecutor's address and the trial judge's directions left the permissible use unclear and invited cross-count reasoning, there was a real and not remote possibility the jury would reason by propensity. The absence of a clear direction that propensity reasoning was impermissible was a miscarriage of justice. Following Hill, a specific direction on the uses to which such evidence must not be put was required. The State did not seek to apply the proviso. Appeal allowed, convictions on counts 2, 3, 5 and 6 set aside, new trial ordered; sentence appeal dismissed as redundant.
whatItMeans: When a complainant volunteers accounts of additional sexual acts that are not charged, flag them clearly in your brief and be explicit about why they matter. If the conduct is serious and provable, consider charging it rather than leaving it as uncharged 'context'. If uncharged acts are to be used as propensity evidence, that pathway runs through s 31A Evidence Act 1906 (WA) and must be identified and pursued from the outset. The Court also noted (following Dann) that evidence of a prior demonstration of sexual interest in the complainant, proximate to the charged offending, may be admissible at common law as circumstantial evidence of motive without s 31A — but that use too has to be identified by the prosecution; it cannot be left as vague 'background'. Do not let the case theory rest on inviting a jury to think the accused is 'the kind of person' who would offend. Be careful with evidence of one complainant being used to prove charges against a different complainant: that requires a linking feature and proper admission. Record dates, places and specifics of each incident as precisely as possible — the count 1 acquittal here is explicable by T's evidence lacking the specificity needed to prove any degree of penetration of the vagina, as opposed to contact with the vaginal area.
verdict: AWARENESS-plus-action: it does not change lawful investigative powers, but it should change how you charge and frame uncharged sexual conduct so the prosecution's use of that evidence is put on a sound, s 31A footing.
flags: District Court indictment number redacted in judgment as 'IND XX of 2018'
Offence dates are a range (01/01/2015 to 12/05/2017) on an unknown single day, per the prosecution case
Complainants and other parties anonymised (T, H, C, P, M) in the judgment

appealFrom: Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Victoria
outcome: Special leave granted; appeal treated as instituted, heard instanter and allowed. Order 2 of the Court of Appeal set aside; appeal to that Court allowed; convictions quashed and judgments of acquittal entered.
weight: High Court of Australia, unanimous seven-member bench — the highest authority in Australia and binding nationally on the unreasonable-verdict test and the appellate treatment of recorded evidence.
oneLine: The High Court quashed PELL's child sexual abuse convictions, holding that unchallenged 'opportunity witness' evidence meant the jury, acting rationally, must have had a reasonable doubt.
whatHappened: George PELL was convicted by a County Court of Victoria jury on 11/12/2018 of one charge of sexual penetration of a child under 16 (Crimes Act 1958 (Vic) s 45(1)) and four charges of an act of indecency with or in the presence of a child under 16 (Crimes Act 1958 (Vic) s 47(1)). The offences were alleged against two 13-year-old choirboys (A and B) at St Patrick's Cathedral, East Melbourne, following Sunday solemn Mass in late 1996 and early 1997, shortly after PELL's installation as Archbishop of Melbourne. B had died before any complaint; A first complained in June 2015. The prosecution case rested wholly on A's evidence. This was a retrial after the first jury could not agree. The Victorian Court of Appeal (majority Ferguson CJ and Maxwell P; Weinberg JA dissenting) dismissed PELL's appeal on 21/08/2019. PELL sought special leave to the High Court on the ground the verdicts were unreasonable and unsupported by the evidence.
whatHeld: The High Court unanimously (seven judges) allowed the appeal. It held there was a significant possibility that an innocent person had been convicted because the evidence did not establish guilt to the requisite standard. On the unreasonableness ground, the correct question is whether the jury, acting rationally, must have entertained a reasonable doubt (applying M v The Queen and Libke v The Queen). Assuming the jury found A credible and reliable, the unchallenged evidence of the 'opportunity witnesses' — placing PELL on the Cathedral steps greeting congregants for at least ten minutes, accompanied by Portelli when he returned to disrobe, and describing constant traffic in and out of the priests' sacristy — created compounding improbabilities that required a reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal majority erred by asking whether it was possible A's account was true, rather than whether the prosecution had negatived the reasonable possibility that PELL did not commit the offences. The Court also held that A's detailed knowledge of the sacristy interior was not corroboration of the assaults. On appellate use of video-recorded evidence, the Court affirmed SKA v The Queen: the mere availability of a recording does not require an appeal court to view it, and demeanour assessment remains the province of the jury.
whatItMeans: This is primarily an evidence-quality lesson for your casework. Where a case depends wholly on one complainant's account, a finding that the complainant is credible does not end the matter — the whole body of evidence must still be capable of excluding a reasonable doubt. Unchallenged evidence of routine, practice and ritual can carry significant probative weight and can defeat a conviction if it is inconsistent with the alleged offending. Build your brief to anticipate 'opportunity' evidence: identify every witness to movements, timings, locks, and practices, and test whether the offending had a realistic opportunity to occur. Remember the correct standard — the prosecution must negative the reasonable possibility that the accused did not do it, not merely show it was possible he did. In historical/delayed-complaint matters, expect the forensic disadvantage from long delay (lost witnesses, memory decay, no chance to make contemporaneous inquiries) to weigh heavily, so preserve and lock down corroborating evidence early. Note too that a complainant's accurate knowledge of a location proves presence, not the offence — it is not corroboration.
verdict: AWARENESS-level but important: it does not change WA charging law, yet it sets the benchmark for how single-witness sexual offence cases are assessed for reasonableness on the whole of the evidence — build your briefs accordingly.
flags: Offences charged under Victorian legislation (Crimes Act 1958 (Vic) ss 45(1), 47(1)); confirm equivalent WA provisions before applying to charging.
Procedural and evidentiary references are to Victorian statutes (Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (Vic), Jury Directions Act 2015 (Vic), Evidence Act 2008 (Vic)) — WA has different legislation.
Judgment noted it was subject to formal revision prior to publication in the Commonwealth Law Reports.

appealFrom: Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Queensland
outcome: Leave to amend the notice of appeal granted; special leave granted on ground 2; appeal dismissed. Conviction on count 2 stands.
weight: High Court of Australia, five-judge bench, majority of four (Nettle J dissenting). Binding and authoritative on the availability and preferred form of Liberato directions.
oneLine: High Court confirms a Liberato direction is not required as a matter of law where the accused does not give sworn evidence, but may be needed where exculpatory answers in a police interview create a real risk the jury will reason wrongly about proof.
whatHappened: DE SILVA was tried in the District Court of Queensland on two counts of rape (digital penetration without consent) against the same complainant on the same occasion, under Criminal Code (Qld) s 349. The prosecution case depended on the complainant's evidence. DE SILVA did not give or call evidence, but his recorded police interview — in which he denied any digital penetration — was in evidence. The trial judge gave conventional onus and standard of proof directions but no Liberato direction (none was requested). The jury acquitted on count 1 and convicted on count 2. The Queensland Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal. He appealed to the High Court.
whatHeld: The appeal was dismissed (Kiefel CJ, Bell, Gageler and Gordon JJ; Nettle J dissenting). A Liberato direction is not required as a matter of law simply because the accused fails to give sworn evidence. However, where the accused's conflicting version is before the jury — including as exculpatory answers in a record of interview — a Liberato direction should be given if the trial judge perceives a real risk the jury might reason that the accused's account can only raise a reasonable doubt if they believe it, or that a preference for the complainant's evidence suffices to establish guilt. The Court endorsed a three-limbed form: (i) if you believe the accused's account, acquit; (ii) if you do not accept it but think it might be true, acquit; (iii) if you do not believe it, put it aside and ask whether the prosecution has proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt on the evidence you do accept. On the facts, the summing-up read as a whole made clear the jury could not convict if the exculpatory answers left them with a reasonable doubt, so no miscarriage occurred. Nettle J dissented, finding the directions likely left the jury thinking they could disregard the exculpatory answers unless satisfied they were "accurate and true".
whatItMeans: This is a trial-directions case, not an investigation rule, so it mainly shapes how the case is run at trial rather than how you gather evidence. The practical point for your casework: a suspect's exculpatory answers in a recorded interview are evidence that can raise a reasonable doubt even if the accused never testifies. Do not treat denials in a record of interview as easily brushed aside — they carry forensic weight. When you build a case that turns on the complainant's account against a denial in interview, expect the defence to rely heavily on that interview, and understand that a jury cannot simply prefer the complainant and convict; the Crown must still prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Conduct thorough interviews and record them accurately, because those answers remain live at trial.
verdict: AWARENESS only — this changes trial directions, not how you investigate or charge, but reinforces that a suspect's recorded exculpatory denials are substantive evidence capable of raising reasonable doubt.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: The State of Western Australia v Jackson
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (BOWDEN DCJ) — The State of Western Australia v Jackson [2019] WADC 91
outcome: Appeal allowed; the primary judge's order for separate trials of counts 3 and 4 set aside; all four counts to be tried together.
weight: Strong. Unanimous judgment of a three-member Court of Appeal (BUSS P, MITCHELL and BEECH JJA), applying High Court authority (McPhillamy, Bauer, Hughes) and settled WA authority on s 31A.
oneLine: Child exploitation material can be cross-admissible propensity evidence proving a touching was deliberate and sexually motivated (indecent) — but not that the touching occurred.
whatHappened: JACKSON faced a four-count indictment. Counts 1 and 2 alleged that on 18/04/2018 he indecently dealt with two 12-year-old girls (triplets) by touching them on the buttocks with the back of his hand as he passed them in a supermarket aisle; he denied any physical contact. Five days later, on 23/04/2018, police searched his home and seized an iPhone and iPad. Count 3 alleged possession of one category 1 child exploitation image (a girl aged about 10–12 in a bikini) and count 4 alleged using a carriage service to access eight category 1 images of girls aged 8–13 in underwear/bikinis in posing photographs — four of which were open in his Safari browser. He admitted accessing images of young girls in bikinis in 'provocative poses', said he found them intriguing, but denied a sexual interest in children. The District Court judge (BOWDEN DCJ) ordered counts 3 and 4 severed and tried separately, finding the images lacked significant probative value for counts 1 and 2. The State appealed the severance.
whatHeld: The Court of Appeal (BUSS P, MITCHELL and BEECH JJA) allowed the appeal and set aside the order for separate trials. The evidence on counts 3 and 4 was cross-admissible propensity evidence under s 31A of the Evidence Act 1906 (WA), but only for a specific purpose. It had significant probative value in proving that any independently established touching was deliberate and sexually motivated, and thus indecent. The images were cogent evidence that, at a time closely proximate to the alleged offences, JACKSON had a sexual interest in pre-adolescent girls. Because jurors would ordinarily assume the vast majority of adult men are not sexually attracted to 12-year-old girls, evidence rebutting that assumption significantly bears on whether the touching was sexually motivated. The Court distinguished McPhillamy: there, tendency-to-act evidence was used to prove conduct occurred; here the propensity evidence is used only after the jury independently finds the touching occurred, to determine state of mind. Critically, the Court held the images did not have significant probative value in proving that the touching in fact occurred — the mere fact an accused has a sexual interest in a class the complainant belongs to is not significantly probative of whether the contact happened, and there was no linking or common feature between viewing images and physically touching children (applying Bauer and McPhillamy). The temporal proximity (five days) and the unusual nature of the sexual interest were key. The Court set out the required jury directions: the images must be disregarded in deciding whether the touching occurred, but may be used to assess deliberateness and sexual motivation once touching is established.
whatItMeans: When you investigate indecent dealing where the physical act is capable of an innocent explanation (like a brush of the hand in a crowded aisle), evidence of a suspect's sexual interest in children — including possession of or access to child exploitation material — can be admissible to prove the touching was deliberate and sexually motivated, which is what makes it indecent. Gather and preserve that CEM evidence: seize and forensically examine devices, capture what was open in browsers, and record admissions about accessing images. Temporal proximity matters — here the images were accessed only five days after the alleged offending, which was central. But be clear about the limits: this kind of evidence will not help prove the touching actually happened — for that you still need the complainants' accounts and other independent evidence, and you would need a genuine linking or common feature between the CEM and the charged conduct. Note the case also confirms the key elements of indecent dealing here: the State must prove the contact was deliberate (not accidental) and sexually motivated. The distinction the Court drew is that the unusual nature of a sexual interest in pre-adolescent girls is what gives it force — the same reasoning would not apply to, say, images of adult women where a defendant is charged with assaulting an adult.
verdict: AWARENESS — this refines when child exploitation material is cross-admissible in contact offending, but does not itself change how you gather evidence; the practical takeaway is to secure device and CEM evidence and note its limited permissible use.

appealFrom: Magistrates Court of Western Australia (Magistrate M RIDLEY), PH 137 of 2018
outcome: Leave to appeal refused; appeal dismissed. The acquittal stands.
weight: Single-judge Supreme Court decision on appeal from the Magistrates Court; persuasive and directly on point for indecent assault charges involving the buttocks, applying binding authority (Drago) and recent Court of Appeal authority (HTD).
oneLine: Whether an assault is indecent turns on the nature and location of the touch plus the actor's motive and context — buttocks are not inherently sexual, so a non-sexual pinch to provoke a photo reaction was not indecent.
whatHappened: On 08/12/2017, at a charity wheelchair basketball event at Wanangkura Stadium, South Hedland, the respondent RAMSDEN — a police officer — ran into a group photo, then pinched the complainant on the side of her right buttock while saying words to the effect of 'I hope you take this the right way'. It was common ground the act was an unlawful assault; the only issue was whether it was indecent under s 323 of the Criminal Code. The prosecution accepted RAMSDEN had no sexual motive, intending only a misguided attempt at humour to provoke a startled reaction for the photo. On 29/03/2018 Magistrate RIDLEY acquitted him after a two-day trial, finding the touch (a pinch to the side of the buttock, not a full cupped grab) was capable of being indecent but was not inherently so, and on the facts was inappropriate but not indecent. The prosecution appealed.
whatHeld: SMITH J refused leave to appeal and dismissed the appeal. 'Indecent' is not defined in the Code; whether an assault is indecent is a question of fact for the trier of fact, requiring a sexual character or connotation. Some body parts (breasts, vagina, penis, testicles, anus) are inherently sexual so that touching them, without explanation, is indecent regardless of motive. The buttocks are not such a part — there is no authority that any touch of the buttocks carries a sexual connotation. Where an act is not inherently sexual, the motive, purpose and surrounding circumstances (nature and location of the touch) are relevant to whether it is indecent (following Drago, Harkin, Court, Gillespie, HTD). The magistrate correctly asked 'why did he do it?' and, with the prosecution not contesting the innocent explanation, was entitled to find the pinch inappropriate but not indecent. Appellate courts should be reluctant to interfere with a magistrate's assessment of community standards. There was no evidence the 'Me Too' movement had changed what the law deems indecent.
whatItMeans: When you are assessing a possible indecent assault under s 323, identify the body part touched. Touching of genitals, anus, or a female breast is inherently sexual — you do not need to prove a sexual motive. For other areas, including the buttocks, the touch is NOT automatically indecent. You must build evidence of the surrounding circumstances, the nature and location of the touch, and the suspect's motive or purpose to establish a sexual connotation. Do not assume a grab or pinch of the buttocks is indecent on its own. Gather and preserve context evidence — CCTV, phone footage, witness accounts, and anything showing intent — because the physical exhibits may be treated as more reliable than memories, and the location of the touch (e.g. side of buttock vs full grab) can be decisive. If the person offers an innocent explanation, test it hard and gather material to rebut it, because an uncontested innocent explanation can defeat the indecency element. Note the buttocks are 'private parts' under the Criminal Investigation (Identifying People) Act 2002, but that definition does not make touching them indecent.
verdict: ACTION — it changes what you gather before you charge: for the buttocks, or any other body part that is not inherently sexual, indecency under s 323 of the Criminal Code is not automatic, so you must evidence the nature and location of the touch, the surrounding circumstances and the suspect's motive or purpose, and test any innocent explanation hard, because an uncontested one defeats the element.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Gibson v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: Supreme Court of WA
outcome: Appeal allowed; manslaughter conviction (on a guilty plea) set aside; judgment of acquittal entered — no retrial. (Orders made 12/04/2017; the Court's reasons, [2017] WASCA 141, were published 28/07/2017.)
weight: WA Court of Appeal — binds WA courts below
oneLine: GIBSON — a Pintupi man with significant cognitive impairment and very little English — pleaded guilty to a manslaughter he likely never understood he could fight. The plea lacked integrity, so the conviction was set aside and a judgment of acquittal entered.
whatHappened: Joshua WARNEKE was found dead beside Old Broome Road in February 2010. GIBSON — an 18-year-old Pintupi man from Kiwirrkurra, unable to read English and with significant cognitive impairment — was charged with murder in 2012. His records of interview were excluded at first instance (not voluntary; Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA) breaches; an interpreter plainly required). With the interviews gone, the case rested on companion witnesses whose accounts kept shifting. Instructions to plead were taken at two rushed conferences — one with no interpreter, one with an interpreter not accredited in his language — and GIBSON pleaded guilty to manslaughter, receiving 7 years 6 months. Official reviews later found the inculpatory witness statements had falsely implicated him.
whatHeld: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal under s 30(3)(c) of the Criminal Appeals Act 2004 (WA): a conviction founded on a guilty plea will be set aside as a miscarriage of justice where the integrity of the plea is impugned — here because GIBSON's significant cognitive impairment and profound language disability meant he did not sufficiently understand the plea or the real choice between pleading guilty and standing trial (where an acquittal would mean release). The recognised categories for overturning a guilty plea are not closed (Vella), and the rule that a plea is a free choice by a person 'of sound mind and understanding' (Meissner) presupposes an understanding he did not have. Because the only inculpatory witnesses were now unreliable and could not properly be led — leaving no case to answer — the Court entered a judgment of acquittal rather than ordering a retrial (s 30(5)(b)).
whatItMeans: Your lessons sit in what went wrong, not the appeal point. Get the interview right: GIBSON's records of interview were thrown out for involuntariness and Criminal Investigation Act breaches, and once they were gone the case had no spine. For a vulnerable or Aboriginal suspect, use a properly accredited interpreter in the right language and a prisoner's friend, and explain the caution phrase by phrase — an untrained community member standing in as interpreter was not enough (read with Anunga). And don't shape your witnesses: the case collapsed because companion accounts shifted and 'critical details' had been introduced by interviewers — keep questions non-leading, corroborate independently, and keep investigating beyond the admission. (The 'reasonable suspicion / suspect status' point you may link to 'Gibson' is actually the separate first-instance ruling that excluded the interviews — The State of WA v Gibson [2014] WASC 240 — not this appeal.)
verdict: ACTION — a wrongful-conviction cautionary tale that drives interview discipline: lawful, voluntary, properly-interpreted records of interview, and witness evidence you have not contaminated.

appealFrom: Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Queensland
outcome: Crown appeal allowed; orders of the Queensland Court of Appeal set aside; appeal to that Court dismissed; jury's murder conviction restored.
weight: Unanimous decision of five Justices of the High Court of Australia; binding and authoritative nationally on circumstantial evidence, intent, post-offence conduct and the review of "unreasonable verdict" appeals.
oneLine: The High Court restored Gerard BADEN-CLAY's murder conviction, holding that a hypothesis of unintentional killing not raised at trial and contradicted by his own evidence could not render the jury's verdict unreasonable.
whatHappened: Allison BADEN-CLAY disappeared from her home overnight on 19/20 April 2012; her body was found on 30/04/2012 under a bridge at Kholo Creek, about 13km away. The respondent had been in a long-running affair with Ms McHugh, had promised to leave his wife by 1 July, and faced the prospect of both women attending the same conference the next day. He had fingernail-type scratches on his cheek (which he claimed were shaving cuts), gave false accounts to police about the affair, and told Ms McHugh to "lie low." Leaves from his home were found on the body and the deceased's blood was in her car. He gave evidence at trial denying any involvement in her death. A Queensland jury convicted him of murder on 15/07/2014. The Queensland Court of Appeal substituted a manslaughter verdict, finding the prosecution had not excluded a hypothesis (raised for the first time on appeal) that he struck her in a struggle and she died from a fall without intent to kill or cause grievous bodily harm. The Crown appealed to the High Court.
whatHeld: The appeal was allowed and the murder conviction restored. The Court held the hypothesis relied on by the Court of Appeal was not open on the evidence — it was mere speculation, contrary to the accused's own sworn evidence (which placed him absent from the death) and contrary to the deliberate tactical way the defence was run at trial. Where an accused gives evidence that excludes a scenario, that scenario cannot found a reasonable doubt; disbelieving an accused does not let an appeal court treat his evidence as never given and substitute its own conjecture. The Court reaffirmed that in a circumstantial case guilt must be the only rational inference on the whole of the evidence, which must be considered as a whole and not piecemeal. It held there is no rule that post-offence concealment and lies are always "intractably neutral" as between murder and manslaughter — the lengths of concealment may support an inference of intent to kill or cause grievous bodily harm. The Court of Appeal erred in dismissing the affair, financial stress and looming exposure as not capable of being relevant to motive and intent. Setting aside a jury verdict as unreasonable is a serious step given the jury's central constitutional role.
whatItMeans: This is a leading authority on building and proving circumstantial murder cases and on the evidentiary value of consciousness-of-guilt evidence. For your casework it confirms that lies, concealment of the body, and post-offence conduct are not automatically neutral on intent — the scale and nature of concealment can support an inference of murderous intent, so gather and document that conduct thoroughly. Motive evidence (relationship strain, an affair, financial pressure, looming exposure) is relevant to proving intent even where there is no premeditation, so build out the surrounding relationship and circumstantial picture. Remember the prosecution must exclude all reasonable hypotheses consistent with innocence, but a "bare possibility" or speculation is not a reasonable hypothesis — and where facts lie solely within a suspect's knowledge, unsupported innocent explanations carry little weight (Weissensteiner). Present the evidence as a whole, not piecemeal.
verdict: AWARENESS authority: it does not change investigative procedure, but it shapes how you assemble circumstantial proof of intent and treat post-offence conduct and lies as probative rather than neutral.

caseName: The State of Western Australia v Gibson
appealFrom: Not an appeal — pre-trial admissibility ruling by a single judge (HALL J) of the Supreme Court of Western Australia before trial.
outcome: All police interviews of 16 and 17 August 2012 ruled inadmissible — not voluntary, obtained in breach of the CIA, and unfair to admit.
weight: Considered, detailed single-judge Supreme Court ruling applying settled High Court authority (McDermott, Lee, Swaffield) and the Anunga guidelines; persuasive and practically instructive, though a first-instance admissibility decision rather than an appellate precedent.
oneLine: Confessions by an Aboriginal partial-English speaker were ruled inadmissible: he was a suspect who should have been recorded and cautioned from the outset, no interpreter was used, and his interview friend pressured him to talk.
whatHappened: GIBSON, a Pintupi man from the remote Kiwirrkurra community, was charged with the murder of Joshua WARNEKE (deceased 26/02/2010). In 2012 multiple witnesses named him as the driver of a stolen car that struck a white man. Detective Sergeant JOHNSTON's inquiry report of 22/05/2012 recommended an audiovisual record of interview so that any confessional evidence was captured in admissible form; the intended interviewing officers, Detective Senior Constables GAZZONE and SHANNON, each prepared a plan (an interview plan and an action plan) contemplating that GIBSON would be arrested on suspicion of murder. The officer in charge, Detective Sergeant WESTERN, reviewed those plans and decided GIBSON would be approached as a witness only. On 16/08/2012 police travelled to Kiwirrkurra, conducted an unrecorded interview without caution or interpreter, and only after GIBSON said 'Mistake. Hit him with car' did they arrest and start a video interview. An interview friend, Mr BUTLER (a senior kin relative), spoke to GIBSON in Pintupi throughout, repeatedly directing him to talk and tell the truth. GIBSON asked to speak to a lawyer; the ALS lawyer (Ms KILBY) told police he did not wish to answer questions, but police continued. He was then held overnight at Kintore and flown to Broome for a further recorded interview the next day, again with no interpreter or interview friend.
whatHeld: Hall J ruled all interviews inadmissible on three independent bases. (1) Not voluntary: as a suspect GIBSON should have been cautioned from the outset but was not; he did not understand the caution when later given; and his will was overborne because Mr BUTLER, an older kin relative, effectively commanded him to answer. (2) Breaches of the Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA): the initial admissions were not recorded contrary to s 118 with no reasonable excuse, and once arrested he was not given a qualified interpreter as required by s 137(3)(d) and s 138(2)(d); the s 155 discretion to admit was refused. (3) Unfairness discretion: it would be unfair to admit the interviews given his severely limited English, no independent interpreter, no interview friend of his choosing, the pressure applied, and the continuation of questioning after his lawyer said he did not wish to answer. The Court held whether a person is a suspect is a question of fact, not a matter of formal police decision — the available information objectively supported a reasonable suspicion of murder, and the interviewing officers in fact held that suspicion before travelling.
whatItMeans: When you decide how to treat a person, remember the court will judge suspect status objectively on the facts, not on the label you attach. If the information before you would support a reasonable suspicion, treat the person as a suspect: caution them and record from the outset. You cannot avoid recording obligations by calling someone a witness — the ready availability of recording gear here meant there was no reasonable excuse under s 118. With any Aboriginal person, and especially remote-community speakers, do not assume English fluency. Casual conversation ability is not the test; ask whether they can understand their rights and complex questions and give their own account. Make proper inquiries, use the COPs manual English-language test, and get a qualified independent interpreter — not a relative. Choose an interview friend who is independent, speaks the person's language and will not push them to answer; a kin relative who directs the suspect to talk can destroy voluntariness. Administer the caution in simple terms and have the person explain it back in their own words — a 'yes' or a nod is not proof of understanding (risk of gratuitous concurrence). When a lawyer tells you clearly the client does not wish to answer, stop; you may seek limited clarification, but pressing on where the client's first language is not English will look coercive.
verdict: ACTION — this pre-trial ruling directly changes how you assess suspect status, record admissions, use interpreters and interview friends, and respond to a suspect's request for silence.
flags: Section references (s 10, s 118, s 137, s 138, s 139, s 140, s 154, s 155, s 28) are taken directly from the judgment text.
This is a pre-trial voir dire ruling; it does not determine guilt and the trial was still to proceed.

The judgment notes the deceased's cause of death was head injury and the pathologist thought injuries unlikely to have come from a motor vehicle — relevant background but not central to the admissibility holding.

caseName: Stubley v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Western Australia ([2010] WASCA 36)
outcome: Appeal allowed; Court of Appeal order set aside; convictions quashed and a new trial ordered.
weight: High Court of Australia — binding and the leading authority on s 31A 'significant probative value'. Caution: the consent analysis is applied to the pre-1992 rape provision (s 325) as it then stood; the statutory definition of consent (now s 319(2)) was not in force for these historical offences.
oneLine: Propensity evidence of uncharged sexual misconduct against three other patients lacked significant probative value where the only live issue was consent, not whether the sex occurred.
whatHappened: Alan John STUBLEY, a consultant psychiatrist, was convicted after a Supreme Court trial of six counts of rape, one of attempted rape and three of unlawful and indecent assault against two former patients, JG and CL, committed in his consulting rooms in the mid-to-late 1970s. The prosecution also called three other former patients — LB, MM and AW — to give evidence of uncharged sexual misconduct against them. No offences involving those three were charged. Through counsel, STUBLEY admitted he had been sexually intimate with JG and CL but asserted the acts were consensual, so the trial ran on consent (and honest and reasonable mistaken belief in consent). The admissibility of the three witnesses' evidence was decided under s 31A of the Evidence Act 1906 (WA). The Court of Appeal (majority) upheld the convictions; STUBLEY appealed to the High Court.
whatHeld: The High Court majority held the evidence of LB, MM and AW did not have significant probative value under s 31A(2)(a) and should not have been admitted. Its value as tendency evidence — showing STUBLEY had sex with patients during consultations — ceased to be significant once the fact that sex occurred with JG and CL was not disputed; only consent was live. Following Phillips v The Queen, whether one complainant consented does not bear on whether another did. None of the three witnesses described threats or intimidation inducing their consent, so their evidence could not rationally affect whether JG's or CL's consent was obtained by threats or intimidation. The Court stressed that proof of psychological dominance or manipulation is not proof of absence of consent: JG and CL were adults not shown to be incapable of consenting. The evidence also could not rationally explain delay in complaint or continued treatment, nor negate honest and reasonable belief in consent. Counsel's opening statement was not a formal admission under s 32, but the fact that sexual activity was undisputed was still material to admissibility. Appeal allowed; convictions set aside; new trial ordered. Heydon J dissented, holding the occurrence of the acts remained a live issue (no valid s 32 admission) and the evidence was admissible.
whatItMeans: When you assemble a brief that relies on tendency, propensity or relationship evidence, first pin down exactly what fact is genuinely in dispute. Propensity evidence only clears the s 31A bar if it can rationally affect a live issue to a significant extent — mere relevance is not enough. If the accused concedes the act happened and only contests consent, evidence going to whether the act happened adds little and risks exclusion. Critically, evidence that other victims felt dominated, manipulated or unable to resist does not, of itself, prove the charged victim did not consent — you need evidence tied to the actual complainant's absence of consent or to a recognised vitiating factor (force, threats, intimidation, fraud). If you want other-victim evidence to carry weight on consent, look for a common method of procuring or overbearing consent (e.g. specific threats), not just a pattern of exploiting vulnerable patients. Also note the practical warning about admissions: loose defence concessions in openings may not formally remove an issue, so keep proving your case fully.
verdict: ACTION — it reshapes how you identify the live issue and how you justify tendering propensity/other-victim evidence under s 31A.
flags: Orders were made on 20/10/2010; reasons for judgment were published on 30/03/2011 — 'decided' uses the reasons date.

The Court analysed consent under the Criminal Code (WA) s 325 as it stood at the material time (pre-1992); the current statutory consent definition (s 319(2), inserted 1992) did not apply — confirm the applicable consent law for any current matter.
Heydon J dissented; the holdings above are those of the majority (Gummow, Crennan, Kiefel and Bell JJ).
Offences were historical (alleged 1975–1978, tried 30+ years later).

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: KMB v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (GROVES DCJ), IND 1264 of 2008
outcome: Appeal against conviction dismissed; appeal against sentence dismissed.
weight: Court of Appeal (three judges) decision applying and citing established authority (HML, Shepherd, PIM, Noto); persuasive and authoritative on s 31A and uncharged-act directions. Sentence aspect expressly turns on its own facts.
oneLine: Court of Appeal confirms uncharged sexual acts were admissible as both propensity and relationship evidence under s 31A Evidence Act 1906 (WA), and that no beyond-reasonable-doubt direction was needed where the complainant gave direct evidence of the charged counts.
whatHappened: KMB was convicted after a District Court trial (before GROVES DCJ) on 23/04/2009 of seven sexual offences against his step-daughter: one count of having a sexual relationship with a child under 16 (Criminal Code (WA) s 321A), three counts of sexual penetration of a child he knew to be his de facto child, and three counts of sexual penetration without consent. The offending ran from when the complainant was about 8 until she was 18, on an almost daily basis. Police arranged a covert pretext meeting on 14/12/2007 in which the complainant wore a recording device and KMB made numerous admissions. He was sentenced on 21/05/2009 to a total effective term of 14 years 6 months. He appealed against both conviction and sentence, arguing the trial judge failed to adequately direct the jury on the evidence of uncharged sexual acts, and that the sentence was manifestly excessive and breached totality.
whatHeld: The appeals against conviction and sentence were both dismissed. On conviction: the evidence of uncharged acts was admissible under s 31A as both 'relationship evidence' and 'propensity evidence' — it showed KMB's ongoing sexual interest in the complainant and the manner and extent to which he acted on it. No direction that the uncharged acts had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt was required because the complainant gave direct evidence of the charged counts, so the uncharged acts were not an indispensable link in a chain of reasoning to guilt (applying Shepherd). The trial judge's directions confined the uncharged-act evidence to background/relationship context and even included a propensity warning — directions the Court described as very favourable to the appellant. Where evidence is admitted generally as propensity evidence under s 31A, no propensity warning is required, though some warning may still be needed to avoid a miscarriage. Experienced trial counsel's decision not to object or seek redirections was a legitimate forensic choice. On sentence: the head sentence and total effective sentence were not manifestly excessive and totality was properly applied; the offending was near the worst category.
whatItMeans: This case is a useful reference on how evidence of uncharged sexual acts is treated in child sexual abuse prosecutions. Build the full picture: evidence of a pattern of uncharged sexual conduct against the same complainant can be admissible under s 31A as relationship and/or propensity evidence, so record and preserve complainant accounts of the wider course of offending, not just the specific charged incidents. Note the effective use of a covert pretext call/meeting — the complainant wearing a recording device produced numerous admissions that strengthened the case; consider this investigative tool where appropriate. The standard-of-proof and jury-direction points are trial-level matters for the DPP, not your casework, but understanding why direct complainant evidence carries the counts (and uncharged acts are supporting circumstantial evidence) helps you focus your brief on solid, specific evidence for each charged count.
verdict: AWARENESS — the core holdings concern admissibility of uncharged acts and jury directions at trial, but it usefully confirms the value of gathering pattern evidence and covert admissions.
flags: Section references (s 321A, s 325, s 329(2) Criminal Code; s 31A Evidence Act) taken from the judgment as reported; verify current wording as s 321A has since been amended.
Individual sentence and count details summarised from the judgment table; confirm against the sentencing remarks if precise figures are needed.

caseName: Carr v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Western Australia
outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction for aggravated armed robbery upheld. Gleeson CJ and the joint reasons (Gummow, Heydon and Crennan JJ) dismissed; Kirby J dissented and would have allowed the appeal and entered an acquittal.
weight: High Court of Australia — binding. Five Justices, 4:1 majority. Authoritative interpretation of s 570D of the Criminal Code (WA), though that provision has since been replaced.
oneLine: Admissions a suspect made in a police lockup, captured by fixed surveillance cameras he didn't know about, were admissible under s 570D of the Criminal Code (WA) because there was a videotape of the admission — consent to recording is not required where a videotape exists.
whatHappened: CARR was suspected of an aggravated armed robbery of the South Perth Commonwealth Bank (08/04/2003). On 30/07/2003 he was arrested, taken to Kensington police station and formally interviewed on videotape in the interview room. He was cautioned, made no real admissions, and repeatedly asked to speak to a lawyer. The recorded interview was then closed. After a cigarette break he was taken to the lockup for routine administrative processing (he was being returned to prison for a parole breach). The lockup had permanently fixed security cameras and microphones. CARR did not know he was being recorded; the officers did know, and realised he didn't. He initiated a wider conversation and boasted about the robbery; officers asked questions to elicit more. He was not re-cautioned. An edited recording (Ex 17) was played to the jury. He was convicted (25/11/2004) and sentenced to six years. The Court of Appeal refused an extension of time. He appealed to the High Court arguing the videotape was inadmissible under s 570D.
whatHeld: Appeal dismissed (Kirby J dissenting). The majority held: (1) 'Interview' in s 570(1) is broad — it means any conversation between a police officer and a suspect about an alleged offence, including an informal conversation initiated by the suspect. No element of formality, and no requirement that the suspect appreciate he is being recorded, is needed. (2) Consent to videotaping is not a precondition to admissibility where a videotape exists. Section 570D(4)(c) merely treats absence of consent as a 'reasonable excuse' for there being no videotape; that is an assumption, not an implication, and cannot be elevated into an extra ground of mandatory exclusion. Once s 570D(2)(a) is satisfied (a videotape of the admission exists), the statutory exclusion does not apply and the qualifications in (b) and (c) never arise. (3) The Court noted s 570D is a threshold/gateway, not an exhaustive admissibility test — common law discretions to exclude for involuntariness, unfairness or public policy remain available, but CARR did not run those arguments here and they had already been rejected below. The majority also observed there is no common law rule requiring a caution; failure to caution only enlivens a discretion to exclude. Kirby J dissented, holding 'interview' requires formality and mutuality and that consent is implied, and would have acquitted.
whatItMeans: For your casework, the lesson is that under the old s 570D regime, a recording of an admission is admissible even if the suspect did not consent to, or did not know about, the recording — provided the conversation is one between police and a suspect about an offence. 'Interview' is read widely and covers informal, suspect-initiated chat. But note three important cautions. First, this case turns on Ch LXA of the Criminal Code, which has been replaced by Pt 11 of the Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA) — that Act requires an 'audiovisual recording' of an 'admission' rather than a 'videotape' of an 'interview', so the precise statutory wording you work under today is different. Treat this case as guidance on principle, not on the current section numbers. Second, clearing the statutory gateway does not guarantee admission: a judge can still exclude on common law grounds of involuntariness, unfairness or public policy. Deliberately taking a suspect off-camera, or exploiting a belief that questioning has ended to bypass a request for a lawyer, invites a fairness/public-policy challenge — CARR survived only because those arguments were not pressed and the conduct was found not improper enough below. Third, watch the Surveillance Devices Act 1998 (WA): the Court found the lockup recording lawful because it was not 'private activity/conversation' and was covered by law-enforcement exceptions, but you should not assume covert recording elsewhere is lawful. Best practice remains: caution, record properly, and where admissions are blurted out off-record, resume a recorded interview and put them to the suspect.
verdict: AWARENESS — important authority on the scope of recorded-admission rules, but decided under the now-repealed Ch LXA; it confirms common law fairness discretions still apply, so it informs rather than directly changes day-to-day practice.

appealFrom: Court of Criminal Appeal of New South Wales
outcome: Appeal against conviction dismissed; convictions for the LOGOZZO offences upheld. The admissions made on 15/05/2002 were properly admitted.
weight: High — unanimous result of the High Court of Australia (4:1 on reasoning, Kirby J dissenting), the apex court.
oneLine: High Court holds covertly recorded admissions to police were not unfair to use under s 90 of the Evidence Act 1995 (NSW), despite a deliberately incomplete caution and the suspect's mistaken belief his words could not be used.
whatHappened: EM was convicted of the murder of Joseph LOGOZZO and related offences arising from a 2002 home invasion in Sydney. Police already had unrecorded admissions from him about a separate home invasion (the KRESS offences, to which he pleaded guilty). On 24/04/2002 EM had refused to be recorded and was released. Police then obtained warrants under the Listening Devices Act 1984 (NSW) and, on 15/05/2002, took EM to a suburban park wearing covert recording devices. They told him he was not under arrest, was free not to talk, and repeatedly assured him they were not tricking him — but deliberately omitted the second part of the caution (that anything he said could be recorded and used in evidence). EM, who believed unrecorded conversations could not be used against him, made admissions about the LOGOZZO killing. The trial judge admitted the first part of the park conversation and excluded the part after a key statement by the detective. The Court of Criminal Appeal upheld that course.
whatHeld: The High Court (Gleeson CJ and Heydon J; Gummow and Hayne JJ agreeing; Kirby J dissenting) dismissed the appeal. It was not unfair under s 90 to use the admissions. Gummow and Hayne JJ reasoned that s 90 operates as a final "safety net" engaged only after the more specific provisions of the Act (ss 84, 85, 137, 138, 139), so that reliability (s 85) and impropriety in obtaining the evidence (s 138) fall to be dealt with under those sections, not s 90. The lead judgment of Gleeson CJ and Heydon J did not adopt that quarantine — it treated reliability as a factor relevant to fairness under s 90, and accepted s 90 can succeed even where no other ground does. EM had in any event failed to invoke or abandoned every other ground. Covert recording under a valid warrant is not made unfair merely because the suspect did not know he was being recorded, and EM conceded as much. His belief that what he said could not be used was inextricably linked to his belief it was not being recorded, so the same concession defeated the broader argument. The detectives merely failed to correct, rather than created, his mistaken belief. There was no legal obligation to caution him in these circumstances (s 139 conditions were not met, as he was not under arrest). The trial judge was also not required to give a special unreliability warning to the jury. Kirby J dissented, holding the deliberately half-given caution, the trickery and the choice of park venue derogated from the right to silence and rendered use of the evidence unfair.
whatItMeans: This case turns on the NSW uniform Evidence Act, which does not apply in WA — so treat it as guidance on principle, not as a rule you apply directly. The underlying message is about the common law unfairness discretion (the Lee/Swaffield line), which does operate in WA. The take-home for you: lawfully authorised covert recording of a suspect, even where the suspect wrongly assumes the chat is "off the record", will not generally be excluded as unfair — secret recording only works because the subject does not know. But note the warnings in this judgment. The majority required strict separation of issues: reliability, impropriety and proper cautioning are dealt with under specific rules, and a court can still exclude on those grounds. Deliberately giving only half a caution drew a strong dissent and is risky. Get and rely on proper authority for any listening device, keep the questioning fair (not hostile, overbearing or unduly persistent), and do not assume a covert operation cures a defective or absent caution where one is required. The safest practice remains a full and proper caution at the point one is legally required.
verdict: AWARENESS — it concerns the NSW Evidence Act unfairness discretion, which does not govern WA, but it usefully shows how appellate courts treat covertly recorded admissions and incomplete cautions.

appealFrom: Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Victoria
outcome: All four appeals dismissed; convictions stand. CLARKE granted leave to amend his notice of appeal but the new discretionary ground rejected.
weight: High Court of Australia, seven-judge bench, 6:1 majority (Kirby J dissenting). Binding and leading authority on the common law of confessions.
oneLine: The High Court (6:1) held that confessions obtained by the undercover "Mr Big"/scenario technique are admissible at common law: gang-impersonating police are not "persons in authority" and the confessions were voluntary.
whatHappened: Four men (TOFILAU, MARKS, HILL and CLARKE) were each suspected of murder in Victoria but there was insufficient evidence to charge. Victoria Police ran undercover "scenario" operations (the Canadian "Mr Big" model): officers posed as a criminal gang, drew each suspect into staged (fake) criminal activity, and offered gang membership, money and protection from prosecution through supposedly corrupt police — on condition the suspect told the gang "boss" the truth about the killing. Each man confessed to an undercover "boss". The confessions were admitted at trial and each was convicted. They appealed, arguing the confessions were involuntary because induced by persons in authority and/or lacked "basal voluntariness". CLARKE also argued discretionary exclusion.
whatHeld: Appeals dismissed (Kirby J dissenting). The undercover officers were not "persons in authority". A person is only a person in authority if the suspect perceives, on reasonable grounds, that they hold the lawful authority of the state to investigate or prosecute. The appellants believed they were dealing with criminals who could corruptly influence police, not with anyone wielding the lawful authority of the state — so the inducement rule was not engaged. The confessions were voluntary ("basal voluntariness" satisfied). There was no duress, intimidation, persistent importunity or sustained/undue pressure of a kind that overbore the will; the men spoke because they hoped to profit and avoid prosecution. Deception or trickery alone does not make a confession involuntary. On the discretion (CLARKE only), the trial judge made no error in admitting the evidence; the seriousness of the crime and the absence of any unlawful conduct by police weighed in favour of admission.
whatItMeans: This is the leading High Court authority validating the "Mr Big"/scenario covert technique for eliciting confessions in serious unsolved crimes. For your casework it means: covert confessions to officers posing as criminals can be admissible, because a suspect who thinks he is confessing to gangsters does not believe he is speaking to a person in authority and is not under state coercion. Two practical levers: avoid feeding the suspect facts only the offender would know (this protects reliability), and ensure the confession is recorded and independently corroborated (e.g. the suspect revealing where the murder weapon/scarf was). Be alert to the discretionary exclusion risk: courts will scrutinise proportionality (these techniques are justified by very serious crime), reliability, and forensic prejudice from showing the jury the suspect's willingness to join a criminal gang. Note this was decided on Victorian common law — confirm the current WA position and any controlled-operations/authorisation requirements before deploying such an operation.
verdict: ACTION — it confirms that scenario/"Mr Big" covert confessions are admissible and tells you exactly why (no person in authority, no overborne will), shaping how you design and document such operations.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: The State of Western Australia v GBT
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (WAGER DCJ), STATE OF WESTERN AUSTRALIA v GBT [2006] WADC 10
outcome: Appeal allowed. Severance order quashed; only count 78 (MLN) severed. All other counts to be tried together.
weight: Court of Appeal (three judges, unanimous). Binding appellate authority on joinder and mutual admissibility in WA.
oneLine: Court of Appeal restores joinder of 77 sexual offence counts across eight complainants, holding the evidence was mutually admissible and severance was wrongly ordered.
whatHappened: GBT was charged on an indictment with 78 counts of sexual misconduct — ranging from unlawful and indecent dealing to sexual penetration — against eight complainants. Twenty-nine counts related to his natural daughter, LKH; most other complainants were friends of LKH who visited and stayed overnight, and one was a friend of LKH's sister. The offending centred on "games" the respondent introduced ("chasey", "squashes", the "typewriter") over many years, involving genital contact, exposure, showing a pornographic video, and, in KMB's case, sexual penetration. On 03/02/2006 WAGER DCJ ordered the indictment severed into separate trials, accepting a defence submission that directing a jury on the admissibility of evidence across so many counts was an unwieldy, insurmountable task that risked compromise verdicts. The State appealed.
whatHeld: The Court of Appeal (WHEELER JA, STEYTLER P and BUSS JA agreeing) allowed the appeal and held severance was wrongly ordered. Much of the evidence on one count was mutually admissible on other counts. LKH's role was critical: her earlier acceptance of the conduct explained why she and other girls did not complain, why she acted protectively of the respondent, and why he believed he could offend with impunity. Evidence of repeated near-identical conduct and identical terminology across complainants rebutted suggestions of fantasy, imagination or innocent/accidental contact. The Court accepted that s 133 prejudice can arise from something other than inadmissible evidence — for example directions of such complexity no reasonable jury could follow them — but held the task here was not of insurmountable difficulty, and that severance would not cure it anyway because the same evidence would be admissible as uncharged acts in any severed trial. Only count 78 (MLN) was to be severed, as that evidence did not currently appear admissible on other counts and risked prejudicial speculation.
whatItMeans: When you build a multi-complainant sexual offence brief, the key question for joinder is mutual admissibility — whether the evidence on one count would be admissible on the others. Map this out carefully before charging and set it out clearly in your brief, because failure to analyse admissibility leaves gaps that drive severance applications. Look for the threads that make evidence cross-admissible: identical terminology, repeated near-identical conduct, patterns explaining delay in complaint, and evidence explaining why an accused believed he could offend undetected. Frequency and similarity of conduct across multiple complainants is powerful in rebutting defences of fantasy, mistaken recollection, or innocent/accidental contact. Be alert that an outlier count — one different in character, complainant, or reaction (as with MLN here) — may need to be treated separately if it isn't cross-admissible and could invite prejudicial speculation. A large number of counts alone does not justify severance.
verdict: AWARENESS-level guidance: this shapes how you assemble and justify multi-complainant briefs, but it is a joinder/admissibility ruling rather than a rule changing your investigative powers.
flags: Judgment refers to s 31A Evidence Act 1906 (WA) in the catchwords and s 133 Criminal Procedure Act 2004 (WA) in the reasons; confirm exact provisions before relying on them.
The indictment had 78 counts; the Court severed count 78, leaving 77 to be tried together.
Admissibility of the MLN count (count 78) was left open and may change depending on the evidence led at trial, particularly from the respondent's former wife.

appealFrom: Court of Criminal Appeal of the Supreme Court of Western Australia
outcome: Appeal allowed. Orders of the Court of Criminal Appeal dated 03/12/2003 set aside; conviction quashed; retrial ordered.
weight: High. Unanimous High Court of Australia decision (joint judgment of four Justices plus Kirby J concurring); leading authority on the whole-case reference power and prosecution disclosure obligations.
oneLine: Prosecution failure to disclose material, potentially exculpatory evidence to the defence produced a miscarriage of justice, quashing MALLARD's murder conviction and ordering a retrial.
whatHappened: Andrew Mark MALLARD was convicted in the Supreme Court of Western Australia of the murder of Mrs Pamela Lawrence, a jewellery shop proprietor at Perth on 23/05/1994. After serving eight years, he petitioned for clemency. The Attorney-General referred the petition to the Court of Criminal Appeal under s 140(1)(a) of the Sentencing Act 1995 (WA), which dismissed it. On appeal to the High Court, it emerged that a significant body of evidence had been in police possession before and during the trial but was not disclosed to the defence — and in some instances actively removed or altered in witness statements. This included a pig's head experiment showing a wrench (the alleged murder weapon per MALLARD's 'confession') could not have caused the wounds; a salt-water clothing experiment contradicting his account of washing clothes in the river; a suppressed witness statement about the whereabouts of his cap; undisclosed eyewitness sketches inconsistent with his appearance; deletion of the 'locked eyes' phrase; and statements about another man wearing a bandanna near the scene. The confessional evidence was largely unrecorded and peculiar in character.
whatHeld: The Court held the Court of Criminal Appeal erred in law by taking too narrow a view of its jurisdiction on an Attorney-General's reference: the words 'the whole case' in s 140(1)(a) require consideration of the whole of the properly admissible evidence — new, fresh or previously adduced, and the words 'as if it were an appeal' only confine the Court to appellate orders, procedures and the s 689(1) proviso. On the facts, the non-disclosure (and in some cases suppression) of material, potentially exculpatory evidence occasioned a miscarriage of justice. The undisclosed evidence was capable of refuting a central plank of the prosecution case (the wrench) and of seriously undermining the reliability of the confessions on which the case heavily depended. The respondent conceded the concessions alone would require quashing unless the proviso applied; the Court held the proviso could not save the conviction. The conviction was quashed and a retrial ordered. Kirby J, agreeing, reviewed extensive domestic and international authority affirming that the prosecution must disclose all material evidence for or against the accused, the touchstone being the accused's right to a fair trial.
whatItMeans: This case is a cornerstone on the prosecution's duty of disclosure. For your casework it means everything relevant in the investigation file must be disclosed — including material that undermines the prosecution theory or helps the defence. You cannot decide unilaterally that inconvenient evidence is irrelevant and leave it out. The judgment specifically condemns the editing or deletion of material from witness statements to remove discrepancies (the cap, the sketches, the 'locked eyes' phrase). Preserve and disclose original handwritten statements, all drafts, and the results of experiments — even failed or unhelpful ones (the pig's head and salt-water tests). Note the strong criticism of unrecorded 'confessions': most interviews here were not recorded despite the ability to do so, which fatally weakened their reliability. Record admissions on videotape — this is now mandatory for serious offences under s 570D of the Criminal Code (WA), which the Court noted was not in force at the original trial but now is. Non-disclosure of exculpatory material can collapse an otherwise sustainable conviction years later.
verdict: ACTION — it directly changes how you must gather, preserve and disclose evidence; treat full disclosure of all relevant material (including unhelpful and original documents) as mandatory.
flags: The original trial date and sentence date are not stated in the judgment text; only the murder date (23/05/1994) and the CCA order date (03/12/2003) are given.
Whether any of the undisclosed material was in the possession of the Director of Public Prosecutions (as opposed to police) was expressly left unresolved by the Court.

court: Supreme Court of WA — Court of Appeal
caseName: Donaldson v The State of Western Australia
appealFrom: District Court of Western Australia (Mazza DCJ)
outcome: Appeal dismissed; refusal to order separate trials confirmed under s 26(7) Criminal Appeals Act 2004. Notice of contention also upheld.
weight: Strong. Unanimous Court of Appeal decision on the merits (three judges agreeing on the s 31A/s 133 construction) and one of the first appellate considerations of the new legislation. A leading authority on propensity/relationship evidence and joinder in WA.
oneLine: Court of Appeal upholds refusal to sever an 18-count sexual offence indictment involving four young complainants, confirming s 31A Evidence Act 1906 propensity/relationship evidence rules override the old Hoch/De Jesus/Pfennig restrictions.
whatHappened: DONALDSON, a swimming/fitness coach, was indicted on 18 sexual offences against four young female complainants (KML, RKL, NDP, CAM) who trained under him between about 1992 and 1999. Each was a female squad member of similar age, offended against while alone with him, after he ingratiated himself with gifts and outings, and while he maintained an atmosphere of normality. Before Mazza DCJ, DONALDSON applied under s 133(3) Criminal Procedure Act 2004 for four separate trials (one per complainant). His Honour refused, holding the evidence of each complainant was mutually admissible as propensity evidence under s 31A Evidence Act 1906. DONALDSON brought a preliminary appeal under s 26 Criminal Appeals Act 2004.
whatHeld: Appeal dismissed. The s 31A and s 133 reforms deliberately overrode the old restrictive authorities (Hoch, De Jesus, Pfennig), so reliance on those cases is misplaced. Propensity and relationship evidence is admissible where it has significant probative value and where, weighed against the risk of an unfair trial, fair-minded people would think the public interest in adducing all relevant evidence of guilt must have priority (s 31A(2)). The possibility of collusion, concoction or suggestion cannot be taken into account by the judge at the admissibility stage — it is a matter for the jury (s 31A(3), s 133(6)). Striking similarity is not required; here an underlying unity, system or pattern in the offending sufficed. Once evidence is mutually admissible there will rarely be prejudice from joinder, and the accused could not point to any other source of prejudice. The evidence was also relationship evidence (widely defined) and admissible to rebut potential innocent-explanation defences, since the prosecution must prove its whole case and cannot split it. On timing, the majority (Wheeler JA, Roberts-Smith JA) held the trial 'starts' for s 26(6) when the jury is sworn and the accused is in its charge, so the appeal was competent; Miller AJA dissented, holding the trial had started on arraignment.
whatItMeans: When you have multiple complainants alleging similar offending by the same suspect — especially child sexual abuse in a position of trust — build the brief so the evidence of each complainant supports the others. You no longer need 'striking similarity': an underlying pattern or system (same type of victim, same grooming, same opportunity, same modus) can carry significant probative value. Do not assume that a possibility the complainants talked to each other will sink joinder — collusion or concoction is now a jury question, not a bar to admissibility, so gather and disclose that material but don't treat it as fatal. Identify and record the likely innocent-explanation defences (e.g. 'my hands were cold', 'I was massaging a muscle', 'helping try on bathers') because the pattern evidence is admissible to rebut them and the prosecution must lead it in its own case. Charge and present multiple complainants together where the material supports it, and make any severance-related issues known early — appeals against joinder rulings must be run before the jury is sworn.
verdict: AWARENESS-plus-ACTION: it changes how you build multi-complainant sexual offence briefs — join and cross-support the evidence, treat concoction as a jury issue — because the Court confirmed s 31A was designed to widen admissibility of propensity and relationship evidence.
flags: The judges divided on when a trial 'starts' for s 26(6) Criminal Appeals Act 2004: the majority (Wheeler JA, Roberts-Smith JA) held it is when the jury is sworn; Miller AJA held it is on arraignment. This point is a matter of appeal procedure/timing rather than investigative practice.
Judgment text at [25] refers to 's 137(7)' of the Criminal Procedure Act while the substantive joinder provision discussed throughout is s 133 — treat the s 133 references as the operative ones.

appealFrom: Court of Criminal Appeal of the Supreme Court of Western Australia
outcome: COATES's appeal allowed, conviction quashed, new trial ordered (off-camera admissions wrongly admitted; no substantial miscarriage of justice not established). NICHOLLS's appeal dismissed (only ground concerned ROSS's evidence, which failed for want of proper foundation).
weight: High — unanimous High Court of Australia decision on appeal from the WA Supreme Court, authoritative on s 570D and the collateral evidence rule, though reasoning on the admissions issue was divided.
oneLine: Off-camera admissions during a 45-minute break in a videotaped police interview were inadmissible where there was no genuine "reasonable excuse" under s 570D Criminal Code (WA), and no notes were kept nor any attempt made to re-record on camera.
whatHappened: COATES and NICHOLLS were convicted of the wilful murder of Clare GARABEDIAN, killed by heroin overdose to stop her giving evidence against COATES and HOY in pending proceedings. The case relied heavily on accomplice Adam DAVIS, who had pleaded guilty. During a videotaped interview, COATES allegedly made inculpatory admissions during a 45-minute "toilet break" when filming was suspended. The admissions were not re-recorded on camera; no contemporaneous notes were taken (notes made next day were lost). Police DSC HAWLEY admitted he encouraged COATES to speak off-camera and "deliberately chose to continue this interview off-camera". The appellants also sought to call witness Joseph ROSS to say DAVIS had told him COATES and NICHOLLS were not involved and that DAVIS intended to give false evidence to secure a police deal.
whatHeld: On the admissions: the High Court held the off-camera admissions were wrongly admitted under s 570D Criminal Code (WA). There was no "reasonable excuse" for the failure to videotape. The Court split 4:3 (Gleeson CJ, Hayne and Heydon JJ would have held them admissible and dismissed COATES's appeal; McHugh, Gummow, Kirby and Callinan JJ found them inadmissible and allowed it), the four-judge majority holding that mere police claims that an accused was "anxious to speak off-tape" or initiated a break cannot constitute reasonable excuse, especially where it was practicable to record, no notes were kept, and no attempt was made to have the admissions repeated on camera. McHugh J held "interview" covers the entire discussion, so refusing to record part did not fall within s 570D(4)(c). On ROSS's evidence (the collateral evidence rule): the appeal was unanimously dismissed on this point. Though the evidence fell within the "corruption" exception to the collateral evidence (finality) rule, it was inadmissible because no proper foundation was laid in cross-examination of DAVIS — the time, place, person and substance of the alleged statements were never sufficiently put to him, breaching s 21 Evidence Act 1906 (WA) and the common law. The Court declined to recast the collateral evidence rule.
whatItMeans: This case is a clear warning about off-camera or unrecorded admissions. Under s 570D (now reflected in current WA recording requirements), if recording equipment is available and working, you cannot rely on a suspect supposedly wanting to talk "off the record" as a reasonable excuse for not recording. If a suspect makes admissions while recording is paused, get them back on camera and have the admissions repeated and adopted on the record. Failing that, the admissions risk exclusion. Always take and keep contemporaneous notes — the loss of notes here was treated as a suspicious circumstance weighing toward exclusion. Encouraging a suspect to speak off-camera will be seen as an unfair attempt to evade the recording regime. On collateral evidence: if you have a witness who will say a key Crown witness admitted lying or intended to give false evidence, the defence (or prosecution) must put the specific occasion — time, place, person and the words used — to that witness in cross-examination before the rebuttal evidence can be called. Vague references to "a conversation" are not enough.
verdict: AWARENESS — this is an appellate evidence-law ruling, but it directly shapes how you should handle interviews; treat it as a practical caution on recording admissions.

appealFrom: Court of Criminal Appeal of Tasmania (Marlow and Kelly (2001) 129 A Crim R 51)
outcome: Appeal dismissed; murder conviction upheld. Majority found the statement admissible; the minority would have excluded it but applied the proviso.
weight: High Court of Australia decision — authoritative on the construction principles (purposive construction, use of definitions) and on the continuing relevance of the McKinney warning, but the specific holding is confined to s 8 of a now-repealed Tasmanian Act.
tags: proviso / no substantial miscarriage of justice
oneLine: High Court holds a suspect's unrecorded admission made after a video interview ended was not "made in the course of official questioning" under Tasmanian law and so was admissible; conviction upheld.
whatHappened: Shane Leslie KELLY was convicted of murdering Tony George TANNER (killed on or about 23/11/1990) by a jury in the Supreme Court of Tasmania. During a video-recorded interview on 04/03/2000 KELLY denied involvement. After the interview was formally concluded at 9.17pm, and 30 to 60 minutes later, as he was about to be driven to hospital for blood and hair samples, KELLY said to police: "Sorry about the interview – no hard feelings, I was just playing the game... I suppose you will make notes of that as well." It was not in response to any question, was not recorded, and police did not take him back to record it. The defence argued this "impugned statement" was a confession or admission inadmissible under s 8(2)(a) of the Criminal Law (Detention and Interrogation) Act 1995 (Tas) because it was not video-taped. The trial judge admitted it; the Court of Criminal Appeal of Tasmania dismissed the appeal.
whatHeld: The majority (Gleeson CJ, Hayne and Heydon JJ) held that "in the course of official questioning" is a temporal expression marking the period from when questioning began to when it ceased. Questioning ended at 9.17pm when the interview was concluded; no further question triggered the statement, so it was not made in the course of official questioning and was admissible. The Court rejected the defence's attempts to read in "custody" or "within a reasonable time after" or "arising out of" — those ideas have no foothold in the statutory language. McHugh J and Kirby J dissented on construction, holding the statement should have been excluded, but agreed the appeal failed because the case against KELLY was overwhelming and the proviso (s 402(2) Criminal Code (Tas)) applied — no substantial miscarriage of justice. In surveying the law, the Court restated the long-standing concern about fabricated and unreliable confessions ("police verbals"); the continuing operation of the McKinney warning to juries about uncorroborated police-custody confessions was affirmed by Kirby J in dissent.
whatItMeans: This case is about how courts read recording-requirement statutes and the perennial danger of unrecorded "verbals". The practical lesson is to capture spontaneous admissions on video promptly — here police could easily have taken KELLY back to the interview room to put the statement to him on tape, and their failure to do so was criticised by every judge. Note carefully that this turns on a Tasmanian provision that has since been repealed, and WA's regime is different: under Criminal Code (WA) s 570D the admissibility of a confession does not turn on whether it was a response to questioning, so the "temporal" reasoning here does not transfer directly to your casework. Treat any post-interview, off-camera admission as fragile — record it or re-engage on camera, and expect the McKinney warning to apply to anything that is not reliably corroborated.
verdict: AWARENESS, not ACTION for WA: the holding construes a repealed Tasmanian section and WA's recording law operates on a different test, so use it for the principles and the recording lesson, not as authority on your charging or admissibility decisions.
